## Introduction

Recent public and policymaker attention has increased on the connection between the mental health of adolescents and their social media use. As rates of social technology use surged during the COVID-19 pandemic due to social distancing measures, schools, clinicians, and parents expressed concerns about the effects of physical isolation from peers and the necessity of online connections due to geographic restrictions. Prior research had also found that some marginalized communities (e.g., adolescents of color, LGBTQ + youth) experienced the beneficial effects, such as fewer in-person bullying and harassment at school [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR1 "Kosciw JG, Clark CM, Menard L. The 2021 National School Climate Survey: The Experiences of LGBTQ + Youth in Our Nation’s Schools. New York, NY: GLSEN; 2022. Available at: 
                  https://www.glsen.org/research/2021-national-school-climate-survey
                  
                ")]. In addition, LGBTQ + youth are early adopters and more frequent users of social media compared to their heteronormative counterparts [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR2 "Charmaraman L, Hodes R, Richer AM. Young sexual minority adolescent experiences of self-expression and isolation on Social Media: cross-sectional survey study. JMIR Ment Health. 2021;8(9):e26207.: 10.2196/26207; PMID: 34524107; PMCID: 8482247.")], which is why understanding this online context is critical to research, practice, and policy. The purpose of this review of LGBTQ + youth using social media in a post-COVID pandemic digital world is to (a) examine how research from different disciplines have framed the use of social media within LGBTQ + youth, (b) what is known about the risks and benefits of social media use particularly related to mental health outcomes, and (c) what needs to be investigated further in future research.

The US Surgeon General recently categorized loneliness as an epidemic exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic and putting isolated populations at greater risk of morbidity and mortality [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR3 "United States Public Health Service, Office of the Surgeon General. Advisory on social media and youth mental health. Washington, DC: US Dept of Health and Human Services; May; 2023.")]. The Surgeon General’s advisory lists young and LGBTQ + communities as disproportionately at-risk groups, as well as marginalized racial and ethnic backgrounds and residents of rural areas. The Surgeon General has also discussed how social media can be a source of social support and community for such marginalized youth [[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR3 "United States Public Health Service, Office of the Surgeon General. Advisory on social media and youth mental health. Washington, DC: US Dept of Health and Human Services; May; 2023."),[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR4 "United States Public Health Service, Office of the Surgeon General. Our epidemic of loneliness and isolation: the U.S. Surgeon General’s Advisory on the Healing effects of social connection and community. Washington, DC: US Dept of Health and Human Services; May; 2023."),[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR5 "Charmaraman L, Hernandez JM, Hodes R. Marginalized and understudied populations using digital media. In: Nesi J, Telzer EH, Prinstein MJ, editors. Handbook of Adolescent Digital Media Use and Mental Health. Cambridge University Press; 2022.")]. For LGBTQ + youth, social media can be an environment for developing their identities, navigating acceptance (or lack thereof) from family and friends, and building a better future through civic engagement as they transition into adulthood.

News coverage has increased regarding political contentions intersecting with this, as 510 bills restricting LGBTQ + rights were introduced across the US in 2023 with 233 bills restricting student and educator rights [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR6 "Mapping Attacks on LGBTQ Rights in U.S. State Legislatures in 2023. American Civil Liberties Union. 
                  https://www.aclu.org/legislative-attacks-on-lgbtq-rights-2023
                  
                . Published January 31, 2023. Accessed September 27, 2024.")]. This number has already been surpassed with 533 bills introduced in fall of 2024 [[7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR7 "Mapping Attacks on LGBTQ Rights in U.S. State Legislatures in 2024. American Civil Liberties Union. 
                  https://www.aclu.org/legislative-attacks-on-lgbtq-rights-2024?impact=
                  
                . Published January 16, 2024. Accessed September 27, 2024.")]. Over 90% of US transgender youth between 13 and 17 years old live in states that have introduced bills or passed laws banning gender affirming healthcare, participation in sports, use of bathrooms, and/or preferred pronoun use [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR8 "Renfield E, Conron KJ, Mallory C. The impact of 2024 anti-transgender legislation on youth. April 2024. Accessed September 27, 2024. 
                  https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/publications/2024-anti-trans-legislation/
                  
                ")]. This legislation is particularly prevalent in the southern US and rural areas where 85% of those in the South and 40% of those in the Midwest live in states with at least one anti-transgender law [[8](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR8 "Renfield E, Conron KJ, Mallory C. The impact of 2024 anti-transgender legislation on youth. April 2024. Accessed September 27, 2024. 
                  https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/publications/2024-anti-trans-legislation/
                  
                ")]. According to the Trevor Project’s 2024 U.S. National Survey on the Mental Health of LGBTQ + Young People (ages 13–24, _n_ = 18,663), almost one third of respondents report attending a school with an anti-LGBTQ + policy, especially Native students and students in the Southern U.S., underscoring the significance of racial and regional differences influencing LGBTQ + youth’s experiences [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR9 "The Trevor Project. 2024 U.S. National Survey on the Mental Health of LGBTQ + Young People. The Trevor Project. 2024. 
                  https://www.thetrevorproject.org/survey-2024/
                  
                ")]. Among older teens and young adult transgender Americans, following the mainstream news coverage, reading news articles, and social media posts about restricting access to affirming health care policies has been associated with worsened rumination, physical health symptoms, depressive symptoms, and fear of coming out [[10](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR10 "Dhanani LY, Totton RR. Have you heard the News? The effects of exposure to News about recent Transgender legislation on Transgender Youth and Young adults. Sex res Social Policy. Published Online April. 2023;5. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s13178-023-00810-6
                  
                .")].

In post-COVID-19 pandemic times when the norms of social technology use have increased exponentially, it is important to understand how this may influence the mental health, identity development, and civic engagement of LGBTQ + adolescents.

## Balancing Social Media’s Multifaceted Impact on Mental Health

### Benefits

There is increasing interest in understanding the associations between social media use and mental health among LGBTQ + youth. To better understand how social media use can affect LGBTQ + youth mental health, a Social Media Benefits Scale (SMBS) was developed through an online survey of LGBTQ + youth to identify motivations and benefits of social media participation for LGBTQ + youth [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR11 "Craig SL, Eaton AD, McInroy LB, Leung VWY, Krishnan S. Can Social Media Participation Enhance LGBTQ + Youth Well-Being? Development of the social media benefits Scale. Social Media + Soc. 2021;7(1). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/2056305121988931
                  
                .")]. They found that younger adolescents used social media more for emotional support, entertainment, and education about LGBTQ + identities, experiencing more significant impacts from social media compared with older adolescents whose social media use decreased and shifted toward enhancing well-being [[11](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR11 "Craig SL, Eaton AD, McInroy LB, Leung VWY, Krishnan S. Can Social Media Participation Enhance LGBTQ + Youth Well-Being? Development of the social media benefits Scale. Social Media + Soc. 2021;7(1). 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/2056305121988931
                  
                .")]. The scale serves as a valuable tool for understanding the positive impact of social media on LGBTQ + youth across different stages of development. It can be used to assess the influence of social media on their wellbeing and the motivations behind their usage, enabling for more personalized interventions.

In a study looking at the effect of gender identity, specifically transgender and nonbinary youth, on social media use and mental health, it was found that active social media use served a protective effect and that deliberate “social media breaks” were associated with increased depression, suggesting that regulating screen time might not be beneficial for the mental health of LGBTQ + youth [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR12 "Coyne SM, Weinstein E, Sheppard JA, et al. Analysis of Social Media Use, Mental Health, and gender identity among US youths. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(7):e2324389. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.24389
                  
                .")]. Additionally, compared to their heterosexual peers, a curated feed, where these youth can be more intentional with the people around them by banning or unfollowing harmful content, and strong media literacy all decreased feelings of depression for LGBTQ + youth [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR12 "Coyne SM, Weinstein E, Sheppard JA, et al. Analysis of Social Media Use, Mental Health, and gender identity among US youths. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(7):e2324389. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.24389
                  
                .")]. LGBTQ + youth can be more deliberate about the community they create online, which might not reflect their home environments.

Social media has also been found to be protective for intersectional identities such as LGBTQ + youth in rural areas who face increased social isolation, a key risk factor for depression [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR13 "Karim S, Choukas-Bradley S, Radovic A, Roberts SR, Maheux AJ, Escobar-Viera CG. Support over Social Media among socially isolated sexual and gender Minority Youth in Rural U.S. during the COVID-19 pandemic: opportunities for intervention research. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022;19(23):15611. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192315611
                  
                . Published 2022 Nov 24.")]. Karim and colleagues found that social media plays a crucial role in providing emotional and informational support, helping to mitigate isolation [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR13 "Karim S, Choukas-Bradley S, Radovic A, Roberts SR, Maheux AJ, Escobar-Viera CG. Support over Social Media among socially isolated sexual and gender Minority Youth in Rural U.S. during the COVID-19 pandemic: opportunities for intervention research. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022;19(23):15611. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192315611
                  
                . Published 2022 Nov 24.")]. Youth sought emotional support in LGBTQ+-specific spaces and used their social media feeds for LGBTQ + information and representation, suggesting that mental health interventions targeting rural LGBTQ + youth, as well as other more marginalized LGBTQ + communities, could effectively use social media platforms, with content-based platforms supporting information-seeking and community-based ones fostering emotional support [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR13 "Karim S, Choukas-Bradley S, Radovic A, Roberts SR, Maheux AJ, Escobar-Viera CG. Support over Social Media among socially isolated sexual and gender Minority Youth in Rural U.S. during the COVID-19 pandemic: opportunities for intervention research. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022;19(23):15611. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192315611
                  
                . Published 2022 Nov 24.")]. Although rural youth have been found to experience similar rates of cyber victimization, critical social supports are more often lacking, such as when facing conflicting family values messaging or religious intolerance [[14](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR14 "Wike TL, Bouchard LM, Kemmerer A, Yabar MP. Victimization and Resilience: Experiences of Rural LGBTQ + Youth Across Multiple Contexts. J Interpers Violence. 2022;37(19–20):NP18988-NP19015. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/08862605211043574
                  
                . Epub 2021 Sep 7. PMID: 34490826.")]. An online interview study looking at LGBTQ + youth in rural areas found that positive representation and connections with LGBTQ + youth groups on social media are crucial for supportive experiences [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR15 "Escobar-Viera CG, Choukas-Bradley S, Sidani J, Maheux AJ, Roberts SR, Rollman BL. Examining Social Media experiences and attitudes toward Technology-based interventions for reducing social isolation among LGBTQ Youth living in Rural United States: an online qualitative study. Front Digit Health. 2022;4:900695. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2022.900695
                  
                . Published 2022 Jun 27.")]. Seeing shared experiences helped reduce isolation and provided useful advice. They found that adolescents use different social media platforms strategically, with some features, like content filtering and privacy settings, making certain platforms feel safer.

### Risks

Social media use has been found to be associated both with protection and risk of suicidal ideation for LGBTQ + adolescents. Increased time spent online with LGBTQ + support groups has been found to be beneficial, especially for Black adolescents who reported significantly fewer depression and anxiety symptoms, and youth who never disclosed their identity online reported less support than those who did [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR16 "Tao X, Fisher C. Associations among web-based Civic Engagement and discrimination, web-based Social Support, and Mental Health and Substance Use Risk among LGBT Youth: cross-sectional survey study. J Med Internet Res. 2023;25:e46604. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2196/46604
                  
                . Published 2023 Jun 26.")]. LGBTQ + youth have also reported to have increased feelings of neglect from their online friends when there is a lack of feedback on personal experiences [[15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR15 "Escobar-Viera CG, Choukas-Bradley S, Sidani J, Maheux AJ, Roberts SR, Rollman BL. Examining Social Media experiences and attitudes toward Technology-based interventions for reducing social isolation among LGBTQ Youth living in Rural United States: an online qualitative study. Front Digit Health. 2022;4:900695. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2022.900695
                  
                . Published 2022 Jun 27.")]. A key theme that emerged from examining the social media experiences of LGBTQ + youth was encountering discriminatory behavior online. Transgender/nonbinary adolescents reported the highest prevalence of web-based discrimination compared to other groups, which may be due to the higher rates of exposure to transphobic public policies (e.g., ban on puberty blockers, removing their identities from school curricula and sports teams) [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR16 "Tao X, Fisher C. Associations among web-based Civic Engagement and discrimination, web-based Social Support, and Mental Health and Substance Use Risk among LGBT Youth: cross-sectional survey study. J Med Internet Res. 2023;25:e46604. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2196/46604
                  
                . Published 2023 Jun 26.")]. As mentioned above, increased use of social media for LGBTQ + education and community-building has been shown to reduce loneliness [[13](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR13 "Karim S, Choukas-Bradley S, Radovic A, Roberts SR, Maheux AJ, Escobar-Viera CG. Support over Social Media among socially isolated sexual and gender Minority Youth in Rural U.S. during the COVID-19 pandemic: opportunities for intervention research. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022;19(23):15611. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192315611
                  
                . Published 2022 Nov 24."), [15](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR15 "Escobar-Viera CG, Choukas-Bradley S, Sidani J, Maheux AJ, Roberts SR, Rollman BL. Examining Social Media experiences and attitudes toward Technology-based interventions for reducing social isolation among LGBTQ Youth living in Rural United States: an online qualitative study. Front Digit Health. 2022;4:900695. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2022.900695
                  
                . Published 2022 Jun 27."), [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR17 "Charmaraman L, Zhang A, Wang K, Chen B. Sexual minorities and loneliness: exploring sexuality through Social Media and Gender-Sexuality Alliance (GSA) supports. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2024;21(3):300. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph21030300
                  
                . PMID: 38541299; PMCID: PMC10970596.")]. However, some youth reported social media as an isolating and rejecting place, which can heighten feelings of exclusion [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR16 "Tao X, Fisher C. Associations among web-based Civic Engagement and discrimination, web-based Social Support, and Mental Health and Substance Use Risk among LGBT Youth: cross-sectional survey study. J Med Internet Res. 2023;25:e46604. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2196/46604
                  
                . Published 2023 Jun 26.")]. This illustrates the clear intricate balance between the protective aspects of the supportive environment that youths can find through social media along with the hostility from being open with their identities online.

In an intensive monitoring study, Hamilton and colleagues found that in a predominantly LGBTQ + sample, more negative experiences on social media in a day led to more likely reports of suicidal ideation while more positive experiences led to less likely reports. This finding corroborates current thoughts on social media, highlighting how negative interactions—such as bullying, harassment, or exposure to distressing content—can significantly worsen mental health outcomes, reinforcing the notion that the quality of online experiences is crucial for overall psychological well-being. Interestingly in this study, they found no significant relation between suicidal ideation the next day from previous social media experiences or screen time [[18](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR18 "Hamilton JL, Dalack M, Boyd SI, et al. Positive and negative social media experiences and proximal risk for suicidal ideation in adolescents. J Child Psychol Psychiatry Published Online May. 2024;13. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.13996
                  
                .")]. In a similar vein, another online study found that LGBTQ + youth who experienced the threat of nonconsensual posting of sexually explicit media had an increased odds of suicidal ideation, planning, attempts, and self-harm among sexual minority adolescents [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR19 "Srivastava A, Rusow J, Schrager SM, Stephenson R, Goldbach JT. Digital Sexual Violence and suicide risk in a national sample of sexual minority adolescents. J Interpers Violence. 2023;38(3–4):4443–58. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/08862605221116317
                  
                .")]. Older age was linked to lower odds of these behaviors, while being female and identifying as Black/African American increased the risk. The effects of social media on youths seems dependent on their intersectional identity, and it is suggested that simply suggesting a one-size-fits-all solution such as minimizing social media time is harmful, especially for some LGBTQ + youth who intentionally create safe spaces online that might not exist offline [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR12 "Coyne SM, Weinstein E, Sheppard JA, et al. Analysis of Social Media Use, Mental Health, and gender identity among US youths. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(7):e2324389. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.24389
                  
                .")]. Additionally, prevention strategies should be tailored to the specific developmental needs of sexual minority adolescents and the evolving nature of digital sexual violence [[19](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR19 "Srivastava A, Rusow J, Schrager SM, Stephenson R, Goldbach JT. Digital Sexual Violence and suicide risk in a national sample of sexual minority adolescents. J Interpers Violence. 2023;38(3–4):4443–58. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/08862605221116317
                  
                .")].

## Victimization and Sense of Belonging in and out of School Contexts

LGBTQ + youth experience higher rates of online and in-person victimization than their peers [[20](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR20 "Valido A, Rivas-Koehl M, Rivas-Koehl D, Espelage DL, Lawrence TI, Robinson LE. Latent class analysis of victimization patterns and Associated Protective factors among LGBTQ Youth. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2022;19:9953. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19169953
                  
                .")]. Adolescents (ages 12–18) interviewed about their perceptions of cyberbullying identified hostile language, such as name calling, and social exclusion as the most common forms of cyberbullying LGBTQ + youth face [[21](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR21 "Ojeda M, Espino E, Elip P, Del-Rey R. Even if they don’t say it to you, it hurts too: internalized homonegativity in LGBTQ + cyberbullying among adolescents. Comunicar: Media Educ Res J. 2023;31(75):21–34. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3916/C75-2023-02
                  
                .")]. Often targeting LGBTQ + identities, online victimization frequently occurs through private direct messages on social media (34.6%), text messages (20.4%), and public social media (19.1%), according to GLSEN’s 2021 National School Climate Survey (ages 13–21) [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR1 "Kosciw JG, Clark CM, Menard L. The 2021 National School Climate Survey: The Experiences of LGBTQ + Youth in Our Nation’s Schools. New York, NY: GLSEN; 2022. Available at: 
                  https://www.glsen.org/research/2021-national-school-climate-survey
                  
                ")]. LGBTQ + youth also frequently reported encountering anti-LGBTQ + microaggressions online, with approximately 76% of participants (ages 14–24) encountering microaggressions making fun of LGBTQ + identities monthly [[22](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR22 "McInroy LB, Beer OWJ, Scheadler TR, Craig SL, Eaton AD. Exploring the psychological and physiological impacts of Digital Microaggressions and hostile online climates on LGBTQ + youth. Current psychology. J Diverse Perspect Diverse Psychol Issues. 2024;43(3):2586–96. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-023-04435-1
                  
                .")].

However, amid anti-LGBTQ + messaging, LGBTQ + youth most frequently identified schools (52%) and online spaces (68%) as affirming places [[9](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR9 "The Trevor Project. 2024 U.S. National Survey on the Mental Health of LGBTQ + Young People. The Trevor Project. 2024. 
                  https://www.thetrevorproject.org/survey-2024/
                  
                ")]. Youth spend most of their daytime hours at schools; thus, it is essential for there to be a group or individual on campus around whom they feel safe regarding their LGBTQ + identity. Following the shutdown of in-person classes and extracurriculars during the peak of COVID-19, it is critical to evaluate how school environments and digital media support LGBTQ + youth–whether they have returned to school in-person from potentially unaccepting home environments, or the schools themselves feel like hostile spaces.

The presence of Gender-Sexuality Alliances (GSAs) and LGBTQ+-inclusive curriculum is associated with lower levels of anti-LGBTQ + victimization [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR1 "Kosciw JG, Clark CM, Menard L. The 2021 National School Climate Survey: The Experiences of LGBTQ + Youth in Our Nation’s Schools. New York, NY: GLSEN; 2022. Available at: 
                  https://www.glsen.org/research/2021-national-school-climate-survey
                  
                ")]. Through GSAs, LGBTQ + students can participate in community engagement, education, and leadership development alongside like-minded peers. GSA participation is associated with lower levels of loneliness, according to students ages 10–17 [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR17 "Charmaraman L, Zhang A, Wang K, Chen B. Sexual minorities and loneliness: exploring sexuality through Social Media and Gender-Sexuality Alliance (GSA) supports. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2024;21(3):300. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph21030300
                  
                . PMID: 38541299; PMCID: PMC10970596.")]. Thus, involvement in GSAs or similar clubs appear to have a positive impact on mental health and LGBTQ + students’ sense of belonging. The absence of such spaces was felt during the height of COVID-19. One health brief analyzing transcripts from the Q Chat Space, a national chat-based support group, discusses the salience of online and school support for LGBTQ + youth, especially as they may be isolated with unsupportive family members during the pandemic [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR23 "Fish JN, McInroy LB, Paceley MS, Williams ND, Henderson S, Levine DS, et al. I’m Kinda Stuck at Home with unsupportive parents right now: LGBTQ youths’ experiences with COVID-19 and the importance of online support. J Adolesc Health. 2020;67(3):450–2. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2020.06.002
                  
                .")]. Some teens described a sense of grief regarding their inability to talk about their LGBTQ + identities with anyone–now that they cannot attend GSA meetings or spend time with friends or mentors at school in-person–as they now run the risk of being overheard by family members during online school meetings [[23](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR23 "Fish JN, McInroy LB, Paceley MS, Williams ND, Henderson S, Levine DS, et al. I’m Kinda Stuck at Home with unsupportive parents right now: LGBTQ youths’ experiences with COVID-19 and the importance of online support. J Adolesc Health. 2020;67(3):450–2. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2020.06.002
                  
                .")]. COVID-19 policies have also seemed to significantly decrease the prevalence of GSAs: although more than 60% of students reported having a GSA at school in GLSEN’s 2019 national survey, less than 40% reported having an active GSA in 2021. GSAs can help spread awareness of online LGBTQ + information, promoting the development and access of digital resources, from referencing LGBTQ + organization websites while organizing GSAs, to creating group chats in which members share online resources among each other. As the numbers of GSAs reduced, students also experienced decreased access to LGBTQ + online information through school computers between 2019 and 2021 [[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR1 "Kosciw JG, Clark CM, Menard L. The 2021 National School Climate Survey: The Experiences of LGBTQ + Youth in Our Nation’s Schools. New York, NY: GLSEN; 2022. Available at: 
                  https://www.glsen.org/research/2021-national-school-climate-survey
                  
                ")].

However, LGBTQ + youth continue to spend a disproportionately greater amount of time online compared to their non-LGBTQ + peers, with additional hours of daily screen time reported for transgender (4.51 h), sexual minority (3.72 h), and gender-questioning (3.41 h) youth [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR24 "Nagata JM, Lee CM, Yang J, et al. Associations between sexual orientation and early adolescent screen use: findings from the adolescent brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. Ann Epidemiol. 2023;82:54–e581. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annepidem.2023.03.004
                  
                ."), [25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR25 "Nagata JM, Balasubramanian P, Iyra P, et al. Screen use in transgender and gender-questioning adolescents: findings from the adolescent brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. Ann Epidemiol. 2024;95:6–11. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annepidem.2024.04.013
                  
                .")]. Because LGBTQ + youth experience higher rates of victimization at school, it is possible that they would avoid extracurriculars and school activities in favor of digital media that feels safer [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR24 "Nagata JM, Lee CM, Yang J, et al. Associations between sexual orientation and early adolescent screen use: findings from the adolescent brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. Ann Epidemiol. 2023;82:54–e581. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annepidem.2023.03.004
                  
                .")]. According to GLSEN, approximately 79% of 2021 National Survey respondents reported avoiding extracurriculars or school events because they felt uncomfortable. While LGBTQ + youth may spend more time online on a regular basis as a form of escapism, seeking refuge from in-person judgment and harassment, their digital access may also simultaneously be an exercise of agency as they strive to cultivate supportive online communities and access essential resources to support their own wellbeing–not only avoiding unsafe individuals and spaces, but moving toward others who have shared their experiences and accept them [[24](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR24 "Nagata JM, Lee CM, Yang J, et al. Associations between sexual orientation and early adolescent screen use: findings from the adolescent brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. Ann Epidemiol. 2023;82:54–e581. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annepidem.2023.03.004
                  
                .")].

Learning about LGBTQ + identities via social media and websites is associated with lower levels of loneliness as well [[17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR17 "Charmaraman L, Zhang A, Wang K, Chen B. Sexual minorities and loneliness: exploring sexuality through Social Media and Gender-Sexuality Alliance (GSA) supports. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2024;21(3):300. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph21030300
                  
                . PMID: 38541299; PMCID: PMC10970596.")]. As youth navigate online spaces, schools can also support their well-being by providing education about social media management and consumption. In a national survey study, participants (ages 10–17) indicated how much they agreed with the statement “My school tries to help us learn how to use our phones or social media in healthy ways” [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR12 "Coyne SM, Weinstein E, Sheppard JA, et al. Analysis of Social Media Use, Mental Health, and gender identity among US youths. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(7):e2324389. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.24389
                  
                .")]. The presence of such digital literacy programming was associated with decreased depressive symptoms in LGBTQ + adolescents [[12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR12 "Coyne SM, Weinstein E, Sheppard JA, et al. Analysis of Social Media Use, Mental Health, and gender identity among US youths. JAMA Netw Open. 2023;6(7):e2324389. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2023.24389
                  
                .")]. Similarly, additional studies have encouraged more tailored digital literacy education that supports youth with marginalized identities, including LGBTQ + youth, rather than assuming that digital media serves similar roles for all young people [[25](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR25 "Nagata JM, Balasubramanian P, Iyra P, et al. Screen use in transgender and gender-questioning adolescents: findings from the adolescent brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study. Ann Epidemiol. 2024;95:6–11. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.annepidem.2024.04.013
                  
                .")].

## Identity Development & Building Online Community

Across platforms, social media can be a positive environment for LGBTQ + youth identity development and community-building [[16](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR16 "Tao X, Fisher C. Associations among web-based Civic Engagement and discrimination, web-based Social Support, and Mental Health and Substance Use Risk among LGBT Youth: cross-sectional survey study. J Med Internet Res. 2023;25:e46604. 
                  https://doi.org/10.2196/46604
                  
                . Published 2023 Jun 26."), [17](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR17 "Charmaraman L, Zhang A, Wang K, Chen B. Sexual minorities and loneliness: exploring sexuality through Social Media and Gender-Sexuality Alliance (GSA) supports. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2024;21(3):300. 
                  https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph21030300
                  
                . PMID: 38541299; PMCID: PMC10970596."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR26 "Bates A, Hobman T, Bell BT. Don’t Decide My Identity For Me: LGBTQ + Youth Experiences of Social Media in Narrative Identity Development. J Adolesc Res. 2020;35(1):51–83. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0743558419884700
                  
                . Let Me Do What I Please With It."), [27](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR27 "Hiebert A, Kortes-Miller K. Finding home in online community: exploring TikTok as a support for gender and sexual minority youth throughout COVID-19. J LGBT Youth. 2023;20:4800–817. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/19361653.2021.2009953
                  
                .")]. LGBTQ + identities are often incongruent to sociocultural expectations regarding gender, sexuality, and relationships, so many adolescents turn to social media as a tool for education on LGBTQ + topics, and learning from organization websites [[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR2 "Charmaraman L, Hodes R, Richer AM. Young sexual minority adolescent experiences of self-expression and isolation on Social Media: cross-sectional survey study. JMIR Ment Health. 2021;8(9):e26207.: 10.2196/26207; PMID: 34524107; PMCID: 8482247."), [26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR26 "Bates A, Hobman T, Bell BT. Don’t Decide My Identity For Me: LGBTQ + Youth Experiences of Social Media in Narrative Identity Development. J Adolesc Res. 2020;35(1):51–83. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0743558419884700
                  
                . Let Me Do What I Please With It.")]. On social media, adolescents can find labels or other terminology to describe who they are [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR26 "Bates A, Hobman T, Bell BT. Don’t Decide My Identity For Me: LGBTQ + Youth Experiences of Social Media in Narrative Identity Development. J Adolesc Res. 2020;35(1):51–83. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0743558419884700
                  
                . Let Me Do What I Please With It.")]. These terminologies may help to normalize their feelings and dismantle internalized stigmas, helping adolescents to build self-confidence in who they are [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR26 "Bates A, Hobman T, Bell BT. Don’t Decide My Identity For Me: LGBTQ + Youth Experiences of Social Media in Narrative Identity Development. J Adolesc Res. 2020;35(1):51–83. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/0743558419884700
                  
                . Let Me Do What I Please With It.")]. They can also curate a social media profile to reflect their “true” identity or ideal self (e.g. subtly posting with a significant other) and adapt this over time through development [[26](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40124-024-00338-2#ref-CR26 "Bates A, Hobman T, Bell BT. Don’t Decide My Identity For Me: LGBTQ + Youth Experiences of Social Media in Narrative Identity Development. J Adolesc Res. 2020;35(1):51–83.

args.key_excerpts: "While some research suggests that social media use and overuse is associated with negative outcomes such as depression and anxiety, many recent studies have found that, for LGBTQ+ youth in particular, social media may be a necessary safe space they have for representation and community building, especially when absent in their physical world.", "Active social media use served a protective effect and that deliberate 'social media breaks' were associated with increased depression, suggesting that regulating screen time might not be beneficial for the mental health of LGBTQ+ youth.", "Simply suggesting a one-size-fits-all solution such as minimizing social media time is harmful, especially for some LGBTQ+ youth who intentionally create safe spaces online that might not exist offline.", "Over 90% of US transgender youth between 13 and 17 years old live in states that have introduced bills or passed laws banning gender affirming healthcare, participation in sports, use of bathrooms, and/or preferred pronoun use.", "LGBTQ+ youth continue to spend a disproportionately greater amount of time online compared to their non-LGBTQ+ peers, with additional hours of daily screen time reported for transgender (4.51 h), sexual minority (3.72 h), and gender-questioning (3.41 h) youth."
args.summary:
This is an academic review article published on January 17, 2025 in Current Pediatrics Reports (Volume 13, Article 3) examining the relationship between social media use and LGBTQ+ youth, focusing on mental health, identity development, and civic engagement in the post-COVID-19 pandemic era.

**Key Context:** The US Surgeon General has identified loneliness as an epidemic, with LGBTQ+ youth as a disproportionately at-risk group. In 2023, 510 bills restricting LGBTQ+ rights were introduced across the US, with 533 introduced by fall 2024. Over 90% of transgender youth aged 13-17 live in states with anti-transgender legislation.

**Mental Health Benefits:** Social media provides crucial safe spaces for LGBTQ+ youth, especially those lacking supportive environments offline. The Social Media Benefits Scale (SMBS) was developed to measure positive impacts. Active social media use was found to be protective for transgender/nonbinary youth, with "social media breaks" actually associated with increased depression. Curated feeds and strong media literacy decreased depressive symptoms. Social media is particularly protective for rural LGBTQ+ youth facing social isolation.

**Mental Health Risks:** Negative online experiences correlate with increased suicidal ideation, while positive experiences reduce it. Transgender/nonbinary adolescents report the highest rates of online discrimination. Digital sexual violence (threat of nonconsensual posting of explicit media) was associated with increased odds of suicidal ideation, attempts, and self-harm among sexual minority adolescents.

**School Context:** LGBTQ+ youth experience higher rates of online and in-person victimization. Approximately 76% of LGBTQ+ youth encounter anti-LGBTQ+ microaggressions online monthly. However, 68% identified online spaces as affirming and 52% identified schools as affirming. Gender-Sexuality Alliances (GSAs) are associated with lower loneliness, but GSA prevalence dropped from over 60% (2019) to under 40% (2021) during COVID-19. LGBTQ+ youth spend disproportionately more time online (transgender: 4.51 hrs/day, sexual minority: 3.72 hrs/day) compared to peers.

**Identity Development:** Social media helps LGBTQ+ youth find terminology, normalize feelings, dismantle internalized stigmas, and build self-confidence. Representation online builds resilience by showing youth they can be openly queer and achieve their goals.

**Conclusions:** The review emphasizes that one-size-fits-all solutions like minimizing screen time may be harmful for LGBTQ+ youth who intentionally create safe spaces online. Future research should examine the granular relationship between social media use and LGBTQ+ adolescent mental health beyond simple comparisons with heterosexual peers, and interventions should be tailored to intersectional identities.

# The Online Experiences of LGBTQ+ Youth

### Contents

[LGBTQ+ Youth Mental Health](#mental-health)

[Media Use Habits of LGBTQ+ Youth](#media-habits)

[Positive Online Experiences – Support and Identity Development](#positive-experiences)

[References](#references)

---

[![Infographic: The Online Experiences of LGBTQ+ Youth](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/wp-content/uploads/202501-brief-infographic.png "Infographic summarizing the key insights of this brief")  
Infographic summarizing the key insights of this brief](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/infographic/lgbtq-youth-experiences-online/)

---

## Introduction

Experts and clinicians, when asked about the impacts of social media on mental health, often highlight the opportunities provided by online spaces specifically for [LGBTQ+](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/family-digital-wellness-guide/glossary/#lgbtqia) youth[1](#1812baba-a0d2-4513-ad79-6d2447c00b21). This research brief explores the current literature about the benefits online spaces confer and the risks of those spaces for young people who identify with a sexual and/or gender minority group, including how these youth find support and community, navigate risks, and explore their identities online.

As much discussion on social media in particular focuses on mental health effects, it is important to recognize that LGBTQ+ youth may be more likely to struggle with mental health concerns like depression and anxiety (CDC, 2024), and often face barriers in accessing care which appropriately meets their needs (Choi et al., 2023). This context is critical for understanding how LGBTQ+ youth navigate online spaces.

Within this framework, this research brief will seek to set the stage with the latest research on the state of mental health of LGBTQ+ youth, followed by an exploration of:

* Which experiences on the internet, and social media more specifically, benefit LGBTQ+ youth?
* Which experiences on the internet, and social media more specifically, increase the risks of harm for LGBT+ youth?

Given that the landscape of online spaces has changed significantly in recent years, in order to best reflect the current online environment, this research brief will primarily evaluate literature from the past five years, 2019-2024.

## Mental Health Experiences of LGBTQ+ Youth

Young people in the LGBTQ+ community have nuanced experiences and unique considerations for their mental, emotional, and social wellbeing. Overall, teens and young adults who identify as LGBTQ+ report more mental health challenges than their cisgender and heterosexual  peers. For example, the Trevor Project’s *2023 National Survey on the Mental Health of LGBTQ Young People* (ages 13-24) found that 67% of respondents reported symptoms of anxiety and 54% reported symptoms of depression (The Trevor Project, 2023). The most recently available *Youth Risk Behavior Survey* data in the United States found that 65% of LGBTQ+ high school students experienced “persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness” during the past year, more than double the rate found among cisgender or heterosexual students (CDC, 2024). LGBTQ+ young people, especially younger adolescents, are also significantly more likely to express suicidal ideation than their cisgender and heterosexual peers (e.g. Miranda-Mendizabal et al., 2017; Ream, 2019).

Unfortunately, unique barriers also exist for LGBTQ+ youth seeking access to mental health care. While 84% of young people identifying as LGBTQ+ reported a desire to engage with a mental health counselor over the past year, 50% of those youth did not receive counseling services (The Trevor Project, 2024). **Geographic location amplifies the challenge. LGBTQ+ youth in the Northeastern United States received access to mental health care (56%) more often than their Southern peers (45%) (The Trevor Project, 2024).****One barrier to accessing care may be a general lack of identity-focused practice: in 2020, only 28% of mental health care facilities in the US offered LGBTQ+-specific services, with coastal states having higher rates of specific care programs than rural areas (Choi et al., 2023). Additionally, many young people noted feelings of fear around talking to someone about their mental health, and almost half of gender-questioning youth did not want to get permission from a parent or caregiver to speak to a counselor (The Trevor Project, 2024; Zullo et al., 2021).** This latter finding is particularly concerning, as acceptance from a parent is associated with a significant decrease in past-year suicide attempt (Green et al., 2021). Addressing barriers to healthcare for LGBTQ+ young people is critical, as access to mental health and/or gender-affirming care can significantly lower suicidal ideation and attempts (Tordoff et al., 2022; The Trevor Project, 2024).

## Media Use Habits of LGBTQ+ Youth

While a significant proportion of young people overall are engaged users of media, LGBTQ+ youth may be more likely to be heavy users both in time spent and spaces visited. One recent analysis of a large longitudinal data set of adolescent screen use in the United States found that identifying with a sexual minority resulted in an average 3.72 hours of additional daily screen time (Nagata et al., 2023). Recent research in the United States and Australia has found that LGBTQ+ young people are more likely to use a greater number of mobile applications and social media platforms, and to hold multiple accounts within a platform, as compared to their cisgender and heterosexual peers (eSafety Commissioner, 2024; Madden et al., 20204; Thorn, 2023). For example, while only 8% of the Australian teen population surveyed used over 10 social media platforms, 25% of LGBTQIA+ teens said the same (eSafety Commissioner, 2024).

Research evaluating the media habits of LGBTQ+ youth has often described their online experiences as a “double edged sword,” including both more positive and more negative experiences for these youth compared to their cisgender and heterosexual peers (e.g. Fisher et al., 2024; Madden et al., 2024). **A majority of LGBTQ+ youth describe social media as both positive (96%) and negative (88%) for their mental health (The Trevor Project, 2021).**

In the United States, sexual minority youth are much more likely than others  to use online resources for sexual exploration and sexual health information (e.g. Delmonaco & Haimson, 2022; Mitchell et al., 2014; Robb & Mann, 2023). While similar patterns of use are found in other countries primarily considered “Western” and developed (e.g. Bradlow et al., 2017; eSafety Commissioner, 2024), far less is known about the online behaviors and experiences of LGBTQ+ youth in areas where queer relationships and gender minority expression are criminalized or face high levels of discrimination, despite the fact that these factors may drive LGBTQ+ people to seek partners online rather than in-person at higher rates (e.g. Thomann et al., 2020).

In the United States, intersectional analyses to compare the media use habits of LGBTQ+ youth who also identify as a racial minority are sparse, though some research has sought to explore the online experiences of multiply-marginalized youth (see: Cho, 2018; Lucero, 2017; Schmitz et al., 2022). As research continues to highlight the unique experiences of LGBTQ+ youth online, it is important to continue developing a context to evaluate how LGBTQ+ youth navigate online spaces with relation to all facets of their identity (i.e. gender, race, sexuality, socioeconomic status), rather than assuming a ubiquitous experience for all gender and sexual minorities independent of other factors.

## Positive Online Experiences – Support and Identity Development

A substantial body of research has explored how LGBTQ+ youth navigate social media to support their identity development, find affinity spaces online, and form connections with peers. In fact, in his 2023 *Advisory on Social Media and Youth Mental Health*, the U.S. Surgeon General called attention to research that suggests that marginalized youth, including sexual and gender minorities, may uniquely benefit from the connection opportunities provided by social media (Office of the U.S. Surgeon General, 2023).

### Exploring LGBTQ+ Identity Online

A recent evaluation of sexual identity milestones (e.g., first attraction, self-identification as sexual minority identity) found that today’s LGBTQ+ youth begin to notice attraction in early adolescence, then self-identify and engage in sexual experiences as they enter later years of adolescence; in contrast, older generations were more likely to have engaged in same-sex behaviors before identifying as a sexual minority (Bishop et al., 2021; Hall et al., 2021). During the adolescent years, young people may use online spaces and resources to understand their feelings and develop their sense of identity. For some young people, especially during early adolescence, online spaces may be a safe place to explore and practice aspects of identity before “coming out” offline. This online information-seeking has been recognized as a common practice for LGBTQ+ young people during their identity formation and “coming out” process for over a decade (e.g. Craig & McInroy, 2014; Fox & Ralston, 2016; Gray, 2009).

Unfortunately, research has found that less than 40% of LGBTQ+ young people find their physical homes to be affirming of their identity (Gardner, 2024; The Trevor Project, 2024), and many young people who are discovering their sexuality may not have access to supportive offline communities or feel comfortable talking about their identity with trusted adults or friends. As a result, online spaces often serve as places where young people feel safer seeking information about and connection around their sexual and/or gender identities. In the United States, over half (54%) of LGBTQ+ young adults say they were out on a dating app before telling friends and family about their identity (Tinder, 2023).

Online fan spaces for connection and creation within pop culture have historically been places where LGBTQ+ teens and young adults find community and support while exploring their interests and sexual identity (see *“Online Fan Spaces” in [Young People’s Sense of Belonging Online](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/research-briefs/young-peoples-sense-of-belonging-online/#fan-spaces)*). Recent work has explored how social gaming, and more specifically [avatar](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/family-digital-wellness-guide/glossary/#avatar) creation, could also provide opportunities for trans and gender diverse youth to feel affirmed and explore different presentations of gender (McKenna et al., 2024; Morgan et al., 2020). For example, one adolescent described avatar creation and gameplay as a way to “test the waters of coming out to people online and see how they respond before doing it IRL [in real life]” (McKenna et al., 2024, pp. 38). While all adolescents are forming and testing out identities, sexual minority identities may feel riskier to present to friends, family, and the offline world as a whole. Online spaces such as social media platforms, forums, and video games, can provide an opportunity for identity development and self-discovery for LGBTQ+ youth who may not feel safe or comfortable first exploring these identities offline.

### Online Support and Community

For teens self-identifying as LGBTQ+, social media in particular can be an outlet for finding others like themselves, providing hope, solace, and connection (Berger et al., 2022; Fish et al., 2020; Hopelab, 2024). While young people frequently have [parasocial relationships](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/family-digital-wellness-guide/glossary/#paraso) with media characters, social media also allows for the formation of parasocial relationships with “influencers” and content creators. While there are some concerns about how parasocial relationships can be exploited to market products, there are also benefits to these relationships, as they can inspire a sense of connection (Lou, 2022; Lou & Kim, 2019; Woznicki et al., 2021). **For LGBTQ+ youth, these relationships may hold particular importance: a recent report found that transgender people with stronger parasocial relationships also had higher levels of transgender pride and community connectedness (Hopelab, 2024). The visibility of trans content creators may help trans youth navigate challenges or feelings of isolation, while witnessing other trans people authentically and joyously living their lives.**

While content creators with large followings may not deeply engage with their viewers, LGBTQ+ youth may be cultivating smaller supportive communities of peers who are navigating similar life experiences. LGBTQ+ youth are more likely than their cisgender and heterosexual peers to join a group or online community, including group chats with online friends or online groups acting as an extension of an in-person group, like a club or support group (Charmaraman et al., 2021). In a survey of LGBTQ+ youth, 68% reported that they have access to affirming spaces online, 14 percentage points higher than the second most-frequently cited space, which was school (The Trevor Project, 2024). LGBTQ+ teenagers who reported that they have found social media to be a place of connection have explained that it allowed them to “make friends like me,” which can sometimes feel safer than trying to find other LGBTQ+ people offline (Fisher et al., 2024, p. 3). For some young people who may not yet feel comfortable sharing their sexual or gender identity with offline friends and family, online friends can seem better at providing emotional support (Ybarra et al., 2015).

Other factors, like the lack of visibility of offline support systems, may also play a role in the perceived value of online social support, with those in rural areas finding increased value in online spaces (Wagaman et al., 2020). This is supported by research exploring the experiences of LGBTQ+ youth who could not access in-person support during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. Young people who identify as LGBTQ+ expressed a sense of loss about the lack of in-person safe spaces during the COVID-19 lockdowns, as well as a sense of gratitude for their online communities (e.g. Fish et al., 2020; Malmquist et al., 2023).

For some, the loss of in-person meeting places was associated with grief. One interviewee from Sweden specifically highlighted how queer culture has often revolved around in-person celebrations or events like Pride celebrations, which were curtailed during the pandemic lockdowns (Malmquist et al., 2023). Other young LGBTQ+ people, including those in rural areas, those who had limited or no familial support, and those where were not yet “out,” reported that they  greatly appreciated the increased availability of online connections within the LGBTQ+community (e.g. Fish et al., 2020; Malmquist et al., 2023).

## Heightened and Unique Risks

### Cyberbullying and Indirect Violence

While there are risks involved with specific media behaviors or features of media platforms,for LGBTQ+ youth, these risks may be amplified or uniquely dangerous for this subgroup of youth. A systematic review of cyberbullying reported that LGBTQ+ young people were at increased risk for online harassment as compared to their cisgender and heterosexual peers (Abreu & Kenny, 2018)**. While nearly half (46%) of teens in the United States report having ever been victims of cyberbullying (Vogels, 2022), 76% of transgender individuals report being harassed online and 47% of LGBTQ+ individuals report having been cyberbullied** ***within the last twelve months*** **(Gardner, 2024).** Over a third of American teenagers (36%, down from the previous year’s 47%) reported that online harassment led to offline harassment within the past year, and a third of teenagers (31%) reported viewing anti-LGBTQ+ content online including that LGBTQ+ individuals are grooming young people (ADL Center for Technology & Society, 2024).

For younger adolescents who may be exploring their identity or beginning the process of coming out, these experiences are unfortunately very common, with 54% of LGBTQ+ middle schoolers in the United States reporting being cyberbullied (The Trevor Project, 2021). These experiences can increase feelings of depression and suicidal ideation, two mental health concerns where LGBTQ+ teens and youth are already at heightened risk (Abreu & Kenny, 2018; CDC, 2024; Miranda-Mendizabal et al., 2017; Ream, 2019). Unfortunately, while online friendships can sometimes provide emotional support, research suggests those friendships do not incur protection from bullying or harassment, unlike in-person support (Ybarra et al., 2015). It is therefore important to continue to increase acceptance of LGBTQ+ adolescents and provide them with both offline and online support systems to decrease experiences of direct victimization.

While direct cyberbullying is an acute and personal risk, hateful and prejudiced rhetoric directed at their community can also affect LGBTQ+ youth online. While slightly over half of cis/heterosexual youth in the United States have encountered transphobic or homophobic comments online, over 75% of LGBTQ+ youth report the same (Madden et al., 2024). As LGBTQ+ youth are more likely to seek support and information online regarding their mental health (eSafety commissioner, 2024), it is critical that they can navigate online spaces and communities in ways that protect and support their mental health.

### Sexting and Sexual Exploitation

While sexting is not uncommon for young people, LGBTQ+ youth often report higher levels of sending and receiving sexual messages. For example, one study found that LGBTQ+ youth in the United States were almost twice as likely to have shared nude images of themselves than their non-LGBTQ+ peers (Mori et al., 2022; Thorn, 2023). However, while sexting behaviors may incur additional risks for the participants, these activities may be seen as a more normalized practice among LGBTQ+ youth, who are more likely to be two-way sexters (both sending and receiving messages), using the opportunity to explore their own sexuality (Foody et al., 2021; Thorn, 2023).

While many LGBTQ+ youth may actively engage in these behaviors for expressive purposes, risky and exploitative online sexual experiences are unfortunately common for sexual minority youth.

**In the United States, 91% of LGBTQ+ youth report that they believe that [grooming](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/family-digital-wellness-guide/glossary/#groomi) online is at least somewhat common, and over 50% of cisgender non-heterosexual male teens have been sent nude photos they did not ask to receive, compared to 26% of their cisgender heterosexual male peers (Thorn, 2023).** In Spain, almost 10% of sexual minority adolescents reported being victims of [sextortion](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/family-digital-wellness-guide/glossary/#sextor), which included sexual coercion and threats (Gamez-Guadix & Incera, 2021). Possibly due to the higher prevalence of victimization, more LGBTQ+ teens are having discussions about things like online sexual predators with their friends; interestingly, for many topics like sexting and sexual predators, LGBTQ+ teens were much more likely than their non-LGBTQ+ peers to turn to online only friends for discussion (Thorn, 2023), continuing to underscore the importance of online information and support-seeking behaviors of LGBTQ+ youth.

### Privacy Concerns and Being “Outed”

Privacy concerns have also been explored within the context of queerness and identity formation; LGBTQ+ youth may manage privacy features differently from their peers depending on their comfort with sharing their identity with friends or family. For many platforms, there is a default expectation of publicness, such as the ability to easily and automatically add people from your phone contacts. While this may make creating an overlapping online/offline network easier for some, for queer youth who are still exploring their identity or who exist in unsupportive physical environments, this raises the risk of being unintentionally outed.LGBTQ+ early adolescents are less likely to report having family members as friends on social media, possibly because of this desire not to share their developing identity publicly online (Charmaraman et al., 2021).

Unfortunately, some youth have experienced unintentional outing to friends and family, attributing those experiences at least in part to the default publicness of platforms like Facebook. **LGBTQ+ young adults described spaces like Facebook as having a high level of surveillance, where they feel unsure about what behaviors (e.g. liking a queer event page) others in their network can see (Cho, 2018).**

**In contrast, teens felt that the platform Tumblr was a space where they could be more expressive, as there was less focus on networking with others known offline and more control over what was seen by whom (Cho, 2018).** Although the structure of Tumblr has changed somewhat since this research, its anonymity still appeals to many LGBTQ+ users, and a significantly higher percentage of LGBTQ+ young people report using the platform (compared to their cisgender and heterosexual peers) to connect with people who share their experience and identity (e.g. eSafety Commissioner, 2024; Nelson et al., 2023; Robards et al., 2020). As of this writing, the welcome page of Tumblr proudly includes “it’s the gay people in your phone,” possibly referencing the site’s historical popularity for queer discourse (Tumblr, 2024). The popularity of a platform like Tumblr speaks to a need to more deeply understand the unique experiences of LGBTQ+ youth navigating the division between their private and public lives; assuming a default publicness as more safe may not be true for all adolescents and young adults.

## Conclusion

[![Infographic: The Online Experiences of LGBTQ+ Youth](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/wp-content/uploads/202501-brief-infographic.png "Infographic summarizing the key insights of this brief")](https://digitalwellnesslab.org/wp-content/uploads/Infographic-LGBTQ-Youth-Experiences-Online.pdf)While LGBTQ+ youth are using media in many of the same ways as their cisgender and heterosexual peers, they engage in online behaviors that highlight the importance of identity-building and connection within queer and/or LGBTQ+ communities and spaces. Importantly, LGBTQ+ youth are not a monolith; while this brief has introduced many of the positive and negative aspects of online engagement for LGBTQ+ youth, there is great variety in the online experiences of different individuals and intersectional identities.

Many existing publications focused on the experiences of adolescents online do not directly compare different minority sexual and gender orientations, instead evaluating the LGBTQ+ adolescent community as a whole. Research that does evaluate separate identity groups (e.g. Nelson et al., 2023; Thorn, 2023) has found a large degree of variation in experience.

It is critical to develop research with increased attention to how specific sexual and gender identities and intersectional identities experience their online environments. In order to best protect marginalized youth online, we must seek to understand their experiences, both positive and harmful, so that platforms can create spaces and features which meet the social needs of all adolescents while mitigating risks that are unique to sexual minority youth.

args.summary:
This research brief from the Digital Wellness Lab at Boston Children's Hospital examines the online experiences of LGBTQ+ youth, highlighting both the benefits and risks of digital spaces for this population.

**Mental Health Context:** LGBTQ+ youth report more mental health challenges than peers. The Trevor Project's 2023 survey found 67% of LGBTQ+ young people (ages 13-24) reported anxiety symptoms and 54% reported depression symptoms. CDC data shows 65% of LGBTQ+ high school students experienced persistent sadness or hopelessness—more than double the rate of cisgender/heterosexual students. Geographic barriers to mental health care exist, with only 28% of US mental health facilities offering LGBTQ+-specific services in 2020.

**Media Use:** LGBTQ+ youth are heavier media users, with sexual minority youth averaging 3.72 additional hours of daily screen time. They use more platforms and maintain multiple accounts. A majority describe social media as both positive (96%) and negative (88%) for their mental health.

**Positive Online Experiences:** Online spaces support identity exploration—over half (54%) of LGBTQ+ young adults were out on dating apps before telling family/friends. Less than 40% find their physical homes affirming. Online communities provide crucial support, with 68% reporting access to affirming online spaces. Transgender youth with stronger parasocial relationships report higher transgender pride and community connectedness. Social gaming and avatar creation offer gender affirmation opportunities for trans and gender diverse youth.

**Risks:** LGBTQ+ youth face heightened cyberbullying risks—76% of transgender individuals report online harassment, and 47% of LGBTQ+ individuals report cyberbullying within the past year. Over 75% of LGBTQ+ youth encounter transphobic/homophobic comments online. Privacy concerns include risk of unintentional "outing" on platforms with default publicness. LGBTQ+ youth are almost twice as likely to have shared nude images, and 91% believe online grooming is common. In Spain, nearly 10% of sexual minority adolescents reported sextortion victimization.

**Conclusion:** The brief emphasizes that LGBTQ+ youth are not a monolith, and calls for more research on specific sexual/gender identities and intersectional identities to better understand and protect marginalized youth online.

## Highlights

*   •Social media spaces offer connection, refuge, and rejection to LGBTQ+youth. 
*   •Discrimination online was associated with more depression, anxiety, and substance use. 
*   •Seeking connection on social media may exacerbate discrimination related stress. 

## Abstract

Social media has been described as both a safe and toxic space for LGBTQ+youth. This mixed-methods online study examined whether differences in youth's open-ended narratives moderate associations between quantitative measures of online discrimination and mental health and substance use. Three thematic groups emerged from open-ended responses of 406 LGBTQ+ 14–18-year-old participants: social media as a source of connection, refuge, or rejection. Moderation analyses indicated that at higher levels of discrimination, youth in the connection narrative group experienced elevated associations between measures of discrimination and depression, anxiety, and substance use compared to the rejection group. The results highlight the significance of a mixed-methods approach, as narratives from LGBTQ+youth about their social media experiences illuminated the quantitative findings. Findings also call for practices that acknowledge the dual-faceted nature of social media and promote connections within LGBTQ+communities to increase LGBTQ+youth's mental health resilience against online discrimination.

# Online Experiences and Mental Health of LGBTQ+ Young People

Most LGBTQ+ young people agreed that they go online to connect with people because it is difficult finding others to relate to and connect with in their daily lives.

#### SHARE
