args.summary:
# Nordic Media Literacy Survey 2025 – Summary

## Overview
This report presents results from the first **Nordic Media Literacy Survey**, conducted in early 2025 by governmental media authorities in Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden, financed by the Nordic Council of Ministers. The survey includes **12,744 responses** – 9,487 adults (16+ years) and 3,257 children/youth (9–15 years) – collected via web panels. It assesses media literacy across eight proficiencies based on Professor Ulla Carlsson's model (adapted from UNESCO's MIL framework).

## Key Findings – Adult Survey

### 1. Understanding Media in a Democratic Society
- **Trust in legacy media is high**: 60–74% of respondents agree TV news provides relevant/important information; 51–69% say the same about daily newspapers. 
- **Trust is age-linked**: Older groups (45+) have higher trust in legacy media; younger groups (16–44) are more ambivalent but not outright distrustful. Outright distrust is low across all ages.
- **Social media is valued for diverse voices but low on credibility**: Social platforms score low on credibility and fair depiction; older respondents are especially sceptical, younger groups more positive.
- **Journalistic roles are highly valued**: Majorities across all countries agree that journalists should scrutinise power, deliver diverse opinions, protect sources, and remain impartial. Importance rises with age.

### 2. Understanding Media Production, Finance, and Regulation
- **Most adults understand editorial responsibility**: Majorities correctly identify that public service companies, daily newspapers, and commercial TV channels have an editor-in-chief.
- **Misconceptions exist**: About 25% of young adults (25–34) incorrectly believe Facebook has an editor-in-chief or a public service mandate.
- **Awareness of reporting mechanisms**: About two-thirds are aware they can report violating posts on social media; one-third are unaware.

### 3. Responsible and Safe Use of Media
- **High sense of personal responsibility** for complying with online regulations. 
- **Younger respondents apply more verification strategies** than older groups, suggesting older citizens may need more fact-checking support.

### 4. Critically Assessing Media Content
- **Paid search rankings**: A majority recognise paid content in search results, but significant shares lack awareness.
- **Identifying content types on news sites**: Uncertainty exists about distinguishing editorial from commercial content.

### 5. Using and Creating Content
- **Fear of attacks limits participation**: ~40% refrain from posting/commenting at least monthly due to fear of attacks; >10% refrain daily.
- **Confidence is generally high** in operating online services, but only one-third feel they receive good information from social media accounts they follow.
- **Older and youngest groups** are less confident in evaluating media trustworthiness.

### 6. AI – Use and Attitudes
- **Close to half** of adults have used an AI service in the last three months.
- **Strong age gradient**: Almost 75% of 16–24-year-olds have used AI vs. <20% of 65+.
- **Younger adults see both positives and negatives**; older adults show high uncertainty ("don't know").
- AI users are more favourable toward AI, but both users and non-users share similar concerns about risks (e.g., complicating truth discernment).

## Key Findings – Youth Survey (9–15 years)

### 1. Understanding Media in Democracy
- Social media is the **greatest news source** for youth, yet trust in it is low. TV news is trusted and seen as beneficial for democracy.
- **High "don't know" rates** (20–47%) regarding newspapers' role.
- Quality journalism is widely endorsed: majorities agree journalists should scrutinise power and ensure accuracy.

### 2. Understanding Media Production
- **Financing models are generally understood** (about half know public service is tax-funded, commercial is ad-funded), but significant groups misattribute.
- **Daily use of age-restricted platforms** is substantial among 9–12-year-olds: about one-third use TikTok and Snapchat daily despite age limits of 13.
- ~66% aware of reporting possibilities; <20% have done so.

### 3. Responsible and Safe Use
- **Most young people take protective actions** (avoiding strangers, blocking accounts, changing privacy settings), but about one-third have taken no action in the last three months.
- **Most have seen false information**; one in five are unsure if they have. Among 9–12-year-olds, this rises to one in three.
- **Only 20% find it easy** to tell if information is genuine. Verification methods: asking trusted people, online searches, comparing with trusted news.

### 4. Critical Assessment
- **Majority correctly identify** paid content in search rankings, but 10–20% fail.
- **Young people struggle** to distinguish news from other editorial sections on news sites.

### 5. Using and Creating Content
- **Most rarely post/comment** (~25% do so weekly). ~20% refrain daily from commenting due to fear of attacks.
- **More agree than not** that it is hard to judge trustworthy sources and stay up to date; ~25% avoid news altogether.
- **Only a minority** assess whether information is genuine before sharing; even fewer use multiple sources.

### 6. AI – Use and Attitudes
- **~40% have used an AI service** in the past three months (half of 13–15-year-olds, one-third of 9–12-year-olds).
- **High "don't know" rates** regarding AI attitudes. Among those with opinions, youth tend to think AI is developing too fast and show limited confidence in its accuracy or democratic benefits.
- Recent users view AI more favourably, but both users and non-users share similar concerns about risks.

## Nordic Perspectives
Separate articles discuss results in each country's context (Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden), noting structural differences in media organisation (e.g., public service funding models) that may affect comparisons.

## Conclusions
The survey provides a foundational knowledge base for media literacy work. Key gaps include: age-related trust divides, misconceptions about media financing, variable awareness of content verification, and high uncertainty around AI. The report emphasises the need for lifelong learning and targeted initiatives to strengthen digital resilience and democratic participation.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
# Youth Wiki

![](/sites/default/files/2021-01/fi.svg)

# Finland



6. Education and Training

## 6.8 Media literacy and safe use of new media

Last update: 19 August 2025

###### On this page

1. National strategy
2. Media literacy and online safety through formal education
3. Promoting media literacy and online safety through non-formal and informal learning
4. Raising awareness about the risks posed by new media

Finland 

Address

Nuorisotutkimusseura ry / Ungdomsforskningssallskapet rf

Finnish Youth Research Society

Kumpulantie 3 A

FI-00520 Helsinki

Tel: +358 44 4165388

E-Mail: [**office@youthresearch.fi**](mailto:office@youthresearch.fi)

Website:

[**https://www.youthresearch.fi/**](https://www.youthresearch.fi/)

###### On this page

1. ###### [National strategy](#121)
2. ###### [Media literacy and online safety through formal education](#122)
3. ###### [Promoting media literacy and online safety through non-formal and informal learning](#123)
4. ###### [Raising awareness about the risks posed by new media](#124)

#### **National strategy**

In alignment with EU Youth Strategy (2019–2027), [Finland’s National Youth Work and Youth Policy Programme 2024–2027](https://julkaisut.valtioneuvosto.fi/handle/10024/165628) (VANUPO) recognises media literacy and critical thinking as a means to support young people.

The policy programme published by the Ministry of Education and Culture explicitly mentions strengthening the functions of the Finnish Safer Internet model. The model operates through the [Finnish Safer Internet Centre](https://www.mll.fi/en/about-mll/media-education/finnish-safer-internet-centre/) (FISIC), a joint project between the National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI), Save the Children Finland (STC), and the Mannerheim League for Child Welfare (MLL).

Finland’s national media literacy policy is grounded on the national media education policy document [Media Literacy in Finland](https://medialukutaitosuomessa.fi/mediaeducationpolicy.pdf), written by Saara Salomaa and Lauri Palsa, National Audiovisual Institute and published by the [Ministry of Education and Culture](https://okm.fi/en/frontpage) in 2019. The document updates and extends th[e original cultural policy guidelines for media literacy](https://julkaisut.valtioneuvosto.fi/handle/10024/75278) (in Finnish) published in 2013. According to the three main objectives of the media education policy, media education in Finland ought to be comprehensive, of high quality and systematic in promoting media literacy, covering all types of media. The 2019 policy document stems from Prime Minister Sanna Marin’s Government Programme (2019–2023), which highlighted the need for media skills in all age groups. The Ministry of Education and Culture’s [press release](https://valtioneuvosto.fi/-/1410845/kansalliset-mediakasvatuslinjaukset-arvioidaan-ja-paivitetaan-1) (in Finnish) on 21 January 2025 stated that the national guidelines will be updated during 2025.

The media education policy document states that there are also several sector-specific strategies necessary for taking media education into account and to provide more detailed guidance for practical actions, such as education curricula and library policies.

The Ministry of Education and Culture supports the promotion of media literacy by allocating resources and providing information guidance. Two agencies operating under the ministry are the [National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI)](https://kavi.fi/en/) and the [Finnish National Agency for Education](https://www.oph.fi/en).

KAVI, established in early 2012, is the only party with a statutory duty to promote media education in Finland. KAVI’s [Department for Media Education and Audiovisual Media (MEKU)](https://kavi.fi/en/media-education/) is responsible for the promotion and coordination of media education at a national level, and the supervision of the provision of audiovisual programmes from the perspective of protecting children. The implementation of the media literacy policy will be regularly studied and evaluated by KAVI in collaboration with stakeholders and the Ministry of Education and Culture.

Other relevant ministries include the [Ministry of Justice](https://oikeusministerio.fi/en/ministry), which promotes media literacy as a part of democracy education. The [Ministry of Transport and Communications](https://www.lvm.fi/en/home) and the [Finnish Transport and Communication Agency](https://www.traficom.fi/en/) (Traficom) co-operate in organising, for example, campaigns such as the [Media Literacy Week](https://www.mediataitoviikko.fi/in-english/), and offering expertise on the safe use of the internet.

#### **Media literacy and online safety through formal education**

The Finnish National Agency for Education promotes media education in formal education. It prepares and makes decisions about the core curricula for basic education and upper secondary education, the core curriculum for early childhood education and care, and frameworks for vocational and competence-based qualifications.

As stated in [Media Literacy in Finland](https://medialukutaitosuomessa.fi/mediaeducationpolicy.pdf), the latest revisions to curricula at all levels from early childhood education to secondary level and basic education for adults have been important for the promotion of media literacy. Firstly, media literacy is developed from the perspective of supporting the objectives and key content of instruction in each subject, such as Finnish and literature, visual arts, social studies, history, and health education. Additionally, media literacy is also developed within the framework of multidisciplinary learning modules where it is understood as being part of multiliteracy.

The [National core curriculum for general upper secondary schools](https://www.oph.fi/sites/default/files/documents/curriculum-for-general-upper-secondary-schools-in-a-nutshell-2020_0.pdf) describes the main topics for learning related to multiliteracy as a multidisciplinary module. Media education and literacy are embedded in various subjects, including mother tongue, language and literature education (e.g., Finnish, sign-language, Swedish, Sami, and Roma languages), visual arts, music, geography (i.e., geomedia), civics, religion, and ethics. The focus is narrowed to critical literacy, being familiar with the key norms related to copyrights and freedom of speech, as well as responsibility in producing, using, and sharing content. Media ethics, media’s role in identity building, and social participation are also represented in the curriculum. In upper secondary education, students may also complete an optional diploma for media studies. The themes of online safety and the dangers of addiction are included in the content of health education as described in the national core curricula. Although not specifically targeted at media education, it is important to note that a revised version of the curriculum will enter into force on 1 August 2025. Section YouthWiki/ Finland 6.6 Social inclusion through education and training can be consulted for more information.

Regarding pedagogical tools, the National Agency for Education offers a platform, [Mediaosaaminen](https://www.oph.fi/fi/mediaosaaminen) (in Finnish), where pedagogical tools and support for media literacy education are available for teachers. Teacher training related to media literacy is also offered by universities and other educational institutions, as well as by some NGOs. The National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI) offers [special grants](https://kavi.fi/mediakasvatus/erityisavustukset/) (in Finnish) for promoting media literacy and education in Finland. In 2025, the grant was 244,904 euros in total. Projects promoting inclusive media activity of adults, AI literacy skills in youth work practices, and animal-rights-based media education for lower and upper secondary education institutions received the grant.

#### **Promoting media literacy and online safety through non-formal and informal learning**

The main top-level national policy for media education in non-formal and informal learning is the previously mentioned policy document [Media Literacy in Finland](https://medialukutaitosuomessa.fi/mediaeducationpolicy.pdf), created in collaboration with the Ministry of Education and Culture and the National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI).

The document recognises that, based on the Act on National Audiovisual Archive (2007), KAVI is responsible for promoting media education at a national level. This duty is realised by KAVI’s [Department for Media Education and Audiovisual Media (MEKU)](https://kavi.fi/en/media-education/). The objectives of the media policy programme are implemented through various long-term measures, such as the Online Media Literacy School and the Finnish Safer Internet Centre (FISIC) projects, which align with the [European BIK+ strategy](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/strategy-better-internet-kids).

The Ministry of Education and Culture also promotes media education and literacy at the NGO level. The [Finnish Society on Media Education](https://mediakasvatus.fi/in-english/), whose work is grounded in the Youth Act, can be regarded as a central NGO in the media education field. The main objectives of the society include raising awareness of research-based information, sharing good practices, training educators, and producing materials, also in [English](https://mediakasvatus.fi/in-english/) and [Swedish](https://mediakasvatus.fi/pa-svenska/). The society is also a global actor and a member of UN Alliance of Civilizations Media Literacy Education Clearinghouse, and works in co-operation with International Clearinghouse on Children, Youth and Media. [Media literacy in Finland](https://medialukutaitosuomessa.fi/mediaeducationpolicy.pdf) also mentions various other actors working with children, youth, and media, including the [Mannerheim League for Child Welfare](https://www.mll.fi/en/), [Save the Children Finland](https://www.pelastakaalapset.fi/en/about-us/who-we-are/save-the-children/), the [Finnish Parents’ League](https://vanhempainliitto.fi/tietoa-liitosta/welcome-to-parental-activity/), the [Finnish 4H Organisation](https://4h.fi/en/), and the [Youth Work Centres of Expertise](https://okm.fi/en/national-youth-centres).

National authorities have also funded and given recognition to innovative initiatives in media education. In 2025, the [Generation AI – consortium project](https://www.generation-ai-stn.fi/en/materials-from/) received the Finnish Open Educational Resource award. The [project](https://uefconnect.uef.fi/en/generation-ai/) is led by Professor Matti Tedre from the [University of Eastern Finland](https://www.uef.fi/en), realised in collaboration between various Finnish universities, educational science institutions and societies, and funded by the [Strategic Research Council (SRC)](https://www.aka.fi/en/). SRC operates in connection with the Research Council of Finland, which again operates under the administrative branch of the Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture. The [Open Science and Research Award](https://avointiede.fi/en/eventpage/open-science-and-research-awards) is granted by the [Federation of Finnish Learned Societies](https://www.tsv.fi/en/), which receives funding from the Ministry of Education and Culture.

#### **Raising awareness about the risks posed by new media**

At a general level, better and safer use of the internet for all age groups, including children and young people, is promoted by the functions of the [Finnish Safer Internet Centre (FISIC)](https://www.betterinternetforkids.eu/sic/finland). Awareness-raising takes place, for example, through the Media Literacy Week, the Safer Internet Day campaign, the Nordic Game Day, and the Media Education Forum. More information on these initiatives is available on the EU subpage [Finnish Safer Internet Centre](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/sic/finland). The [free English language resources for media education](https://mediataitokoulu.fi/en/home/), provided by [KAVI](https://kavi.fi/en/), also provide educational information on topics such as ‘media fears’ and ‘deepfake’. The project is co-financed by the European Union.

Promoting media literacy is also supported by the [Creative Europe funding programme](https://commission.europa.eu/funding-tenders/find-funding/eu-funding-programmes/creative-europe_en). [According to the Finnish National Agency for Education](https://www.oph.fi/fi/uutiset/2025/suomeen-ennatysmaara-eu-rahoitusta-medialukutaidon-ja-journalismin-vahvistamiseen) (in Finnish), the following projects with Finnish participants received funding in the 2024 application round:

* [Endgame project](https://endgameproject.github.io/) (coordinated by the [University of Eastern Finland](https://www.uef.fi/en), participants include [Factbar](https://faktabaari.fi/in-english/))
* [PRIME - Primary Information](https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/projects-details/43251814/101187582) (participants include [Factbar](https://faktabaari.fi/in-english/) and the [European School of Helsinki](https://www.eshelsinki.com/))
* [Media Education project and the Content Analysis and Research Lab (CARL)](https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/projects-details/43251814/101180139/CREA2027?order=DESC&pageNumber=1&pageSize=50&sortBy=es_SortDate&keywords=Reaching%20journalism%20sustainability%20through%20understanding%20content%20data&isExactMatch=true) (Participants include [Savo-Karjalan Media Oy](https://keskisuomalainen.com/alueyhtiot/savo-karjalan-media-oy/))

The funded projects also provide tools for young people to interact in online environments in a responsible way. For example, the [PRIME –programme’s](https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/projects-details/43251814/101187582) goals include ‘developing interactive toolkits for the online environment’.

**Grooming**

[Save the Children Finland](https://www.pelastakaalapset.fi/en/) aims to combat grooming through the [Finnish Hotline Nettivihje](https://www.pelastakaalapset.fi/en/finnish-hotline-nettivihje/), where material and activity related to online child sexual abuse can be reported. Save the Children Finland has also hosted [webinars](https://better-internet-for-kids.europa.eu/en/sic/finland) and provides information regarding grooming, harassment, and abuse online, as well as self-help material for individuals experiencing sexual interest in children.

In addition to Save the Children Finland, [Loisto settlement ry’s](https://loistosetlementti.fi/english/) (based in the Helsinki area) programme [For You on Social Media](https://suavartensomessa.fi/in-english/) (Sua varten somessa, in Finnish) is another example of an initiative targeting children and young people aged 8–21 years, aiming to decrease sexual harassment and violence against them on social media. Young people are able to contact youth workers through social media and receive support and guidance. The programme has been awarded the [Youth Work Recognition Award](https://valtioneuvosto.fi/-/1410845/sua-varten-somessa-hanke-sai-nuorisotyon-tunnustuspalkinnon) in 2022 by the Minister of Education and Culture, Antti Kurvinen.

In September 2024, the Finnish Government reported that the [Recognise, learn, report!” campaign seeks to prevent crime occurring online](https://valtioneuvosto.fi/en/-//25235045/the-recognise-learn-report-campaign-seeks-to-prevent-crime-taking-place-online). It is described that the ‘campaign will increase awareness and call attention to the importance of discussions about digital everyday activities’. The campaign is realised by the National Police Board, the National Bureau of Investigation, Save the Children Finland and the Protect Children association, and focuses on recognition, reporting and prevention of crimes in online environments. Helping young people recognise online sexual violence is recognised as a special focus area.

**Cyberbullying**

At the moment, as stated on the Council of Europe’s subpage [Finland – Cyberviolence](https://www.coe.int/en/web/cyberviolence/finland), ‘Finland doesn’t have specific provisions regarding online offences/cyberbullying offences either. The coverage of these offences is to some degree unclear but nevertheless it’s possible to say that acts like these are covered by many Criminal Code provisions ‘.

FINEEC’s Evaluation of methods that prevent bullying and improve wellbeing and the working atmosphere [final report](https://www.karvi.fi/en/evaluations/pre-primary-and-basic-education/thematic-and-system-evaluations/evaluation-methods-prevent-bullying-and-improve-wellbeing-and-working-atmosphere) (2023) noted that bullying on digital platforms does not come to the attention of school personnel as easily as bullying in the physical school environment.

In addition, the Mannerheim League for Child Welfare (MLL) published a report, [Youth and Cyberbullying 2025](https://www.mll.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/nettikiusaamiskysely_2025_A4.pdf) (in Finnish), which examined experiences of cyberbullying among 13–18-year-old young people. According to the report, cyberbullying has increased on social media platforms, with 20% of the participants encountering online bullying daily. TikTok was specifically highlighted as a platform where cyberbullying is common.

# Finland: Media Literacy and Safe Use of New Media (Youth Wiki)

## National Strategy

Finland's media literacy policy is grounded in the 2019 national policy document "Media Literacy in Finland" (by Salomaa & Palsa, National Audiovisual Institute, published by the Ministry of Education and Culture). The document has three main objectives: media education should be **comprehensive, high quality, and systematic** in promoting media literacy across all media types. The Ministry of Education and Culture announced on 21 January 2025 that these national guidelines will be updated during 2025.

The policy aligns with the **EU Youth Strategy (2019–2027)** and Finland's **National Youth Work and Youth Policy Programme 2024–2027 (VANUPO)**. The **National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI)** is the only party with a statutory duty to promote media education in Finland, operating through its Department for Media Education and Audiovisual Media (MEKU). The **Finnish Safer Internet Centre (FISIC)** operates as a joint project between KAVI, Save the Children Finland, and the Mannerheim League for Child Welfare.

## Media Literacy Through Formal Education

The **Finnish National Agency for Education** promotes media education in formal education through core curricula at all levels (early childhood to upper secondary). Media literacy is embedded across subjects (Finnish, visual arts, social studies, history, health education) and within multidisciplinary learning modules as part of **multiliteracy**. A revised upper secondary curriculum entered into force on 1 August 2025.

Pedagogical tools are available via the **Mediaosaaminen** platform. KAVI offers special grants for promoting media literacy (€244,904 total in 2025).

## Non-Formal and Informal Learning

The **Finnish Society on Media Education** is a central NGO in the field, grounded in the Youth Act. Other actors include the Mannerheim League for Child Welfare, Save the Children Finland, the Finnish Parents' League, the Finnish 4H Organisation, and Youth Work Centres of Expertise.

The **Generation AI consortium project** (led by Prof. Matti Tedre, University of Eastern Finland) received the Finnish Open Educational Resource award in 2025.

## Raising Awareness About Risks

**Finnish Safer Internet Centre (FISIC)** raises awareness through Media Literacy Week, Safer Internet Day, Nordic Game Day, and the Media Education Forum. KAVI provides free English language resources covering topics like "media fears" and "deepfake."

**EU-funded projects** (2024 Creative Europe round) include: Endgame (University of Eastern Finland & Factbar), PRIME - Primary Information (Factbar & European School of Helsinki), and the Media Education/CARL project.

**Grooming:** Save the Children Finland operates the **Nettivihje hotline** for reporting online child sexual abuse material. The **"For You on Social Media"** programme (Loisto settlement ry) targets youth aged 8–21 to decrease sexual harassment on social media; it received the Youth Work Recognition Award in 2022. In September 2024, the Finnish Government launched the **"Recognise, learn, report!"** campaign to prevent online crime, focusing on recognition, reporting, and prevention.

**Cyberbullying:** The Council of Europe notes Finland has no specific provisions for online/cyberbullying offences, though such acts are covered by Criminal Code provisions. MLL's **Youth and Cyberbullying 2025** report found that 20% of youth (13–18) encounter online bullying daily, with TikTok highlighted as a common platform. FINEEC's 2023 evaluation noted that bullying on digital platforms is less visible to school personnel.

# How Nordic countries differ in children’s media guidelines

![](https://medialukutaitosuomessa.fi/wp-content/uploads/iStock-2159343013.jpg)

The conversation around children’s and young people’s media use has evolved significantly in recent years across the globe. In the Nordic countries, the topic has gained particular momentum. Smart device use in schools has been restricted, and partly strict recommendations have been issued to families regarding children’s and adolescents’ media habits. This country-specific review highlights how media use is recommended or regulated across the Nordic region.

**Finland Leads with Legislation on Smart Devices in Schools**

Finland is currently developing recommendations for children’s and adolescents’ leisure-time digital media use through broad stakeholder collaboration, coordinated by the Finnish National Agency for Education and the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare. The primary audience for these recommendations is parents and guardians. Guidelines for children under 13 will be published in early 2026, with those for adolescents expected later that year.

A new law came into effect in August 2025, prohibiting the use of personal mobile devices during lessons, except for pedagogical or health-related reasons. Schools retain autonomy over device use during breaks and meals and define disciplinary measures in their own rules. While schools already had the authority to restrict phone use, educators and school leaders sought a stronger legal framework.

**Sweden Sets Clear Screen Time Guidelines**

The Swedish Public Health Agency released [recommendations for children’s and adolescents’ digital media use](https://www.folkhalsomyndigheten.se/contentassets/ab9cc71603f84f048dadf4c2851032f6/recommendations-childrens-adolescents-digital-media-use.pdf) in September 2024. These guidelines offer advice on screen time limits, considerations for family media habits, and reflections on parents’ own media behavior. The recommendations are based on the earlier report [Digital Media and the Health of Children and Adolescents](https://www.folkhalsomyndigheten.se/publikationer-och-material/publikationsarkiv/d/digitala-medier-och-barns-och-ungas-halsa-kunskapssammanstallning/) (in Swedish). Additional materials will be produced in autumn 2025 in collaboration with the Swedish Media Authority to engage both parents and professionals.

Regarding smartphone use, a government inquiry has proposed a national ban on mobile phones in schools starting 1 July 2026. The proposed legislation closely mirrors Finland’s law. Schools will determine practical arrangements, such as phone storage, through their internal policies.

**Norway Considers Raising the Age Limit for Social Media**

Norway adopted the World Health Organization’s screen time recommendations in 2022. In 2024, the government appointed a committee to examine children’s media use. The committee’s [comprehensive report](https://www.regjeringen.no/contentassets/c252947398de4fb0aea9349f011eb410/no/pdfs/nou202420240020000dddpdfs.pdf) (in Norwegian) includes recommendations for leisure-time media use, school settings, and daycare environments. However, it avoids setting strict time limits, citing limited scientific evidence and varying family circumstances. Instead, the emphasis is placed on parents’ role in guiding media use, particularly before bedtime.

Norway is also considering raising the age limit for data protection from 13 to 15, which would prohibit children under 15 from creating social media accounts.

While there is no national law banning personal phone use during the school day, nearly all primary schools prohibit phone use during lessons through school rules, and more than half of upper secondary schools have adopted similar policies.

**Denmark’s Guidelines Extend to Adults**

The Danish Health Authority published [updated recommendations](https://www.sst.dk/da/Borger/En-sund-hverdag/Sk%C3%A6rmbrug) (in Danish, with a website translation tool) for leisure-time screen use in June 2024. These guidelines apply to children, adolescents, and parents. Denmark follows the WHO’s approach to time limits, acknowledging the limited scientific evidence. Time-based suggestions are presented as flexible guidelines, supported by practical advice for implementation. Update 26th of November: In Denmark, the government plans to ban the use of social media by people under the age of 15.

Denmark does not currently have a national law banning phone use during the school day. However, the government is planning legislation that would require all school boards to establish a local anti-smartphone policy.

**Iceland Sets Time Limits Only for the Youngest Children**

Although Iceland lacks formal national guidelines, the health authority has compiled [comprehensive instructions](https://www.heilsuvera.is/efnisflokkar/throskaferlid/throski-og-uppeldi-barna/skjarinn-og-bornin/) on screen time and media use for children on the health service website Heilsuvera (in Icelandic, with a translation tool). These guidelines were developed in collaboration with the Media Literacy Department at the Icelandic Media Commission. While no strict time limits are imposed, screen use is not recommended at all for children under 18 months. The site also offers concise recommendations for three age groups, created in partnership with multiple stakeholders.

The Icelandic government is preparing to regulate phone use in schools in the coming months. Many schools across the country have already implemented bans during the school day.

Text: Julia Alajärvi, National Audiovisual Institute

Photo: [Jacob Wackerhausen](https://www.istockphoto.com/fi/portfolio/PeopleImages?mediatype=photography) / iStock

**Sources:** Nordic media regulators meeting in Helsinki, September 11–12, 2025; [*National Recommendations and Guidelines in the Nordic Countries*](https://nordicwelfare.org/en/national-recommendations-and-guidelines-in-the-nordic-countries/) by Nordic Welfare Centre; various national authority websites; Helsingin Sanomat, Yle, Euronews, BBC.

***Note:** The National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI) and the Arts Promotion Centre Finland (Taike) will merge into the Finnish Arts and Culture Agency as of 1 January 2026. This merger is part of the Ministry of Education and Culture’s Administration 2030 reform initiative.*

This article, published on November 4, 2025 by the Finnish National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI), examines how Nordic countries differ in their approaches to children's media guidelines and smart device use in schools.

**Finland** leads with a new law (August 2025) banning personal mobile devices during lessons, with exceptions for pedagogical or health reasons. Schools retain autonomy over device use during breaks. National recommendations for children's leisure-time digital media use are being developed, with guidelines for under-13s due in early 2026 and adolescents later that year.

**Sweden's** Public Health Agency released screen time recommendations in September 2024, including time limits, family media habit guidance, and parental self-reflection. A government inquiry proposes a national ban on mobile phones in schools starting July 1, 2026.

**Norway** adopted WHO screen time recommendations in 2022 and published a comprehensive report in 2024 focusing on parental guidance rather than strict time limits. Norway is considering raising the data protection age from 13 to 15, which would prohibit children under 15 from creating social media accounts. Nearly all primary schools prohibit phone use during lessons through school rules.

**Denmark** updated screen time recommendations in June 2024 for children, adolescents, and parents, following WHO's flexible approach. The government plans to ban social media for under-15s and require all school boards to establish local anti-smartphone policies.

**Iceland** lacks formal national guidelines but has compiled instructions on the health service website. Screen use is not recommended for children under 18 months. The government is preparing to regulate phone use in schools, with many schools already implementing bans.

The article notes that the National Audiovisual Institute (KAVI) and the Arts Promotion Centre Finland will merge into the Finnish Arts and Culture Agency as of January 1, 2026.

# Media literacy in finland – national media education policy

---

![](/creativity/sites/default/files/styles/paragraph_medium_desktop/public/structured_data/dce002/5664648_framework_pmp_goal1_1405.png.webp?itok=kalSTLBJ)

**Where**

**When**

**Who**  
 National audiovisual institute, ministry of education and culture

**Website of the policy/measure**  
  [Website](http://julkaisut.valtioneuvosto.fi/handle/10024/162065)

**Read the full report**  
  [Go to full report](https://media.unesco.org/sites/default/files/webform/dce002/QPR_2020_FI_5ba21a05-ed07-418a-96b1-2b0d53477ae3_9.pdf)

## Description of the policy/measure

Media literacy in finland is the media literacy policy and the national media education policy document, published by the ministry of education and culture in 2019. the document updates and extends the cultural policy guidelines for media literacy published in 2013. the media literacy in finland policy document aims to clarify the field of media education and describe the strengths, values and principles of media education in finland. this document also highlights areas for improvement and the related social, cultural and technological development trends. according to the three main objectives of the media education policy, media education in finland is comprehensive, of high-quality, and systematic. to support the implementation of the policy media literacy in finland portal introduces the policy and provides insights to the finnish media literacy initiatives. kavi (the finnish media education authority), a subordinate of the finnish ministry of education and culture, has a legal task to promote media education, children's media skills and the development of a safe media environment for children . kavi actively participates in international collaboration and represents finland in the european commission media literacy expert group and safer internet for children expert group, for example. since 2012 kavi has organised annually media education forum, event that supports networking between the different actors and the development of the sector. kavi's media literacy school is a portal for educators with information and exercises that support media education activities in schools, libraries, youth centres, etc. all resources are free of charge, and many of them are available in english. kavi also implements and actively develops film education as part of the promotion of audiovisual culture. every year in february finland celebrates media literacy week . the aim of the initiative is to advance the media literacy skills, as well as to support professional educators, guardians and other adults in their important media educational tasks. in 2019, the week was organized as a series of 30 different materials and campaigns created together by 55 partner organisations from all sectors of society. media literacy week is part of the finnish safer internet centre -project coordinated by kavi and co-funded by the european commission. another major awareness raising campaign part of the project is finnish game week. game week comprises of hundreds of individual events organized around finland. in the finnish education system media literacy and media education is integrated to the following national core curricula: early childhood education and care, pre-primary education, basic education, basic education for adults, general upper secondary education, extended and general syllabus for the basic art education (studies in media arts). curricula are mandatory for the education providers. university of lapland provides international master degree studies in media education. in two-year english-taught master's degree programme the students will build expertise in three major themes: media in teaching and learning, media in society and media and psychosocial well-being. univeristy of lapland's media education hub (meh) is a unit for education and research with fifteen years of experience of carrying out interdisciplinary research projects and developing educational models for different contexts. the hub also coordinates for example the ikaihme -project (2018-2020) funded by the ministry of education and culture that aims to develop teacher education of adult educators - targeting older people's media education. established in 2017, the european centre of excellence for countering hybrid threats is an international hub, which unites its member states (24 countries as of november 2019) , the eu and nato institutions to assist them in better understanding and defending against hybrid threats. it includes the work on resilience against disinformation as a part of wider concept of hybrid threats. in finland there are many active civil society organizations promoting media literacy. a large proportion of the active organisations in media education in finland are members of the finnish society on media education. the finnish society on media education raises awareness and spreads information and best practices of media literacy; organises events; publishes materials; implements development projects; contributes to the public debate and provides opportunities to share media education experiences online and offline nationwide. the society publishes a newsletter with information on the latest projects, events and research in finland. a long-term promoter of media education among companies in the media sector is yle, the finnish public service media company, which actively produces media education materials on its websites. as an example, the digitreenit (digital training) website offers citizens a wide range of freely available materials for independent learning, and the yle uutisluokka (yle news class) media education activities are targeted at adolescents between 11 and 18 years of age.

args.summary: This UNESCO webpage describes Finland's national media education policy ("Media Literacy in Finland"), published by the Ministry of Education and Culture in 2019, updating a 2013 policy. The policy aims to make media education in Finland comprehensive, high-quality, and systematic. Key implementing body is KAVI (the Finnish Media Education Authority), which promotes media education, children's media skills, and safe media environments. KAVI organizes the annual Media Education Forum (since 2012) and Media Literacy Week (each February), and runs a free media literacy school portal for educators. Media literacy is integrated into national core curricula from early childhood through upper secondary education. The University of Lapland offers an international master's degree in media education and runs the Media Education Hub (MEH). Other notable initiatives include the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats (established 2017), the Finnish Society on Media Education (a civil society network), YLE's public media education materials (including Digitreenit and Yle Uutisluokka), and the Finnish Game Week campaign. The policy is part of the 2005 UNESCO Convention on the Protection and Promotion of the Diversity of Cultural Expressions and aligns with SDGs 4, 8, 16, and 17.

# Social-media age verification needs Europe to work in step, Norway’s Tung says

By **[Sara Brandstätter](#)**

October 29, 2025, 09:06 GMT | Comment

Norway is moving ahead swiftly in the debate over children's use of social media as it develops a plan for a strict minimum age of 15, the country's digital minister has said. Australia is the poster child for banning social media, but Norway is now a European pioneer. Karianne Oldernes Tung spoke to MLex about the thinking behind the proposal, the challenges of age-verification measures that will be needed, and why Europe must coordinate its approach.

Norway's plans to introduce a minimum age limit for social media by next summer attracted headlines in 2024. But with a draft law in the works and results of public feedback now being analyzed, much work will be needed to make it feasible.   
  
Key factors will be the creation of a robust age-verification system and stronger cooperation across Europe, the country's minister of digitalization and public governance told MLex.  
  
In an exclusive interview, Karianne Oldernes Tung discussed Norway's active role in the growing debate over social media use among children, but stressed a need for collective action.   
  
“It is important that all European countries are engaged in developing age-verification systems, so that we can implement this across the continent. Norway is a small country, so we can’t necessarily do this alone,” Tung said.  
  
Although Norway isn’t a member of the EU, it is part of the European Economic Area, which means it adopts most EU laws linked to the single market. The country already applies the General Data Protection Regulation and is now implementing the EU’s Digital Services Act, the bloc's high-profile content-moderation law.  
  
“We see that it’s not enough,” Tung said, adding that the GDPR already sets a minimum age limit of 13, but that the rule isn’t adequately enforced, as children as young as nine are on social media.  
  
That’s why Norway's government, led by the center-left Labour Party, has proposed a new law, besides implementing the DSA and the existing GDPR, with an absolute age limit for social media and a clear definition of what constitutes social media.   
  
It also wants to raise the GDPR's minimum age for processing of children's data from 13 years old to 15 — something that each EU member state can decide on its own.   
  
The government is currently analyzing feedback from a public consultation that drew more than 8,000 submissions. "People in Norway are very engaged in this," Tung said.  
  
Protecting children from online harms is climbing the political agenda around the world. Australia is in the vanguard — a social media ban for under-16s will take effect there on Dec. 10 — while EU countries such as France, Denmark and Greece are also developing national laws.   
  
At the same time, the EU is facing growing pressure to deliver a bloc-wide solution (see [here](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/articles/2391751/social-media-platforms-could-face-age-restrictions-in-eu-von-der-leyen-says) and [here](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/articles/2403349/macron-renews-multi-nation-push-for-social-media-age-limits)). Most recently, influential lawmaker Christel Schaldemose highlighted a [European Parliament](/mlex/search?q=&per_page=20&facet_added=agency:%22European%20Parliament%22) report calling for an EU-wide age limit of 16,unless a parent or guardian authorizes the use (see [here](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/articles/2399630/eu-wide-social-media-age-limit-is-a-must-lawmaker-schaldemose-says)).  
— EU-wide or national —  
  
Tung attended a meeting of digital ministers in Denmark earlier this month, where she raised Norway's ambitions with counterparts in the EU (see [here](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/articles/2398498/eu-countries-want-stronger-protections-for-minors-online-differ-on-approach)).   
  
In her view, developing an effective age-verification system is the key area for international cooperation. Verifying a user’s age can be done in several ways, including ID checks, facial age estimation, or behavior-based assessment tools that infer age from online activity patterns. But some experts say the technology for that isn’t yet ready.   
  
“If we're not able to agree on setting the [minimum] at 15, for instance, we should at least agree on having an age-verification system that enables everyone to set their own national limits,” Tung said, adding that tech companies “have the smartest brains on board, they have the most money on board.”   
  
The Norwegian minister said she's optimistic about finding a common European pathway, pointing to earlier success in reaching agreement on the DSA. “I think we're on the path to agree on verification systems, and then hopefully we also will agree on setting a common age or minimum age limit as well.”  
  
For Norway, setting the age limit at 15 has been both a political and evidence-based decision, Tung said. The choice aligns with other national legal thresholds, such as the age of criminal responsibility, the right to choose one’s education, join a religious community and enter into a work contract.  
  
— Who is included? —  
  
When it comes to regulating social media, there is a need to define which platforms and apps are considered social media, and which aren’t.  
  
That’s why the Norwegian government wants to define social media in the proposed law: “It's hard work,” Tung said, stressing that the definition would need to be futureproofed to work in an area of constant developments.  
  
“We might have to change the definition. But I really believe in starting this hard work protecting children better, and then we have to make sure that we are making it more and more perfect the more we know about it.”   
  
The definition in the draft law, still open to change after a public consultation currently under way, says that social media services are defined “as information society services which let users create a profile and connect with other user profiles.” Moreover, these services must store and disseminate content uploaded by users without editorial oversight to the public.   
  
There will also be specific exemptions in the law, for example for computer games, platforms that are used for buying and selling services or products, or platforms with closed groups being used for educational purposes or spare time. “In Norway, for instance, we have a very popular app called Spond,” which will be exempted, Tung said. Spond is mostly used to coordinate sports activities.  
  
Defining which platforms fall within the scope of a ban has proved to be universally challenging. In Australia, for instance, regulators have faced similar difficulties, with platforms such as [YouTube](/mlex/search?q=&per_page=20&facet_added=company:%22YouTube%20Inc.%22) and [Snapchat](/mlex/search?q=&per_page=20&facet_added=company:%22Snap%20Inc.%22) arguing that they should be excluded from the proposed restrictions (see [here](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/articles/2335869/google-pushed-for-youtube-exemption-under-social-media-ban-law-in-australia) and [here](https://www.mlex.com/mlex/articles/2404426/snapchat-says-australia-s-online-safety-watchdog-misclassified-it-as-social-media)).  
  
— Open questions —  
  
Tung said concerns voiced by child safety groups — that a social-media ban could adversely affect marginalized groups by limiting channels for connection — resonate with her. To deal with the “digital divide within Europe and Norway,” she said, it’s important to work together, such as by sharing common solutions.  
  
"Social media is a positive thing ... because it enables children, adults, citizens to connect." But governments must strike a balance between protecting children and citizens and recognizing the democratic and inclusive value that social media can offer, Tung said.    
  
Another big concern is around age verification and how data protection can be safeguarded. Any system capable of verifying users’ ages would likely involve processing sensitive personal or biometric information, raising questions about privacy, transparency and oversight.  
  
Tung said this issue is at the top of her list. “It has to be our number-one job to protect privacy, human rights, transparency and non-discrimination,” while coming up with age-verification models to enforce the social-media ban, she said.

- The government is analyzing feedback from a public consultation that received over 8,000 submissions.
- A key challenge is developing a robust age-verification system, and Tung emphasizes the need for European coordination: "Norway is a small country, so we can’t necessarily do this alone."
- Norway wants to raise the GDPR's minimum age for processing children's data from 13 to 15, which each EU member state can decide individually.

- Privacy and data protection in age-verification systems is a top concern, with Tung stating it must be "our number-one job to protect privacy, human rights, transparency and non-discrimination."
- Australia's social media ban for under-16s (effective Dec. 10, 2025) is noted as a global precedent, and EU countries like France, Denmark, Greece, and the European Parliament are also pushing for age limits.

On November 7, 2025, the government of Denmark announced a plan to ban social media for children under the age of 15, as part of a 14-point agreement to better protect minors online. # Denmark proposes banning social media for kids under 15

![](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/c5327d73-f685-4dce-a068-8057c8da7539/phone-as-er-251008_1759952270870_hpMain_16x9.jpg?w=992)

The country of Denmark is proposing a [social media ban](https://www.goodmorningamerica.com/family/story/florida-house-representatives-approves-bill-ban-social-media-106672586) for children under the age of 15.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday at the [opening of the Folketing](https://www.ft.dk/aktuelt/webtv/video/20251/salen/1.aspx?as=1), the Danish parliament, saying social media platforms are "stealing our children's childhood."

"The reality is that we have let a monster loose. Never before have so many children and young people suffered from anxiety and depression," Frederiksen said in part, as [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2025/10/08/tech/denmark-children-social-media-ban-scli-intl) reported.

![PHOTO: A child looks a phone screen in this undated stock photo. ](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/c5327d73-f685-4dce-a068-8057c8da7539/phone-as-er-251008_1759952270870_hpMain.jpg)

Frederiksen called out the negative impacts of [cellphones](https://www.goodmorningamerica.com/family/story/nyc-expands-school-cellphone-ban-include-smartwatches-tablets-124027667) and social media on children, including on their mental health; adverse impacts on reading skills and concentration; and online safety concerns.

The Danish proposal would allow for an exception, giving parents the choice to approve social media use for their kids starting at the age of 13, if they wish.

![](https://i.abcnewsfe.com/a/02f13397-7409-4616-bc8d-038049eb1d12/denmark-rt-er-251008_1759952438514_hpEmbed_3x2.jpg)

The proposal follows a successful vote by Danish lawmakers in September to ban cellphones from elementary schools and after-school programs in the Scandinavian country, according to CNN.

Denmark is not the only country to ban social media or propose such restrictions.

[Australia banned social media accounts](https://www.goodmorningamerica.com/video/116316943) for children under 16 in November 2024, becoming the first country in the world to do so.

The law gave platforms such as Facebook, Snapchat and TikTok one year to abide by the law or be subjected to fines of up to $33 million.

# Denmark to ban social media for children under 15

[Dmytro Hubenko](/en/dmytro-hubenko/person-38682181) with AP, Reuters

November 7, 2025

Most parties in the Danish parliament said they support implementing a 15-year-old minimum age requirement for social media. It is not yet known which social media platforms will be affected.

https://p.dw.com/p/53I5i

According to the Danish government, the platforms most used by children in Denmark include Snapchat, YouTube, Instagram, and TikTokImage: Yui Mok/dpa/picture alliance

Advertisement

The [Danish](/en/denmark/t-19249216) government has reached an agreement to implement a minimum age requirement of 15 years old on certain social media platforms, it announced on Friday.

The move follows Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen's call for [restrictions on children's use of social media](/en/phone-free-childhood-is-growing-up-without-social-media-still-possible/a-74484730) in her opening speech to Parliament last month, due to concerns over youth mental health. A majority of parties in parliament said they would support the plan.

"As one of the first countries in the EU, Denmark is now taking a groundbreaking step towards introducing age limits on social media," said the country's digitalization ministry in a statement. "This is done to protect children and young people in the digital world."

"As a starting point, children under the age of 15 should not have access to platforms that may expose them to harmful content or harmful features," the statement said.

## Behind the growing movement for a phone-free childhood

The ministry did not specify which social media platforms are affected or how the ban will be enforced.

However, exceptions can be made if parents believe their child should have access to social media at an earlier age. According to the statement, parents will have the opportunity to consent to their children's access, if their children are as young as 13.

## What other activities are planned?

The agreement also envisages allocating 160 million Danish kroner (€21.4 million; $24.8 million) to 14 initiatives aimed at strengthening the protection of children and young people online and creating a better framework for their digital lives.

As part of the agreement, EU's [Digital Services Act](/en/digital-services-act-dsa/t-73446203) supervision will be strengthened, and funds will be allocated to support the development of alternative social media platforms. Additionally, extra efforts will be made to combat illegal marketing by influencers, the statement mentioned.

A coalition of lawmakers "are making it clear that children should not be left alone in a digital world where harmful content and commercial interests are too much a part of shaping their everyday lives and childhoods," the ministry said.

"Children and young people have their sleep disrupted, lose their peace and concentration, and experience increasing pressure from digital relationships where adults are not always present," it said. "This is a development that no parent, teacher or educator can stop alone."

## How harmful is social media for children?

"Denmark is now leading the way in Europe with a national age limit for social media and a concerted effort to strengthen the digital wellbeing of children and young people," Digitalization Minister Caroline Stage said.

"We are taking a necessary stand against a development where large tech platforms have had free rein in children's rooms for far too long."

## Australia leads the world in banning social media for children

This Danish plan follows [Australia's lead](/en/australia-youth-social-media-ban-mental-health-will-it-work/a-73230182). In December, Australia is set to become the first country [to ban social media for children](/en/australia-launches-bill-banning-social-media-for-under-16s/a-70838309), setting the minimum age at 16.

In September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told a United Nations forum in New York that she was "inspired" by Australia's "common sense" decision to enact age restrictions.

The legislation subjects social media platforms to fines of up to 50 million Australian dollars (€30 million; $32.3 million) for allowing children under 16 to create accounts.

On Wednesday, [Australia](/en/australia/t-18172340) announced that it had added the message board Reddit and the livestreaming service Kick to its list of social media platforms that must prohibit children under 16 from having accounts.

These platforms will join Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, X, and YouTube in facing a world-first legal obligation to shut down accounts belonging to younger Australian children on December 10, according to Communications Minister Anika Wells.

COPENHAGEN, Nov 7 (Reuters) - Denmark will ban the use of social media for children under the age of 15, the Danish government said on Friday, although parents will be allowed to give dispensation for youngsters down to the age of 13 to access certain platforms.

The move follows Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen's call in her opening speech to parliament last month for social media restrictions for children due to concerns over youth mental health.

"The so-called social media thrive on stealing our children's time, childhood and well-being and we are putting a stop to that now," Digitalization Minister Caroline Stage Olsen said.

A majority of parties in parliament said they would back the plan ahead of a formal vote.

The platforms most used by children in Denmark include Snapchat, YouTube, Instagram and TikTok, the government said.

According to an analysis from the Danish competition and consumer authority from February this year, youngsters in the Nordic country spend on average 2 hours and 40 minutes every day on social media.

Denmark follows the likes of Australia, which last year imposed a ban on social media for children under 16.

URL: https://www.easternmirrornagaland.com/a-study-on-the-effect-of-social-media-usage-on-mental-health-among-teenagers

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Eastern Mirror Nagaland (published Oct 28, 2025) examines the effects of social media usage on the mental health of teenagers, authored by Dr. Ranjit Paul (Academic Dean, Public College). It covers both positive and negative impacts, underlying psychological mechanisms, empirical findings, and recommendations.

**Positive effects:** Social media enables communication, learning, community building, and emotional support for isolated or anxious teens. It also spreads awareness campaigns on mental health and body positivity.

**Negative effects:** Constant comparison, unrealistic lifestyle exposure, and validation-seeking lead to low self-esteem, body image issues, anxiety, and depression. Excessive screen time causes sleep deprivation, poor concentration, academic decline, loneliness, and cyberbullying risks.

**Psychological mechanisms:**
1. Social Comparison Theory (Festinger, 1954) – Teens compare themselves to curated, idealized content, leading to inadequacy and envy.
2. Dopamine reward system – Intermittent positive reinforcement (likes/comments) creates addiction-like loops, especially in developing adolescent brains.
3. Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) – Leads to compulsive checking, stress, anxiety, and sleep disturbances.
4. Online Disinhibition Effect – Anonymity encourages impulsive/aggressive behavior, increasing cyberbullying.
5. Emotional contagion – Algorithms amplify emotionally charged content, affecting emotional regulation.

**Empirical findings:**
- A 2021 JAMA Psychiatry study found teens spending 3+ hours daily on social media were twice as likely to experience anxiety/depression compared to those under 1 hour.
- A 2022 Pew Research Center report found 46% of teens felt overwhelmed by pressure to post content that gains positive attention.
- University of Pittsburgh (2020) research linked Instagram use to body dissatisfaction, especially among teenage girls.
- UK's Royal Society for Public Health (2019) ranked Instagram and Snapchat as most harmful for mental health due to poor sleep and anxiety.
- UNICEF (2022) reported nearly one in three teenagers worldwide has experienced cyberbullying.
- A 2020 Oxford Internet Institute study found moderate use (1-2 hours/day) can enhance social connectedness; active/purposeful engagement improves well-being while passive scrolling harms it.

**Recommendations:** Parents and educators should encourage open communication, screen time management, digital literacy, and offline activities. Social media companies should introduce digital well-being features, content filters, and anti-bullying measures. The key is responsible, mindful use rather than outright rejection.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 19: Screen time: impacts on education and wellbeing - Education Committee ---
URL: https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5804/cmselect/cmeduc/118/report.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Summary: Screen Time: Impacts on Education and Wellbeing

This is a House of Commons Education Committee report (Fourth Report of Session 2023–24), published 25 May 2024, investigating the impact of screen time on children's educational outcomes and wellbeing.

## Key Findings

### Scope of the Problem
- Children are owning smartphones at progressively younger ages; one in five children aged 3–4 have their own mobile phone, rising to almost all children by age 12
- Time spent online by 5–15 year olds rose from 9 hours/week (2009) to 15 hours/week (2018)
- 18% of children aged 7–16 had a probable mental health disorder in 2022 (up from 12.1% in 2017)
- Nearly 25% of children and young people use smartphones in a way consistent with behavioural addiction
- Screen time increased 52% between 2020 and 2022

### Mental Health Impacts
- Children encounter online harms including cyberbullying, racism, misogynistic abuse, pornography, and self-harm material
- 79% of children encountered violent pornography before age 18; children see pornography from as young as 7
- Sexual crimes against children online rose 400% since 2013
- 60% increase in self-generated pornographic images from 7–10 year olds
- Instagram made body image issues worse for 1 in 3 teenage girls (Meta research)
- 81% of girls aged 7–21 experienced threatening or upsetting behaviour online
- One in five children (19%) aged 10–15 experienced cyberbullying

### Educational Impacts
- Schools report smartphones disrupt learning; it can take up to 20 minutes to refocus after non-academic activity
- Children with >2 hours daily recreational screen time had worse working memory, processing speed, attention, language skills, and executive function
- Prolonged screen use linked to diminished attention capacity and heightened distractibility
- Mobile phone bans improve test scores by 6.41% (with wide compliance); low-achieving students improved by 14.23%

### Physical Health Impacts
- Concerns about sedentary lifestyle, digital eye strain, myopia epidemic
- Excessive screen time linked to hand/wrist weakness, grip strength issues, sleep deprivation
- Late bedtimes (linked to social media use) predict poorer academic and emotional outcomes

### Vulnerable Children
- Children in care, care leavers, young carers, children in poverty, and those with additional needs are more susceptible to online harms
- 79% of young women experienced online harm in 2021
- Online platforms described as "foundation of county lines recruitment" for criminal exploitation

## Key Recommendations

### Mobile Phone Bans in Schools
- The Government issued non-statutory guidance on 19 February 2024 banning mobile phones throughout the school day
- **The Committee recommends formal monitoring** of implementation and effects, not just informal monitoring
- If non-statutory ban proves ineffective, next Government must introduce statutory ban
- Guidance must not prevent parents contacting children during commute; should not insist phones left at home
- Government should set out approximate costs of implementation approaches (e.g., secure storage)

### Support for Parents
- **Next Government should produce cross-departmental guidance** for parents on managing screen time
- Guidance should focus on known harms (e.g., no screens after bedtime, incorporating physical activity)
- Advice for parents of babies/young children should emphasize face-to-face interaction

### Digital Literacy & Educational Apps
- Over half a million apps claim to be educational but no quality standards exist
- **Next Government should commission guidance** for parents/schools on educational apps within a year
- Should support a kitemarking scheme for educational resources
- Should engage tech companies to introduce standards for educational labels

### Overall Conclusion
The Committee found that harms of screen time significantly outweigh benefits for young children, while limited, educational use can benefit older children. Screen time should be minimal for younger children and better balanced with face-to-face socialization and physical activity for older ones.
</summary>

This webpage from Klippa (a document processing and identity verification company) is a blog post titled "Age Assurance for Online Platforms: Protecting Sellers, Buyers & Youth," published in 2026. It discusses the global shift from voluntary safety measures to mandatory compliance regarding age assurance on digital platforms.

**Key Context:** By 2026, teenagers aged 15-18 spend roughly 7.5 hours/day on screens, and governments worldwide have moved from suggesting safety measures to mandating them with heavy penalties. The rise of AI-generated deepfakes and automated grooming bots has amplified risks, and countries like Australia implemented landmark bans on social media for children under 16.

**Types of Age Assurance Methods:**
- **Age Estimation (Soft):** AI-driven facial analysis (video selfie, ±1.5-year margin) and behavioral analysis algorithms.
- **Age Verification (Hard):** NFC chip scans of passports/IDs, EU Digital Identity Wallet ("Mini-Wallet") with Zero-Knowledge Age Tokens, and Open Banking (bank confirms age without revealing financial data).
- **Device & OS-Based Signals:** iOS/Android provide verified age signals to websites, making verification invisible to users.

**Benefits:**
- **For Sellers:** Legal "Safe Harbor" and liability shield. Fines under EU's DSA and UK's Online Safety Act can reach 6-10% of global annual turnover. Certified tools meeting Ofcom guidelines provide legal protection.
- **For Buyers:** Privacy-first experience via Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP) and "Verify Once, Use Everywhere" tokens. Users are 40% more likely to engage with verified accounts.

**Overview of the Online Safety Act 2023**

The Online Safety Act 2023 received Royal Assent on 26 October 2023 and is being implemented by Ofcom in three phases, with full implementation expected by 2026. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) published a draft statement of strategic priorities for Ofcom in November 2024, focusing on safety by design, transparency, agile regulation, inclusivity, and technology/innovation.

**Key Provisions**

- **Illegal content:** All platforms must implement measures to reduce risk of illegal activity and remove illegal content. Priority offences include child sexual abuse, terrorism, fraud, extreme sexual violence, intimate image abuse, promoting suicide, and selling illegal drugs/weapons.
- **Protecting children:** Platforms must remove illegal content quickly, prevent children from accessing harmful/age-inappropriate content (including pornography, suicide/self-harm content, eating disorder content, bullying), enforce age limits with age-checking measures, publish risk assessments, and provide clear reporting mechanisms.
- **Protecting adults:** A "triple shield" approach: (1) remove illegal content, (2) enforce platform terms and conditions, (3) allow users to filter unwanted content.
- **Enforcement:** Companies can be fined up to £18 million or 10% of global revenue (whichever is greater) for non-compliance.

**Implementation Timeline**

- **16 December 2024:** Ofcom's draft illegal content codes of practice were laid before Parliament. Providers have three months to complete illegal content risk assessments. Once codes come into force, statutory safety duties begin and Ofcom can enforce compliance.
- **16 January 2025:** Ofcom published guidance on "highly effective age assurance" methods (open banking, photo ID matching, facial age estimation, etc.) and confirmed that self-declaration of age is not sufficient. Services must complete children's access assessments by 16 April 2025.
- **By July 2025:** Services allowing pornography must have age checks in place; services likely accessed by children must conduct children's risk assessments.
- **Spring 2025:** Ofcom to consult on additional measures including automated detection tools.

**Threshold Conditions for Categorisation**

Draft regulations (laid 16 December 2024) set thresholds for service categorisation:
- **Category 1:** Services with >34M UK users AND content recommender system, OR >7M UK users with recommender system AND content forwarding/sharing functionality.
- **Category 2A:** Search services with >7M UK users (excluding vertical search engines).
- **Category 2B:** User-to-user services with >3M UK users AND direct messaging functionality.

Secretary of State Peter Kyle chose not to include "small but risky" services in threshold conditions, stating the decision was evidence-based, but welcomed Ofcom's dedicated "small but risky" supervision taskforce.

**Criticism of the Act**

- **Online Safety Act Network:** Criticised Ofcom's failure to deliver "safe by design" requirements, omission of livestreaming risk measures, and slow pace of change. Argued threshold conditions allow small risky platforms to avoid stringent regulation.
- **Internet Watch Foundation (IWF):** In January 2025, IWF Chair Catherine Brown urged the Prime Minister to strengthen regulation, noting that 291,270 child sexual abuse webpages were removed in 2024 (a 5% increase). Criticised the "technically feasible" loophole and the act's failure to mandate moderation of private communications.
- **Molly Russell Foundation:** Ian Russell called Ofcom's implementation a "disaster," arguing the regulatory model is structurally weak and failing to address preventable harms. Called for strengthened primary legislation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Effects of Social Media Use on Youth and Adolescent Mental Health: A Scoping Review of Reviews ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12108867

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This scoping review of reviews, published in Behavioral Sciences (2025), examines the effects of social media use on youth and adolescent mental health. The authors—Agyapong-Opoku, Agyapong-Opoku, and Greenshaw from the University of Alberta—analyzed 43 review articles (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, narrative reviews, umbrella reviews) published between July 2020 and July 2024, drawn from PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Scopus.

**Key Findings:**

- **Negative Effects:** The majority of studies linked social media use to adverse mental health outcomes, particularly depression (13 studies) and anxiety (7 studies). Associations were also found with suicidal ideation/self-harm (6 studies), body dissatisfaction/eating disorders (5 studies), and ADHD. Problematic/passive social media use was most strongly associated with negative effects, with a "dose-response" relationship noted between time spent on social media and depression/anxiety symptoms.

- **Active vs. Passive Use:** Passive consumption (scrolling, viewing content, appearance-based activities) was associated with negative outcomes, while active use (one-to-one communication, self-disclosure in mutual friendships) was largely associated with increased wellbeing. The review emphasizes that social media itself does not inherently pose a threat—it is problematic use patterns that are harmful.

- **COVID-19 Context:** During the pandemic, social media's impact was mixed. Negative effects included increased anxiety and depression, but positive effects included humorous content and positive exchanges that alleviated loneliness and stress.

- **Positive Effects:** Social media can provide social support, reduce isolation, foster community, enhance empathy, and provide access to mental health resources. Adolescents who sought and received social support via social media reported improved depressive symptoms.

- **Null Effects:** Some studies found no significant relationship between social media use and mental health.

**Moderating Factors:** The relationship is highly individualistic and context-specific, influenced by patterns of usage, gender (girls more affected by passive use; effects of social media on self-harm greatest among girls), and the type of engagement.

**Implications:** The authors recommend more longitudinal studies, enhanced digital literacy education, parental involvement, collaboration between social media companies and mental health professionals, and the development of features that foster healthy interactions. The review notes that in November 2024, Australia banned social media for individuals under 16, underscoring the importance of clear evidence in this domain.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The nature of social media's impact on adolescent mental health is highly individualistic and influenced by moderating factors, "The nature of social media's impact on adolescent mental health is highly individualistic and influenced by moderating factors." "The majority of studies linked social media use to adverse mental health outcomes, particularly depression and anxiety." "Social media use was not significantly associated with self-harm or depression among boys." "The bottom line from this review of reviews is that social media exposure may have positive or negative effects, but context is important, and we do not have a clear understanding of determinants of the net impact of social media on youth and adolescent mental health." "For each hour of increase in social media use among adolescents, there was a 13% increased risk of depression, an association which was more robust for adolescent females than males."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The Relationship Between Social Media Use, and Mental Health Disorders in Adolescents and Young Adults: A Scoping Review - Lauren Corke, Kateryna Maksyutynska, Jennifer M. Jones, Tony P. George, 2025 ---
URL: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10401237251344098

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scoping review published in Volume 36, Issue 3 of a journal, examining the relationship between social media use and mental health disorders in adolescents and young adults (AYAs) during the COVID-19 pandemic. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in OVID Medline, Embase, and PsychInfo (2020-2023), yielding 16 studies meeting inclusion criteria (N=150,810 participants, ages 12-40). The primary finding was that social media use was positively associated with severity of depression and anxiety among AYAs. Key mediating factors identified included: online discrimination, self-comparison, reliance on social media for social approval, and cyberbullying, all of which were associated with poorer mental health outcomes. Eight of fourteen studies found positive associations between duration/frequency of social media use and depression. Studies also found that participants spent 2-4 hours daily on social media, with 98.3% of 18-29-year-olds using Instagram at least once daily. Several studies examined factors beyond time spent, including emotional investment, social comparison, self-presentation, cyberbullying, and online racial discrimination—all demonstrating detrimental impacts on mental health. Two studies (Charmaraman et al., 2022; Sewall et al., 2022) did not find significant results. The review notes that most studies were cross-sectional (limiting causal conclusions), with 5 longitudinal studies included. Quality assessment using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale found 14 studies to be good or very good quality. The authors conclude that social media use during the COVID-19 pandemic may have negatively impacted mental health outcomes in AYAs, and that further research is needed to understand mechanisms and develop interventions.
</summary>
