## Research Article: "Adolescent Emotional Well-Being and Social Media Addiction: The COVID-19 Pandemic's Influence on Mental Health"

**Authors:** Andreas P. Mulder, Kristine T. Kingsley, PsyD, ABPP, Diego Fernando Rivera Camacho, PhD, Juan Arango Lasprilla, PhD

### Background & Objectives
The study investigates how COVID-19 lockdowns impacted patterns of social media addiction (SMA) in adolescents before, during, and after the pandemic. Objectives included evaluating post-pandemic mental health status, analyzing SMA development across these three time periods, and identifying correlations between demographic factors and mental health/SMA levels.

### Methodology
- **Survey:** Administered via Google Forms through Amazon MTurk
- **Participants:** N=850 individuals aged 10-24 (WHO definition of adolescence)
- **Instruments:** Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale (BSMAS), PHQ-9 (depression), GAD-7 (anxiety), DASS-21 (stress), and Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL)
- **Analysis:** ANOVA, Linear Mixed Effects models, and linear regression for predictive variables

### Key Demographic Findings
- 83.1% of participants were aged 19+
- 53.5% female, 45.2% male, 1.5% non-binary
- 60.4% enrolled in college/university; 82.3% from the United States
- 74.9% Caucasian; 51.6% from double-parent households

### Smartphone Usage Patterns
- 47% used phones several times daily; 27% almost constantly
- Social media was the most common phone use (38.4%)
- 38.1% spent 2-4 hours daily on phones; 49.6% primarily used phones from 6pm-12am
- 53.5% had experienced cyberbullying; 46.3% believed social media had a positive impact on their mental health

### Longitudinal Analysis of Social Media Addiction
- **Significant increase** in BSMAS scores during vs. before the pandemic (p<0.001)
- **No significant change** between during-pandemic and post-pandemic periods (p=0.5481)
- Contrary to hypothesis, SMA levels did not decrease after lockdown ended

### Mental Health Results
- Most participants reported low levels of depression, anxiety, and stress
- PHQ-9, GAD-7, and DASS-21 distributions were slightly right-skewed (lower scores)
- PedsQL scores indicated generally high quality of life
- **GAD-7 results:** Minimal anxiety (25%), Mild (29%), Moderate (35%), Severe (11%)

### Predictive Factors

**For Higher Social Media Addiction (BSMAS):**
- Attending college/university
- Primary smartphone use for entertainment or social media
- History of cyberbullying
- Perceiving social media as having a positive impact (cognitive dissonance noted)
- Age 13-15 and 19+ showed negative association

**For Higher Depression (PHQ-9):**
- Primary smartphone use for entertainment/social media
- History of cyberbullying (strongest predictor, t=7.416)
- Females showed higher scores than males/non-binary
- Mid-range GPA (3.0-3.5) and frequent smartphone use were associated with lower depression

**For Higher Anxiety (GAD-7) and Stress (DASS-21):**
- Primary smartphone use for entertainment
- Primary smartphone use for social media
- History of cyberbullying (strongest predictor for both)

**For Quality of Life (PedsQL):**
- Older adolescents (16+) reported higher quality of life than younger teens
- Age 13-15 showed negative association with quality of life

### Key Conclusions
1. SMA levels increased significantly during the pandemic and did not decrease post-pandemic
2. Despite sustained SMA levels, adolescent mental health showed improvement post-pandemic
3. Cyberbullying was the most consistent predictor of negative outcomes across all questionnaires
4. The study found cognitive dissonance: those most addicted to social media perceived it as having a positive impact
5. Using smartphones for entertainment/social media predicted both higher depression and higher SMA

### Limitations
- PHQ-9 was modified (self-harm question omitted)
- Only stress-related DASS-21 questions were included
- Recall bias possible for BSMAS (participants recalled behaviors from 2+ years prior)
- Potential selection bias due to access barriers for lower-income households

- **Most common weekly threat**: Misinformation (44.2%)

- **Protective factors**: Emotional intelligence and family support were associated with encountering social media threats less frequently

  - Anxiety symptoms

- Fixed effects regression models applied
- Nine threats measured: cyberbullying, sexual harassment, racism, unauthorized distribution of sensitive material, phishing attempts, misinformation, sale/distribution of drugs, harmful social media challenges, content causing appearance pressures

1. **No significant longitudinal association**: In adjusted analysis, there was a non-significant trend showing more time spent on social media was related to poorer mental health 2 years later (β=.21, 95% CI −0.43 to 0.84; P=.52).

4. **Significant predictors** of mental health at ages 14-15: baseline mental health, year of survey participation, and ethnicity.

URL: https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2026/06/growing-up-in-the-social-media-age_be0c75c6/a1132839-en.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This OECD Digital Economy Paper (No. 385, published 2026) examines the impacts of social media use on young people, focusing on 15-year-olds using PISA 2022 data. Key findings include:

**Social Media Usage:** On average across the OECD, 15-year-olds spend almost 35 hours per week on social media, exceeding time spent on homework and school lessons. About 95% browse social media daily and 88% communicate/share content. Girls spend more time (37.2 hours/week) than boys (31.8 hours). Usage varies from under 26 hours in Japan to over 45 hours in Chile.

**Academic Performance:** A "Goldilocks hypothesis" is observed — moderate social media use (under 3 hours/day) is associated with higher test scores, while excessive use correlates with declining academic performance. Mathematics performance declines steadily beyond 3 hours/day. Disadvantaged students spend more time on social media but the performance decline associated with heavy use is more pronounced for advantaged students (37-point drop at 35 hours/week vs. 19-point drop for disadvantaged).

**Creative Thinking:** Moderate browsing (1-3 hours/day) is associated with better creative thinking scores. However, more than 1 hour/day of active communication/sharing content is linked to declining creative thinking scores.

**Social Connection:** Social media complements rather than substitutes in-person interaction. Students who see friends daily after school spend close to 40 hours/week on social media vs. 30 hours for those who rarely meet friends. However, students who feel lonely at school use more social media.

**Policy Approaches:** Several countries restrict mobile phones in schools, though enforcement is challenging — 29% of students in schools with bans still use phones several times daily. Some countries (e.g., Australia) have enacted minimum age laws for social media accounts. The paper emphasizes that policy should balance opportunities with risks while safeguarding freedom of expression, privacy, innovation, and fair competition.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Summary: Screen Time: Impacts on Education and Wellbeing

This is a House of Commons Education Committee report (Fourth Report of Session 2023–24), published 25 May 2024, investigating the impact of screen time on children's educational outcomes and wellbeing.

## Key Findings

### Scope of the Problem
- Children are owning smartphones at progressively younger ages; one in five children aged 3–4 have their own mobile phone, rising to almost all children by age 12
- Time spent online by 5–15 year olds rose from 9 hours/week (2009) to 15 hours/week (2018)
- 18% of children aged 7–16 had a probable mental health disorder in 2022 (up from 12.1% in 2017)
- Nearly 25% of children and young people use smartphones in a way consistent with behavioural addiction
- Screen time increased 52% between 2020 and 2022

### Mental Health Impacts
- Children encounter online harms including cyberbullying, racism, misogynistic abuse, pornography, and self-harm material
- 79% of children encountered violent pornography before age 18; children see pornography from as young as 7
- Sexual crimes against children online rose 400% since 2013
- 60% increase in self-generated pornographic images from 7–10 year olds
- Instagram made body image issues worse for 1 in 3 teenage girls (Meta research)
- 81% of girls aged 7–21 experienced threatening or upsetting behaviour online
- One in five children (19%) aged 10–15 experienced cyberbullying

### Educational Impacts
- Schools report smartphones disrupt learning; it can take up to 20 minutes to refocus after non-academic activity
- Children with >2 hours daily recreational screen time had worse working memory, processing speed, attention, language skills, and executive function
- Prolonged screen use linked to diminished attention capacity and heightened distractibility
- Mobile phone bans improve test scores by 6.41% (with wide compliance); low-achieving students improved by 14.23%

### Physical Health Impacts
- Concerns about sedentary lifestyle, digital eye strain, myopia epidemic
- Excessive screen time linked to hand/wrist weakness, grip strength issues, sleep deprivation
- Late bedtimes (linked to social media use) predict poorer academic and emotional outcomes

### Vulnerable Children
- Children in care, care leavers, young carers, children in poverty, and those with additional needs are more susceptible to online harms
- 79% of young women experienced online harm in 2021
- Online platforms described as "foundation of county lines recruitment" for criminal exploitation

## Key Recommendations

### Mobile Phone Bans in Schools
- The Government issued non-statutory guidance on 19 February 2024 banning mobile phones throughout the school day
- **The Committee recommends formal monitoring** of implementation and effects, not just informal monitoring
- If non-statutory ban proves ineffective, next Government must introduce statutory ban
- Guidance must not prevent parents contacting children during commute; should not insist phones left at home
- Government should set out approximate costs of implementation approaches (e.g., secure storage)

### Support for Parents
- **Next Government should produce cross-departmental guidance** for parents on managing screen time
- Guidance should focus on known harms (e.g., no screens after bedtime, incorporating physical activity)
- Advice for parents of babies/young children should emphasize face-to-face interaction

### Digital Literacy & Educational Apps
- Over half a million apps claim to be educational but no quality standards exist
- **Next Government should commission guidance** for parents/schools on educational apps within a year
- Should support a kitemarking scheme for educational resources
- Should engage tech companies to introduce standards for educational labels

### Overall Conclusion
The Committee found that harms of screen time significantly outweigh benefits for young children, while limited, educational use can benefit older children. Screen time should be minimal for younger children and better balanced with face-to-face socialization and physical activity for older ones.
</summary>

This policy brief from the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC), published in 2025, examines the need for a common definition of cyberbullying to support the forthcoming EU Cyberbullying Action Plan (planned for 2026).

# Romanian Children Facing Europe's Highest Cyberbullying Rates

## Key Findings
Romania has recorded among the highest cyberbullying rates in Europe. As early as 2018, over 37% of Romanian adolescents reported being cyberbullied—the highest rate among seven European countries compared, well above Greece (27%) and Spain (13%). More recent national surveys (2021-2023) confirm online harassment remains widespread, with victims reporting anxiety, school withdrawal, and difficulty maintaining friendships.

## Prevalence and Demographics
- In 2021, nearly half of Romanian students said they had been bullied, and over 80% witnessed classmates experiencing it.
- In 2023, the national child helpline received 1,167 calls related to cyberbullying.
- Younger teenagers (early-to-mid adolescence) are most vulnerable; those over 16 had nearly 50% lower odds of victimization.
- Children spending more than 2 hours daily on social media faced an 83% greater chance of being bullied online.

## Digital Spaces and Platforms
Three in four victims were bullied on Facebook, two in five on Instagram, and nearly one in five through video games. Girls were more often targeted on Facebook and Instagram, while boys experienced more bullying on YouTube and gaming platforms.

## Inadequate Legal Framework
Romania remains one of the few EU countries where cyberbullying is not defined as a general criminal offence. It is addressed only indirectly through:
- Law No. 106/2020 (amending domestic violence legislation to include "cyber violence")
- National Education Law No. 1/2011 (prohibiting actions endangering children's health)
- A 2020 regulation defining cyberbullying in school contexts

In contrast, Ireland (Coco's Law), France, Italy (Law No. 71/2017), Austria, and Slovakia have enacted direct and comprehensive cyberbullying legislation.

## Recent Policy Developments (2025)
- June 2025: Proposed bill to set digital age of consent at 16, requiring parental approval for social media accounts.
- July 2025: National Cyber Security Directorate (DNSC) adopted Regulation on social media platforms, focusing on cybersecurity but mentioning cyberbullying only indirectly.

## Consequences
Strong links exist between cyberbullying and depression among Romanian adolescents. Factors such as loneliness, low self-esteem, and aggressive parenting are closely tied to both victimization and perpetration.

## Recommendations
The article calls for a comprehensive national strategy including: clear reporting procedures for cyberbullying, integration of media literacy into curricula, dedicated mental health services for victims, and mechanisms empowering children's voices in shaping online safety policies.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Eastern Mirror Nagaland (published Oct 28, 2025) examines the effects of social media usage on the mental health of teenagers, authored by Dr. Ranjit Paul (Academic Dean, Public College). It covers both positive and negative impacts, underlying psychological mechanisms, empirical findings, and recommendations.

**Positive effects:** Social media enables communication, learning, community building, and emotional support for isolated or anxious teens. It also spreads awareness campaigns on mental health and body positivity.

**Negative effects:** Constant comparison, unrealistic lifestyle exposure, and validation-seeking lead to low self-esteem, body image issues, anxiety, and depression. Excessive screen time causes sleep deprivation, poor concentration, academic decline, loneliness, and cyberbullying risks.

**Psychological mechanisms:**
1. Social Comparison Theory (Festinger, 1954) – Teens compare themselves to curated, idealized content, leading to inadequacy and envy.
2. Dopamine reward system – Intermittent positive reinforcement (likes/comments) creates addiction-like loops, especially in developing adolescent brains.
3. Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) – Leads to compulsive checking, stress, anxiety, and sleep disturbances.
4. Online Disinhibition Effect – Anonymity encourages impulsive/aggressive behavior, increasing cyberbullying.
5. Emotional contagion – Algorithms amplify emotionally charged content, affecting emotional regulation.

**Empirical findings:**
- A 2021 JAMA Psychiatry study found teens spending 3+ hours daily on social media were twice as likely to experience anxiety/depression compared to those under 1 hour.
- A 2022 Pew Research Center report found 46% of teens felt overwhelmed by pressure to post content that gains positive attention.
- University of Pittsburgh (2020) research linked Instagram use to body dissatisfaction, especially among teenage girls.
- UK's Royal Society for Public Health (2019) ranked Instagram and Snapchat as most harmful for mental health due to poor sleep and anxiety.
- UNICEF (2022) reported nearly one in three teenagers worldwide has experienced cyberbullying.
- A 2020 Oxford Internet Institute study found moderate use (1-2 hours/day) can enhance social connectedness; active/purposeful engagement improves well-being while passive scrolling harms it.

**Recommendations:** Parents and educators should encourage open communication, screen time management, digital literacy, and offline activities. Social media companies should introduce digital well-being features, content filters, and anti-bullying measures. The key is responsible, mindful use rather than outright rejection.

--- SOURCE 19: Screen time: impacts on education and wellbeing - Education Committee ---
URL: https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5804/cmselect/cmeduc/118/report.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Summary: Screen Time: Impacts on Education and Wellbeing

This is a House of Commons Education Committee report (Fourth Report of Session 2023–24), published 25 May 2024, investigating the impact of screen time on children's educational outcomes and wellbeing.

## Key Findings

### Scope of the Problem
- Children are owning smartphones at progressively younger ages; one in five children aged 3–4 have their own mobile phone, rising to almost all children by age 12
- Time spent online by 5–15 year olds rose from 9 hours/week (2009) to 15 hours/week (2018)
- 18% of children aged 7–16 had a probable mental health disorder in 2022 (up from 12.1% in 2017)
- Nearly 25% of children and young people use smartphones in a way consistent with behavioural addiction
- Screen time increased 52% between 2020 and 2022

### Mental Health Impacts
- Children encounter online harms including cyberbullying, racism, misogynistic abuse, pornography, and self-harm material
- 79% of children encountered violent pornography before age 18; children see pornography from as young as 7
- Sexual crimes against children online rose 400% since 2013
- 60% increase in self-generated pornographic images from 7–10 year olds
- Instagram made body image issues worse for 1 in 3 teenage girls (Meta research)
- 81% of girls aged 7–21 experienced threatening or upsetting behaviour online
- One in five children (19%) aged 10–15 experienced cyberbullying

### Educational Impacts
- Schools report smartphones disrupt learning; it can take up to 20 minutes to refocus after non-academic activity
- Children with >2 hours daily recreational screen time had worse working memory, processing speed, attention, language skills, and executive function
- Prolonged screen use linked to diminished attention capacity and heightened distractibility
- Mobile phone bans improve test scores by 6.41% (with wide compliance); low-achieving students improved by 14.23%

### Physical Health Impacts
- Concerns about sedentary lifestyle, digital eye strain, myopia epidemic
- Excessive screen time linked to hand/wrist weakness, grip strength issues, sleep deprivation
- Late bedtimes (linked to social media use) predict poorer academic and emotional outcomes

### Vulnerable Children
- Children in care, care leavers, young carers, children in poverty, and those with additional needs are more susceptible to online harms
- 79% of young women experienced online harm in 2021
- Online platforms described as "foundation of county lines recruitment" for criminal exploitation

## Key Recommendations

### Mobile Phone Bans in Schools
- The Government issued non-statutory guidance on 19 February 2024 banning mobile phones throughout the school day
- **The Committee recommends formal monitoring** of implementation and effects, not just informal monitoring
- If non-statutory ban proves ineffective, next Government must introduce statutory ban
- Guidance must not prevent parents contacting children during commute; should not insist phones left at home
- Government should set out approximate costs of implementation approaches (e.g., secure storage)

### Support for Parents
- **Next Government should produce cross-departmental guidance** for parents on managing screen time
- Guidance should focus on known harms (e.g., no screens after bedtime, incorporating physical activity)
- Advice for parents of babies/young children should emphasize face-to-face interaction

### Digital Literacy & Educational Apps
- Over half a million apps claim to be educational but no quality standards exist
- **Next Government should commission guidance** for parents/schools on educational apps within a year
- Should support a kitemarking scheme for educational resources
- Should engage tech companies to introduce standards for educational labels

### Overall Conclusion
The Committee found that harms of screen time significantly outweigh benefits for young children, while limited, educational use can benefit older children. Screen time should be minimal for younger children and better balanced with face-to-face socialization and physical activity for older ones.
</summary>

This is a Springer Nature academic article page for "European Youth and Digital Engagement: Attitudes, Skills, and Civic Participation," published in the Journal of Applied Youth Studies (Volume 8, pages 219–247, 2025). The article is open access and was published on March 11, 2025.

**Authors:** Eva Tsouparopoulou, Maria Symeonaki, Dimitris Parsanoglou, and Aggeliki Kazani (affiliated with Greek institutions).

**Main Topic:** The study investigates how young Europeans (aged 15–35) perceive digital communication, focusing on digital skills, digital citizenship, and civic engagement. It uses data from the European Social Survey (ESS) Round 10 (2020) across over 30 European countries, analyzing the ESS's rotating module on "Digital social contacts in work and family life."

**Key Research Areas:**
- Digital skepticism and optimism among youth
- Digital skills and their link to civic participation
- Exposure to misinformation and online political engagement
- Socio-demographic factors (education, gender, parental education, migration background, life satisfaction, Internet usage)

**Methodology:** Statistical analysis including chi-square tests, multiple regression analysis, and correspondence analysis. The study examines three key questions: whether young people possess digital skills, how they use ICTs for civic participation, and how attitudes toward ICT vary across European countries.

**Key Findings/Themes:**
- ICTs play a significant role in young people's daily lives—education, leisure, work, and civic engagement
- Digital skills do not develop spontaneously; young people need resource-intensive interventions to acquire them
- Internet use encourages political participation but also exposes youth to misinformation and fake news
- The digital divide paradigm (access, skills, economic opportunity, democratic divide) affects civic participation
- Education is a significant factor in the overall digital divide
- Social media provides platforms for civic engagement and affects political behavior both online and offline
- The study constructs a latent variable called "beneficial Internet time" (log of product of time spent online × digital skills level)

**Context:** The research builds on the DigiGen project, which examined youth online civic participation in Estonia, Greece, and the UK. The paper aims to systematically assemble indicators capturing young people's attitudes toward digital communication and examine their interconnections across European countries.

- Making use of the EU's age verification blueprint
- Drawing up implementation plans
- Cooperating with Digital Services Coordinators, the Commission, researchers, and civil society
- Ensuring compliance with cybersecurity and privacy standards through third-party scrutiny

Additionally, the Commission will create an EU Age Verification Scheme outlining governance, trust model, and requirements for entities wishing to act as issuers. --- SOURCE 12: Implementation of the Online Safety Act - Commons Library ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**Overview of the Online Safety Act 2023**

The Online Safety Act 2023 received Royal Assent on 26 October 2023 and is being implemented by Ofcom in three phases, with full implementation expected by 2026. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) published a draft statement of strategic priorities for Ofcom in November 2024, focusing on safety by design, transparency, agile regulation, inclusivity, and technology/innovation.

**Key Provisions**

- **Illegal content:** All platforms must implement measures to reduce risk of illegal activity and remove illegal content. Priority offences include child sexual abuse, terrorism, fraud, extreme sexual violence, intimate image abuse, promoting suicide, and selling illegal drugs/weapons.
- **Protecting children:** Platforms must remove illegal content quickly, prevent children from accessing harmful/age-inappropriate content (including pornography, suicide/self-harm content, eating disorder content, bullying), enforce age limits with age-checking measures, publish risk assessments, and provide clear reporting mechanisms.
- **Protecting adults:** A "triple shield" approach: (1) remove illegal content, (2) enforce platform terms and conditions, (3) allow users to filter unwanted content.
- **Enforcement:** Companies can be fined up to £18 million or 10% of global revenue (whichever is greater) for non-compliance.

**Implementation Timeline**

- **16 December 2024:** Ofcom's draft illegal content codes of practice were laid before Parliament. Providers have three months to complete illegal content risk assessments. Once codes come into force, statutory safety duties begin and Ofcom can enforce compliance.
- **16 January 2025:** Ofcom published guidance on "highly effective age assurance" methods (open banking, photo ID matching, facial age estimation, etc.) and confirmed that self-declaration of age is not sufficient. Services must complete children's access assessments by 16 April 2025.
- **By July 2025:** Services allowing pornography must have age checks in place; services likely accessed by children must conduct children's risk assessments.
- **Spring 2025:** Ofcom to consult on additional measures including automated detection tools.

**Threshold Conditions for Categorisation**

Draft regulations (laid 16 December 2024) set thresholds for service categorisation:
- **Category 1:** Services with >34M UK users AND content recommender system, OR >7M UK users with recommender system AND content forwarding/sharing functionality.
- **Category 2A:** Search services with >7M UK users (excluding vertical search engines).
- **Category 2B:** User-to-user services with >3M UK users AND direct messaging functionality.

Secretary of State Peter Kyle chose not to include "small but risky" services in threshold conditions, stating the decision was evidence-based, but welcomed Ofcom's dedicated "small but risky" supervision taskforce.

**Criticism of the Act**

- **Online Safety Act Network:** Criticised Ofcom's failure to deliver "safe by design" requirements, omission of livestreaming risk measures, and slow pace of change. Argued threshold conditions allow small risky platforms to avoid stringent regulation.
- **Internet Watch Foundation (IWF):** In January 2025, IWF Chair Catherine Brown urged the Prime Minister to strengthen regulation, noting that 291,270 child sexual abuse webpages were removed in 2024 (a 5% increase). Criticised the "technically feasible" loophole and the act's failure to mandate moderation of private communications.
- **Molly Russell Foundation:** Ian Russell called Ofcom's implementation a "disaster," arguing the regulatory model is structurally weak and failing to address preventable harms. Called for strengthened primary legislation.
</summary>

<summary>
This chapter from the World Happiness Report 2026 investigates the relationship between Problematic Social Media Use (PSMU) and adolescent wellbeing across 43 countries, and how this relationship varies by family socioeconomic status (SES). The study uses data from the Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study from 2018 and 2022, covering six regions: Anglo-Celtic, Caucasus-Black Sea, Central-Eastern Europe, Mediterranean, Nordic, and Western Europe.

Key findings include:
- PSMU is associated with more psychological complaints and lower life evaluation in all 43 countries examined. These associations are strongest in Anglo-Celtic and Central-Eastern European countries and weakest in the Caucasus-Black Sea region.
- The negative relationship between PSMU and wellbeing is stronger among adolescents from lower SES backgrounds compared to higher SES peers. Low-SES adolescents bear the greatest costs of compulsive digital behaviors.
- SES differences in the PSMU-wellbeing relationship are more pronounced for life evaluation than for psychological complaints.
- Younger adolescents (ages 11–12) are more vulnerable to the negative effects of PSMU than older adolescents (ages 13–16).
- Between 2018 and 2022, the negative association between PSMU and adolescent wellbeing intensified across all socioeconomic groups and most regions, likely influenced by the COVID-19 pandemic's acceleration of digital engagement.
- The Anglo-Celtic region shows the most pronounced SES gaps, while Mediterranean countries show smaller SES differences, possibly due to stronger family ties and community networks.
- The study uses the Family Affluence Scale (FAS) to measure SES and the Cantril Scale for life evaluation, alongside a 9-item PSMU scale.
- The authors caution that the cross-sectional nature of the data cannot establish causality, and call for policies addressing both PSMU risks and the unequal burden on disadvantaged adolescents, including family support, digital literacy programs, and accessible mental health services.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"For adolescents, Problematic Social Media Use (PSMU) is associated with more psychological complaints and lower life evaluation in all 43 countries we examined. These associations are most pronounced in Anglo-Celtic countries and least problematic in the Caucasus-Black Sea region.", "Globally, the relationship between PSMU and lower wellbeing is stronger among adolescents from lower socioeconomic backgrounds than among their higher-status peers.", "Low-SES adolescents bear the greatest costs of compulsive or addictive digital behaviours, while their more advantaged peers are relatively more protected from these harms.", "Between 2018 and 2022, the negative association between PSMU and adolescent wellbeing intensified. This increase occurred across all socioeconomic groups and in most of the regions examined.", "Younger adolescents appear more vulnerable to the negative wellbeing consequences of problematic digital engagement."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 19: Associations of time spent on different types of digital media with self-rated general and mental health in Swedish adolescents | Scientific Reports ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-83951-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study published in *Scientific Reports* (2025) investigated the association between time spent on different types of digital media and self-rated general and mental health in Swedish adolescents. The cross-sectional population-based study included 3,566 high school students aged 16–17 from Östergötland County, Sweden. Data came from the "Om mig" web survey conducted in 2019.

**Key methods:** Time spent on digital media was categorized into four types: social media, gaming, watching movies/series/video clips, and digital schoolwork. Usage was categorized as low (≤1 h/day), moderate (2–3 h), high (4–5 h), and very high (≥6 h). Health outcomes measured included general health, self-esteem, symptoms of worry/anxiety, low mood/depression, trust in others, head/neck/shoulder pain, and sleep quality. Logistic regression models adjusted for sociodemographic variables and health behaviours.

**Key findings:**
- Very high use (≥6 h/day) of any digital media except schoolwork was associated with poor self-esteem, low mood/depression, and poor sleep (ORs 1.35–2.93).
- Spending ≥6 h/day on social media or gaming was associated with worry/anxiety.
- Social media, watching movies/series/video clips, and schoolwork at ≥6 h/day were associated with head/neck/shoulder pain.
- Gaming at ≥6 h/day was associated with poor general health and low trust.
- High use (4–5 h/day) of watching movies/series/video clips was associated with daily low mood/depression, neck/shoulder pain, and low trust.
- Moderate use (2–3 h/day) showed few or weak associations with adverse outcomes.

The study indicates a dose-response relationship between digital media use and adverse health outcomes in adolescents, with adverse associations starting to appear after 4–5 hours, particularly for watching movies/series/video clips. The authors call for further longitudinal studies, randomized controlled trials, and public health interventions focused on healthy and balanced use of digital media.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In the adjusted models, spending very high amounts of time (≥6 h/day) on any digital media, except schoolwork, was associated with poor self-esteem, symptoms of low mood/depression and poor sleep (ORs 1.35–2.93, p<0.05).", "This study indicates a dose-response relationship between digital media use and adverse health outcomes in adolescents, where adverse associations start to appear after 4–5 h, particularly for watching movies/series/video clips.", "Almost 3 out of 4 participants (73%) reported spending three hours or more daily with at least one type of digital media (social media, movies/series/video clips, or gaming) in their leisure time.", "On average, participants reported high daily usage of all digital media categories: social media, movies/series/video clips, schoolwork, and gaming.", "The study included 3566 Swedish high school students aged 16–17 years."

--- SOURCE 20: Teens, screens and mental health ---
URL: https://www.who.int/europe/news/item/25-09-2024-teens--screens-and-mental-health

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**WHO Report: Teens, Screens and Mental Health (September 25, 2024, Copenhagen)**

A new WHO Regional Office for Europe report based on the Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study—surveying nearly 280,000 adolescents aged 11, 13, and 15 across 44 countries in Europe, central Asia, and Canada in 2022—reveals a sharp rise in problematic social media use among adolescents, increasing from 7% in 2018 to 11% in 2022. Additionally, 12% of adolescents are at risk of problematic gaming.

**Key findings:**
- Problematic social media use is defined as addiction-like symptoms: inability to control usage, withdrawal symptoms, neglecting other activities, and negative daily-life consequences.
- Previous research links problematic social media use to lower mental and social well-being, higher substance use, less sleep, and later bedtimes.
- 34% of adolescents play digital games daily, with 22% playing at least 4 hours on gaming days. 68% were non-problematic gamers, but 12% were at risk of problematic gaming.
- Boys show higher rates of daily gaming and are more likely to develop problematic gaming habits.
- Heavy but non-problematic social media users reported stronger peer support and social connections.

**WHO calls to action:**
- Improve digital literacy education, which remains inadequate in many countries.
- Implement age-appropriate, gender-sensitive, and culturally tailored interventions.
- Policy-makers, educators, and healthcare providers should prioritize adolescent digital well-being.
- Empower adolescents to make informed decisions about online activities, balancing online and offline worlds.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"It's clear that social media can have both positive and negative consequences on the health and well-being of adolescents," noted Dr Hans Henri P. Kluge, WHO Regional Director for Europe. "As millions of children across the Region return to school after the summer holidays, some countries are considering restrictions or outright bans on social media for children up to a certain age. It's clear we need immediate and sustained action to help adolescents turn the tide on potentially damaging social media use, which has been shown to lead to depression, bullying, anxiety and poor academic performance.", "This study reveals both the promise and the pitfalls of digital engagement for our young people," said Dr Natasha Azzopardi-Muscat, Director for Country Health Policies and Systems, WHO Regional Office for Europe. "In short, they should rule social media, and not have social media ruling them.", "The gender differences in gaming patterns are striking. Boys not only show higher rates of daily gaming but are also more likely to develop problematic gaming habits. This highlights the need for targeted interventions that consider gender-specific motivations and risk factors in gaming behaviour", Dr Claudia Marino, one of the report authors at the University of Padova, noted., "Ultimately, what we are seeking to achieve for our children is a solid foundation for life in the digital age, something social media companies and young people alike are beginning to acknowledge and act upon around the world," concluded Dr Kluge. "Digital literacy in the context of child development and well-being, informed by the right knowledge at the right time along with the right health and other support services, are critical."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 21: European Digital Education Hub & EU Digital Education Action Plan ---
URL: https://learnworkecosystemlibrary.com/initiatives/european-digital-education-hub-eu-digital-education-action-plan

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The webpage from the Learn & Work Ecosystem Library provides a comprehensive overview of two interrelated European Union initiatives: the European Digital Education Hub and the EU Digital Education Action Plan (2021-2027), last updated January 16, 2025.

**European Digital Education Hub:** Launched in June 2022, this is an online collaborative community connecting digital education stakeholders across Europe. It offers a voluntary platform for sharing best practices, peer learning, and cross-sector collaboration. Membership includes school educators, teacher trainers, policymakers, and school representatives. By January 2025, the Hub had grown to over 5,500 members, with more than 100 publications and 200 activities. Most activities occur online, primarily in English.

**EU Digital Education Action Plan:** Adopted September 2020, this strategic framework (2021-2027) supports the sustainable digital transformation of education and training systems across Europe. It is part of the broader European Education Area initiative. Key areas of activity include:

- **Enhance digital skills and competencies** – basic digital literacy, advanced digital skills (AI, cybersecurity), and teacher training.
- **Build a high-performing digital education ecosystem** – strengthen digital infrastructure and access to secure tools.
- **Develop robust digital infrastructure** – address gaps in remote/rural areas, foster public-private partnerships.
- **Promote digital inclusion** – reduce the digital divide for disadvantaged groups.
- **Enhance collaboration** – cross-border cooperation among EU Member States.
- **Drive innovation and research** – support initiatives like the Hub, fund pilot projects.

Work focuses on developing a European Digital Education Content Framework, introducing self-assessment tools for digital competencies, and promoting open educational resources (OER). The plan is a key enabler for achieving a European Education Area by 2025, originally endorsed at a 2017 Social Summit in Sweden. It also contributes to the European Skills Agenda, European Social Pillar Action Plan, and the 2030 Digital Compass. The plan is supported by EU funding programs including Erasmus+, Horizon Europe, and the Digital Europe Programme.
</summary>

The European Digital Education Hub is an online collaborative community that connects digital education stakeholders across Europe and beyond. --- SOURCE 22: ETUC Position on Digital Education Action Plan 2021-2027 | ETUC ---
URL: https://www.etuc.org/en/document/etuc-position-digital-education-action-plan-2021-2027

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) adopted a position on the European Commission's Digital Education Action Plan 2021-2027 at its Executive Committee Meeting of 28-29 October 2020. The ETUC argues that digital skills training and lifelong learning are tools, not ends in themselves, and must be paired with quality jobs, fair salaries, and decent working conditions for a just digital transition.

Key demands include: 
- Effective upskilling and reskilling strategies defined by EU member states and companies, with employers taking responsibility for training workers (including paid training during working hours, per the European Social Partners Framework Agreement on Digitalisation)
- Training must be recognised, certified, and lead to full qualifications, not replaced by short courses or micro-credentials
- Achieving the target of 70% of adults (16-74) having basic digital skills by 2025, with targeted support for low-skilled, low-qualified, and unemployed people
- Inclusion of social partners in policy development and implementation of digital skills strategies
- Ensuring the right to quality and inclusive education, training, and lifelong learning for all, with equal access for disadvantaged learners and women
- Sustainable public budgets for digital tools in VET, protecting VET school autonomy from dependence on digital companies
- Full implementation of the European Framework of Quality and Effective Apprenticeship to prevent exploitation of apprentices as cheap labour
- Linking digital education with the Green Deal, including measures to reduce digital waste
- Not limiting the European Digital Competence Framework and Digital Skills Certificate to high-level IT skills; digital competence should also support everyday life, not just the labour market

The ETUC criticises the Commission's Communication for not providing solutions for digitalisation in the VET sector for adults and employees, and for not mentioning the involvement of social partners. It calls for effective social dialogue, respect for labour rights, and worker information and consultation on digital skills development.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Quality jobs, fair salary and working conditions are prerequisites for a just transition towards fair digitalisation for long-term and sustainable growth, productivity, and innovation. Digital skills training and lifelong learning are only tools to achieve these goals.", "Employers need to take their responsibility to upskill and reskill workers, in particular within jobs undergoing digitalisation.", "Where an employer requests a worker to participate in a job-related training that is directly linked to the digital transformation of the enterprise, the training is paid by the employer or in line with the collective agreement or national practice. This training can be in-house or off-site and takes place at an appropriate and agreed time for both the employer and the worker, and where possible during working hours.", "We regret that the Commission's Communication does not mention the involvement of social partners in policy developments and implementation of digital skills strategies.", "The Digital Education Action Plan 2021-27 should impose ensuring the right of all Europeans to quality and inclusive education, training and lifelong learning on digital skills and competences on EU member states in line with the first principle of the European Pillar of Social Rights."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 23: Digital Education Action Plan: policy background ---
URL: https://education.ec.europa.eu/focus-topics/digital-education/actions/plan

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Digital Education Action Plan (2021-2027) is a European Commission policy initiative that sets out a strategic vision and 14 actions to foster high-quality, inclusive and accessible digital education across Europe. Adopted in 2020 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the plan aims to help national education and training systems adapt to the digital age by addressing challenges and opportunities from digital transformation.

Key figures highlight the need for action:
- Fewer than 40% of EU educators felt ready to use digital technologies in teaching (OECD, 2018)
- Over 40% of 13-14-year-olds in the EU lack basic digital skills, falling short of the EU's 2030 goal of reducing this below 15% (ICILS, 2023)
- 20% of low-income households lack access to computers and broadband (Eurostat, 2020)
- 95% of public consultation respondents said COVID-19 marked a turning point in educational technology use (2020)

The Action Plan is a key component of the European Education Area and contributes to several Commission priorities including A Europe fit for the Digital Age, Next Generation EU, the Union of Skills, and the 2030 Digital Compass. A 2030 Roadmap on the future of digital education and skills will build on a review of this plan, complementing other initiatives like the Action Plan on Basic Skills and the STEM Education Strategic Plan. The plan builds on the first Digital Education Action Plan (2018-2020).
</summary>

These guidelines are a flagship initiative of the Digital Education Action Plan (2021–2027) and align with the Union of Skills commitment. Later in 2026, the Commission will adopt a broader Education Package and a 2030 Roadmap on the future of digital education and skills.

Methodology ......................................................................................................... 111 3 1. Introduction Ofcom’s Online Nation report is an annual publication that looks at what people are doing online, how they are served by online content providers and platforms, and their attitudes to and experiences of using the internet. There is an accompanying interactive report with additional data to what is included in this report. In October 2023 Ofcom became the regulator of online safety in the UK under the Online Safety Act. Regulated services will have to follow various rules, including protecting users from illegal content and activity online, as well as protecting children from harmful content and activity online. The terminology, and the categorisation of the services and potential harms discussed in this report, do not necessarily align with the Online Safety Act definitions and should not be considered a reflection of any policy position that Ofcom may adopt. A range of Ofcom and third-party sources have been used to provide context and information on the UK’s use of online services and people’s experiences of being online. Two sources played a major role in the production of this report: Ofcom’s Online Experiences Tracker (OET)1 and Ipsos iris.2 The Online Experiences Tracker (OET) is Ofcom’s biannual quantitative tracking survey that examines people’s attitudes to and experiences of using online services. Ipsos iris is the UKOM-endorsed currency for the measurement of online audiences and provides data that is representative of the UK online adult (18+) population, giving a snapshot of both reach and time spent on websites and apps, across smartphones, tablets and computers in May 2024. It compares year-on-year trends since May 2022, and is used to explore monthly trends where notable changes are occurring. A note on research methodology and terminology regarding ‘potential harms’ used in the report The OET survey seeks to understand the experiences of encountering potential harms online by UK internet users aged 13 and over. Not all occurrences of potentially harmful content or behaviour online result in actual psychological (or financial) harm, so in this report they are referred to as ‘potential harms’. The data relating to the type and prevalence of potential harm relates to the responses from internet users encountering a ‘potential harm’ in the four weeks before completing our OET survey; their ‘most recent encountered potential harm’. Further OET data relating to the location and impact of, and response to a potential harm, relate to this ‘most recent encountered potential harm’. To capture these figures, survey participants in the OET are prompted with a list of potential harms, and their responses are based on their recall and judgement of the content and behaviours which they consider align with those listed in the questionnaire. The list of potential harms in the OET questionnaire covers content that is harmful to children, falling within the scope of the Online Safety Act, and also extends to other types of potentially harmful content and behaviour, in order to capture a wide range of experiences online.3 1 The Online Experiences Tracker (OET) is created by Ofcom, run by YouGov on its online panel. More information and data from each wave can be found here: Experiences of using online services. 2 Ipsos iris measures participants’ online behaviours and activities on their personal devices. For more information see the Ipsos iris website and the methodology annex below. 3 A full list of potential harms used to prompt participants can be found in the questionnaire. 4 2. Overview Time spent online In May 2024, UK adults spent an average of 4 hours 20 minutes a day online, across smartphones, tablets and computers Young adults spent the most time online, with 18-24-year-olds spending a daily average of 6 hours 1 minute online, and those aged 65+ spending the least time online (3 hours 10 minutes). Women spent more time online than men across all adult age groups. The daily average for women was 4 hours 36 minutes, 33 minutes more than men (4 hours 3 minutes). The difference was highest among ‘Gen Z’ women aged 18-24, who spent more than an hour longer online than their male counterparts (6 hours 36 minutes vs 5 hours 28 minutes). Almost half (48%) of the time UK adults spend online is on services owned by Alphabet or Meta In May 2024, UK adults spent an average of 2 hours 4 minutes a day on services owned by these two organisations. Alphabet remains the highest reaching organisation visited by almost all online adults (99%), with 94% visiting YouTube, spending an average of 47 minutes a day on it. Meta was not far behind as the second highest reaching organisation (96%). In total, 70% (33 million) of UK online adults visited all top three Meta-owned platforms – Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram. Although Facebook and Messenger was Meta’s highest-reaching service among adults (at 91%), there is a notable difference in the time spent on it by adult age groups. Facebook users aged 18-24 are the least engaged with the service, spending an average of 15 minutes a day on the platform, much lower than the average time spent by adults overall (39mins). Online sectors Social media Reddit was the fastest-growing large social media platform in the UK, reaching more than half of UK online adults by June 2024 Reddit experienced a 47% year-on-year increase in reach among UK online adults, rising to 22.9 million (48% UK online adults) by May 2024 (May 2023: 15.6m, 33%), overtaking X (formerly Twitter) and LinkedIn to become the fifth highest-reaching social media service among adults. This increase was predominantly driven by young adults, resulting in Reddit appearing in the top ten online organisations for young online adults for the first time (age 18-24: 71%; age 25-34: 63%). This is a notable increase since May 2023 (18-24%: 58%, 25-34: 49%). Reddit increased its reach further in June 2024, reaching 24.6 million (52%) of UK online adults. A year after its release, Meta’s microblogging service Threads became the 12th highest-reaching social media service, reaching 5.3 million (11%) UK online adults in July 2024. Although X remains the highest-reaching microblogging service, its average monthly adult reach continues to decline: from 27.9 million in 2021 to 26.5 million in 2022 and 23.8 million in 2023. The monthly 2024 average up to August 2024 was 22.2 million, down by a further 1.6 million adult visitors. 18-24-year-old TikTok and Snapchat visitors spent on average about an hour per day on each service About three-quarters (74%, 2.0m) of online 18-24-year-olds visited TikTok in May 2024, spending an average of 64 minutes per day on the service and accounting for 39% of the total time UK adults 5 spent on the service. Women aged 18-24 who visited TikTok spent on average 1 hour 17 minutes on it, while men spent 35 minutes less on average (48 minutes). Snapchat skews even more heavily towards young adults, with users aged 18-24 accounting for 64% of the total time spent by UK adults on Snapchat in May 2024, averaging 55 minutes per day. Two-thirds of the total time spent by UK adults on Snapchat in May 2024 was by women; women aged 18-24-year who visited Snapchat spent over an hour (67 minutes) on average on the service per day, while men spent 42 minutes. Messaging and calling Forty-three per cent of UK Snapchat messenger users aged 16+ sent a disappearing image or video on the service in July 2024 An Ofcom survey in July 2024 found that 57% of 16-24-year-olds had sent a disappearing image or video on Snapchat. WhatsApp and Telegram also offer ‘view once’ or disappearing image/video functionalities, and these had been used by 9% and 12% of UK internet users aged 16+ respectively. Ipsos iris data showed that WhatsApp continued to be the highest-reaching messaging service, reaching 87% of UK online adults in May 2024. Sixty-four per cent of UK online adults accessed WhatsApp daily, up from 58% in May 2023. Generative artificial intelligence ChatGPT was the most popular generative AI tool, with 37% of British online 8-15s and 33% of UK internet users aged 16+ saying they had used it in the past year An Ofcom survey conducted in June 2024 revealed that over half (54%) of British online 8-15s and 41% of UK online aged 16+ users said they had used a generative AI tool in the past year. UK online males aged 16+ were more likely than females to have used a generative AI tool in the past year (50% vs 33%). Ipsos iris data found that ChatGPT had continued to expand its reach, with 4.2 million (9%) UK online adults visiting it in May 2024, increasing to 4.4 million (9%) by July 2024. ChatGPT adult reach was highest among UK online 18-24-year-olds (27%, 1.4m) in May 2024. Although ‘finding information or content’ is the most popular reason for using a generative AI tool, only a minority believe the information provided is reliable The most popular reason for using a generative AI tool in the past year was to find information or content, reported by 48% of internet users aged 16+ and 31% of British online 8-15-year-olds. Despite this, only 18% of those aged 16+ said they thought the information from generative AI was reliable, while a third of 8-15s said they were confident in the information they got from these tools. Search engines Search engines are still widely used; 90% of UK online adults visited at least one of the top ten highest-reaching search engines in May 2024 Google Search remained the highest-reaching search engine, with 83% of UK online adults visiting it in May 2024, down from 86% in May 2023. Microsoft’s Bing was the next highest-reaching, at 39% in May 2024, down from 46% in May 2023. Both Google and Microsoft have incorporated generative AI into their search sites – Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. Fifteen per cent of UK internet users aged 16+ said they had used Copilot, the second-highest-reaching generative AI tool, in the past year, while 10% said they had used Google Gemini, which became the fourth-highest-reaching AI tool only six months after its launch. Dating One in ten UK online adults visited a dating service in May 2024, in line with May 2023 (11%), although there has been a decline in UK adult use of popular dating services 6 Visitors to dating services was highest among 18-24-year-olds (18%) and 25-34-year-olds (17%). Tinder continued to be the highest reaching, at 1.9 million (4%) UK online adults. However, its reach had declined by 600k from 2.5 million visitors (5%) the year before. Hinge, the second-highest-reaching service, reached 1.4 million UK online adults (3%) in May 2024, down 131k from the year before. While men still outnumbered women on online dating services overall, Hinge was more popular among women in May 2024. Pornographic content services Twenty-nine per cent of UK online adults accessed a pornographic content service in May 2024 Twenty-nine per cent (13.8m) of UK online adults accessed a pornographic content service in May 2024, in line with the previous two years (May 2023: 29%, May 2022: 31%). For the first half of 2024, the monthly average time spent on pornographic content services by UK adult visitors was 1 hour 33 minutes, an 11% decrease (-11 minutes) compared to the first half of 2023 (monthly average 1 hour 41 minutes). Men remained far more likely to visit a pornographic content service, comprising 72% of the UK adult audience in May 2024, consistent with the previous year (May 2023: 73%). Pornhub continued to be the highest-reaching pornographic content service across nations, genders and age groups, visited by 18% (8.4m) of UK online adults in May 2024. Retail Amazon remained the UK’s leading online retailer visited by 35% UK online adults per day in May 2024 Eighty-eight per cent (41.5m) of UK online adults visited Amazon in May 2024, consistent with the same period in the previous two years (May 2022: 88%, May 2023: 87%). On average, 16.4 million (35%) UK online adults visited Amazon per day in May 2024. Three quarters of the UK online population aged 16+ said they had used an online marketplace in Q2 2024. Ebay was the top reaching online marketplace (57%) followed by 40% saying they used Facebook Marketplace in Q2 2024. The online experience Two-thirds (67%) of online adults agree that for them the benefits of being online outweigh the risks, a decrease from June 2023 (71%) and January 2024 (68%) Younger adults aged 18-24 (11%) and those in a minority ethnic group (10%) were more likely to agree that the risks outweighed the benefits of being online. Although more users felt that the personal benefits of being online were high (67%), fewer felt that the internet was good for society (40%). Women (34%), white individuals (39%), those in the lower C2DE socio-economic group (36%) and those with a limiting condition (36%) were less likely than average to feel that the internet was good for society. Young adults were less likely than older people to think they had a good balance between their online and offline lives, and older children were more concerned than younger ones about the time they spent online Ofcom’s Media Literacy research found young adults were more likely than older adults to disagree that they had a good balance between their online and offline lives (21% of 18-24-years vs 7% of over-54s). A separate Ofcom survey showed that children’s concern about their time spent online increases with age: 35% of 8-9-year-olds, 46% of 10-12-year-olds, and 51% of 13-15-year-olds reported concern about the amount of time they spent on at least one service type. Children were worried about the mental (49%) and physical (46%) health effects of spending too much time online. 7 Misinformation remained the most prevalent potential harm, with 39% of users aged 13+ saying they had encountered it in June 2024 In June 2024, three in ten UK internet users aged 13+ said they had seen something in the past four weeks that had made them feel uncomfortable, upset or negative, an increase since June 2023 (27%). Despite the increase, the proportion of users who had encountered at least one of the harms listed in our OET survey remained the same as in previous years (68%); Younger adults (18-24: 80% vs 65+: 55%) were more likely than average to have come across potential harms online. Misinformation was the most prevalent potential harm with 39% of internet users aged 13+ saying they had encountered it. The types of misinformation that internet users saw fluctuated according to the topical news and current affairs when the survey was run. Following the announcement of the UK General Election, on 22 May 2024, there was a small but significant increase in June 2024 of internet users aged 13+ saying they had encountered political or electoral misinformation (25%), up from 22% in January 2024. In January 2024, reports of misinformation about conflicts rose significantly (to 21% from 6% in June 2023), probably linked to the war in Gaza which began in October 2023. Although these numbers fell in the June 2024 survey, they are still significantly higher than in June 2023, at 16%. More online adults are encountering hateful, offensive or discriminatory content UK adult internet users reporting seeing hateful, offensive or discriminatory content has increased over the past year, from 23% in June 2023 to 26% in June 2024. The types of hateful online content reported fluctuates according to the news and current affairs at the time of the survey. In January 2024, reports of content hateful towards people because of their ethnicity or religion rose sharply, to 36% and 33% respectively, up from 25% and 16% in June 2023. In June 2024 these figures remained higher than in the previous year, both for ethnicity (33%) and religion (30%). There were some gender disparities in regard to the types of potential harms that were encountered online. Men were more likely than women to report that they had encountered misinformation (41% vs 37%), scams or fraud (36% vs 31%), hateful content (27% vs 24%), fake or deceptive content (20% vs 16%) and paid for/sponsored content that is not marked as such (19% vs 15%). Women were more likely than men to report encountering unwelcome friend or follow requests (30% vs 26%), misogynistic content (23% vs 19%) and body-image-related content (21% vs 13%). One in five 8-15 year-olds have a user age of at least 18 on a social media platform but there are indications that there are more frequent efforts from services to verify their date of birth Ofcom’s user age research, conducted in August 2024, suggests that 22% of 8-17-year-olds (and 20% of 8-15s) with a social media profile on at least one of the platforms listed in our study, have a user profile age of at least 18, meaning they are at greater risk of seeing adult content. This has remained consistent with data from February 2024 and September 2023 (8-17s: 21% and 22%, 8-15s: 20% for both). Compared to September 2023, children aged 8-17 in August 2024 were more likely to say that they had been asked to verify their date of birth on their profile (Facebook: 25% vs 10%, Instagram: 18% vs 9%, Snapchat: 14% vs 9%, TikTok: 19% vs 13%, X: 20% vs 10% and YouTube: 14% vs 10%). Among online teens, generally offensive or ‘bad’ language4 was the most prevalent potential harm encountered, although their reported exposure has declined over the past year 4 Although generally offensive or bad language’ is not separately recognised as a harm in the Online Safety Act 2023, this was included as part of a list of potential harms within our OET survey as we wanted to capture the wider online user experience. 8 Thirty-five per cent of users aged 13-17 said in June 2024 that they had come across generally offensive or ‘bad’ language online. The proportion of 13-17s encountering this potential harm has decreased over the past year, with 47% citing this harm in June 2023 and 40% in January 2024. Teenage boys were more likely to encounter content showing dangerous stunts, while girls were more likely to encounter potential harms relating to body image There were gender differences in the prevalence of potential harms that teen users were exposed to. Teenage boys were more likely than girls to encounter content showing dangerous stunts (29% vs 19%). Encounters with potential online harms relating to body image are more common among girls than boys; this includes content stigmatising certain body types (25% vs 11%), content promoting excessive or unhealthy eating/exercise (19% vs 9%), group shaming (19% vs 10%) and content relating to eating disorders (17% vs 5%). Teen girls were also more likely than boys to say they had encountered unwelcome friend or follow requests (33% vs 21%) and misogynistic content (23% vs 14%). Facebook remains the most likely service on which adult users encountered a potential harm (29%) in the past year, while TikTok (22%) and YouTube (13%) are the services where teen users were most likely to encounter a potential harm Social media was the type of service on which users aged 13+ most commonly reported encountering their most recent potential harm online (56%). Facebook (29%) was the most likely platform on which adult users encountered potential harms, followed by X (June 2024: 18%, down from 23% in June 2023). Older adults were significantly more likely to have encountered their most recent potential harm on Facebook, (55+: 45% vs. 18-24: 8%). Users aged 18-24 were more likely than older adults to encounter their most recent potential harm on X (23%), Instagram (20%), TikTok (20%), Snapchat (3%) and Tumblr (1%), and less likely on Facebook (8%). Children aged 13-17 were significantly more likely than adults to have encountered their most recent potential harm on TikTok (22% vs 9%), YouTube (13% vs 4%), Snapchat (7% vs 1%) and WhatsApp (7% vs 2%). In June 2024, 35% of adults said they had reported or flagged content in response to encountering a potential harm online in the past four weeks Thirty-eight per cent of adults who chose to report or flag the content or activity were aware of the outcome of their report, an increase since the last two waves of the survey (32% in January 2024, 30% in June 2023). Women were more likely to say that they had ‘not heard anything yet’ in response to their report, compared to men (55% vs 46%). Men were more likely to say they had received a written response (11% vs 7%) and more likely to say the reported content had been removed (25% vs 18%). Satisfaction following reporting potential harmful content has increased, from 31% in June 2023 to 40% in June 2024. There has also been an increase in awareness of the result of reporting content (e.g. content removal, written response, etc.), from 30% in June 2023 to 38% in June 2024. Two-fifths of adult users believe the onus is on the website/app (39%) and on search engines (41%) to keep users safe online Women were more likely than average to say the onus is on the website or app that hosts user generated content (40%) and on search engines (45%), while 38% of men said this for both websites and apps that host user generated content and search engines. Twenty per cent of adult users thought the onus was on the individual to ensure that what they posted is appropriate for other users. 9 More online adults in June 2024 than in June 2023 said it was important for sites to monitor and delete offensive views to protect other users (26%, compared to 24% in June 2023). However, 38% of online adults agreed that ‘the internet has an important role in supporting free speech’. Men were more likely to be advocates of free speech: 47% agreed with this statement, compared with 30% of women. There was an increase in the proportion of online adults who believed that further safety measures are needed online (44%, compared to 42% in January 2024 and 40% in June 2023). This belief is especially prevalent among women, people aged 55+ and heterosexuals. In contrast, men, younger adults and those identifying as LGB+ are more likely to say that the existing safety measures are sufficient. 10 3. args.summary:
Ofcom's Online Nation 2024 report, published 28 November 2024, examines UK online behavior, platform usage, and user experiences. Key findings include:

**Time Spent Online:** UK adults averaged 4 hours 20 minutes daily online in May 2024. Young adults (18-24) spent the most time (6 hours 1 minute), while 65+ spent the least (3 hours 10 minutes). Women spent more time online than men across all age groups (4 hours 36 mins vs 4 hours 3 mins). Smartphones accounted for 75% of online time.

**Top Platforms:** Nearly half (48%) of UK adult online time is spent on Alphabet or Meta-owned services. Alphabet reaches 99% of online adults, with YouTube at 94% reach (47 mins/day). Meta reaches 96%, with 70% visiting all three top platforms (Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram). Reddit grew 47% year-on-year, reaching 48% of UK online adults by May 2024, overtaking X and LinkedIn.

**Generative AI:** 41% of UK adults and 54% of 8-15-year-olds had used a generative AI tool in the past year. ChatGPT was the most popular (37% of 8-15s, 33% of 16+). Only 18% of adults thought AI information was reliable.

**Potential Harms:** Three in ten UK internet users aged 13+ encountered something upsetting online in the past four weeks (June 2024). Misinformation remained the most prevalent harm (39%). Hateful content reports increased from 23% (June 2023) to 26% (June 2024). Facebook was the most common platform for adult harm encounters (29%), while TikTok (22%) and YouTube (13%) were most common for teens.

**Children:** 20% of 8-15-year-olds with social media profiles have a user age of at least 18. Teen girls were more likely to encounter body-image-related harms; boys were more likely to encounter dangerous stunts content.

**Safety:** 67% of adults agree benefits outweigh risks (down from 71% in June 2023). 44% believe further safety measures are needed (up from 40% in June 2023). 40% of adults who reported content were satisfied with the outcome (up from 31% in June 2023).

**Other Sectors:** 29% of UK online adults accessed pornographic content services. Dating service visits declined (Tinder down 600k visitors). Amazon was visited by 88% of UK online adults. 5% of UK individuals lack home internet access, with cost cited by 27% of those without.
