## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475)Abstract

### Purpose of Review

Social media use (SMU) and other internet-based technologies are ubiquitous in today’s interconnected society, with young people being among the commonest users. Previous literature tends to support that SMU is associated with poor sleep and mental health issues in youth, despite some conflicting findings. In this scoping review, we summarized relevant studies published within the past 3 years, highlighted the impacts of SMU on sleep and mental health in youth, while also examined the possible underlying mechanisms involved. Future direction and intervention on rational use of SMU was discussed.

### Recent Findings

Both cross-sectional and longitudinal cohort studies demonstrated the negative impacts of SMU on sleep and mental health, with preliminary evidence indicating potential benefits especially during the COVID period at which social restriction was common. However, the limited longitudinal research has hindered the establishment of directionality and causality in the association among SMU, sleep, and mental health.

### Summary

Recent studies have made advances with a more comprehensive understanding of the impact of SMU on sleep and mental health in youth, which is of public health importance and will contribute to improving sleep and mental health outcomes while promoting rational and beneficial SMU. Future research should include the implementation of cohort studies with representative samples to investigate the directionality and causality of the complex relationships among SMU, sleep, and mental health; the use of validated questionnaires and objective measurements; and the design of randomized controlled interventional trials to reduce overall and problematic SMU that will ultimately enhance sleep and mental health outcomes in youth.

**Keywords:**Social media use, Sleep, Mental health, Youth, Adolescent

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475)Introduction

Youth population, which typically refers to individuals between the ages of 15 and 24, experience substantial changes in their neurobiology, physical development, behavior, and emotions, making it a vulnerable stage for the development of both sleep and mental health problems [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR1)–[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR3)]. In Hong Kong, approximately 64.5% of adolescents sleep less than 8 h during weekdays [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR4)] and 29.2% have reported insomnia symptoms [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR5)]. Both cross-sectional and longitudinal studies have demonstrated that sleep loss and disturbances in youth lead to significant personal distress, increase risk of psychiatric illnesses, and risky behaviors such as drug abuse and dangerous driving [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR5), [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR6)]. In addition to sleep disturbances, mental health problems are highly prevalent among the youth population. Evidence suggested that nearly 75% of psychiatric illnesses have their age onset during adolescence [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR7), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR8)].

There are multiple risk factors that commonly contribute to sleep and mental health problems, including being female, heavy school workload, physical inactivity, and worse general health [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR9)]. Recently, a growing number of studies indicate that social media use (SMU) is associated with both sleep and mental health problems in youth [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR10)•]. In particular, identity development and peer acceptance during adolescence are important developmental needs, at which social media may apparently serve as a convenient means to meet these needs. A previous study reported that over 80% of adolescents (16–19 years) use electronic devices near bedtime [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR11)]. On the other hand, excessive SMU can have detrimental health effects [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR12), [13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR13)], and contribute to various negative repercussions such as cyberbullying [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR14)], gender stereotypes [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR15)], self-objectification [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR16)], and exposure to inappropriate content, such as unsolicited violent and sexual contents [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR17)]. The effect becomes more prominent in young people who are considered as digital native [[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR18)]. Nevertheless, SMU also comes with some potential benefits [[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR19)] such as increased self-esteem [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR20)], increased social capital [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR21)], identity presentation and sexual exploration [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR22)], and social support [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR23)].

Despite the emerging evidence supporting the link among SMU, sleep, and mental health, the relationship and directionality are complex and inconsistent. For example, two recent studies did not find significant associations among SMU, sleep, and mental health [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR24), [25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR25)•]. Nonetheless, a US study reported that greater SMU was significantly associated with sleep disturbances [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR26)], and some also reported bidirectional relationship at which poor sleepers tend to use electronic devices as a sleep aid [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR27)]. In general, it is believed that youth are at a higher risk of experiencing the negative impacts of SMU as they are more susceptible to peer pressure and fear of missing out (FOMO). FOMO refers to the perception of missing out on enjoyable experiences, followed up with a compulsive behavior to maintain these social connections with others to avoid being excluded from those experiences [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR28)–[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR30)]. Hence, understanding the association and directionality among SMU, sleep, and mental health is crucial for developing public health strategies on how to cultivate healthy SMU habits and develop effective interventions targeting inappropriate and excessive SMU.

This scoping review summarized recent studies on SMU, sleep, and mental health in youth (Fig.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#Fig1)) and explored the potential underlying mechanisms of how SMU affects sleep and mental health in youth (Fig.[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#Fig2)). Finally, we have put forward several potential avenues for future research and recommendations in this area. Search terms including #adolescent, #social media, #sleep, and #mental health were used to search for relevant studies that were published between January 2020 and July 2023 in MEDLINE. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475)Overview of SMU

SMU refers to the act of engaging with online platforms specifically designed for social interaction, whereas electronic media use (or digital use, digital media, internet use, screen time) is a broader term that encompasses various forms of media delivered electronically, including but not limited to social media. In this scoping review, we focus on SMU.

Over the past decade, subjective measures have been the primary tool to investigate individual perceptions, opinions, or personal experiences of SMU. For example, a self-report scale was developed to assess compulsive use of social media and its severity [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR31)]. Besides, there are several platform-specific scales for social media addiction features such as salience, mood modification, tolerance, withdrawal, conflict, and relapse. The Bergen Facebook Addiction Scale, for instance, focuses specifically on addiction to Facebook [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR32)•], while the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale has emerged to examine a broader scope, including social media platforms beyond Facebook [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR33)•, [34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR34)]. Indeed, more researchers used general metrics to measure SMU across multiple platforms collectively such as the Social Media Disorder Scale which measures aspects of social media addiction features, such as preoccupation with social media, excessive time spent, withdrawal symptoms, and negative consequences [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR35)–[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR37)]. Other SMU experiences are also captured including social comparison on social media and negative experiences such as bullying, FOMO, and extensive negative feedback [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR32)•].

In addition, the duration and timing of SMU also have significant implications for sleep and mental health, as excessive or inappropriate use of social media at certain timing, for example at bedtime, can potentially contribute to negative biopsychosocial effects. The Socio-Digital Participation Inventory includes four items to measure the frequency of SMU on a seven-point frequency scale (1 = never, 2 = a couple of times a year, 3 = monthly, 4 = weekly, 5 = daily, 6 = multiple times a day, 7 = all the time) [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR25)•]. The total time spent on SMU (in daytime and night-time) are usually captured by questionnaires and social media time use diary [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR38)•]. In view of the limitation of self-reported measures, there has been a shift towards incorporating more objective measures in addition to subjective self-report scales. Increasing number of studies used time tracker via specific apps (installed on participants’ devices used for online activity) to reduce recall bias [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR33)•]. Other objective features, such as the number of followers, likes, comments, shares, bookmarks, and total interactions, which can be retrieved from various social media platforms [[39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR39)•] were also used to reflect social medica engagement. In addition, the content (e.g., educational vs non-educational) posted, read, and shared on social media platforms plays a significant role in shaping user experiences, engagement levels, and the overall impact of SMU. It is worth to note that no included studies attempted to measure multi-device SMU as it can be challenging due to the wide range of devices that people use to access social media platforms. Traditional research methods often rely on self-reporting, surveys, or tracking software installed on specific devices, which may not capture the full extent of multi-device usage. Some individuals may switch between multiple devices throughout the day, making it challenging to track their overall social media engagement accurately.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475)Overview of Recent Studies

### Study Characteristics

A total of 33 studies were included in this scoping review, with 26 of them were cross-sectional in nature, indicating a snapshot overview of the relationship between SMU, sleep, and mental health. Moreover, only a few studies utilized representative samples [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR35), [36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR36), [40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR40), [41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR41)], as outlined in Table[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#Tab1). It is also worth noting that the sample sizes varied significantly across studies, ranging from 54 to 195,668 participants.

### Measurement of SMU

In terms of the measurement of SMU, all studies used either self-developed questionnaires (e.g., “in a typical school week, how often do you check social media?” and “on a normal weekday, how many hours you spend on social medias, write blogs/read each people blogs, or chat online?”) or validated self-report questionnaires (e.g., the 26-item Chinese Internet Addiction Scale-Revised and the Online Civic Engagement Behavior Construct). Different dimensions of SMU were measured such as overall and night-time SMU, problematic SMU, emotional investment in social media, racial discrimination, and racial justice civic engagement on social media. Only a limited number of studies incorporated more reliable measurements such as ecological momentary assessment [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR42)] and total message count [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR43)].

### Measurement of Sleep and Mental Health

In terms of sleep outcome assessment, most of these studies employed subjective instruments such as sleep diary [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR32)•], self-developed self-report questionnaires (e.g., “How many hours did you sleep over the past week?”) [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR43)], and validated self-report questionnaires (e.g., the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and the Insomnia Severity Index) [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR44), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR45)•] to measure different sleep outcomes including sleep quality, sleep duration, sleep displacement, bedtime, and sleep-onset latency. In addition to these subjective instruments, 3 studies have utilized objective devices such as actigraphy and other wearable devices to capture objective sleep data [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR43), [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46), [47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR47)]. While for mental health aspects, depression and anxiety are the main outcomes. Most of the recent studies utilized standardized questionnaires such as the Short Mood and Feelings Questionnaire, the Depression Anxiety Stress Scales 21, and the Suicidal Behaviors Questionnaire-Revised to measure the symptoms of depression and anxiety.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475)Synthesis of Recent Findings

### SMU and Sleep

Both longitudinal and cross-sectional studies tend to support the association between SMU and sleep disturbances (Table[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#Tab1)). A total of 17 cross-sectional studies observed an association between SMU and various sleep parameters in youth. Of these studies, a total of 16 reported a significant association between different dimensions of SMU (internet addition, duration of screen use, inappropriate time use (near bedtime), with one additionally measure parent control of technology) and poor sleep outcomes (both subjectively and objectively measured sleep parameters, such as bedtime, sleep-onset latency, sleep duration, and sleep quality) [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR31), [32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR32)•, [35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR35), [36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR36), [40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR40), [42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR42)–[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR44), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR45)•, [47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR47)–[53](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR53)]. Nevertheless, a study of 101 undergraduate students did not find that bedtime SMU was detrimental to sleep [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46)]. However, in the subgroup analysis, the authors found that youth with increased levels of depressive symptoms are at higher risk of experiencing negative impacts of bedtime SMU on sleep [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46)].

Among the three cohort studies, two indicated that higher levels of SMU predicted later bedtime and shorter sleep duration in youth after 1–2 years of follow-up [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR37), [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR54)]. These studies revealed that both frequent and problematic use of SMU could result in later bedtime [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR37), [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR54)]. In addition, Richardson and colleagues further found that SMU predicted greater daytime sleepiness in adolescence [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR54)]. In addition, adolescents with evening chronotype preference and shorter sleep duration were found to have longer usage of social media, suggesting a potential bidirectional relationship between SMU and sleep duration [[54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR54)]. Another cohort study conducted by Maksniemi and colleagues did not find a significant association between SMU and bedtime among 426 youth aged between 13 and 19 [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR25)•]. Interestingly, subgroup analyses indicated that significant associations were only observed in early adolescence (at age 13 and 14), but not in middle (at age 14 and 15) nor late adolescence (at age 17 and 18) [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR25)•]. This finding highlights the importance of considering the developmental stages of youth in order to unravel the complex relationship between SMU and sleep [[55](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR55)].

### SMU and Mental Health

A total of 9 cross-sectional studies examined the relationship between SMU and mental health [[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR33)•, [34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR34), [38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR38)•, [39](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR39)•, [56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR56)•, [57](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR57)–[60](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR60)]. A greater amount of time spent on social media was associated with an increased risk of depression, self-harm, and lower self-esteem. On the other hand, adolescents who exhibited mental health issues tended to spend more time on social media platforms, suggesting a potential bidirectional relationship between SMU and mental health. However, it is important to point out that despite appealing hypotheses, actual effect size estimates of SMU on various mental health outcomes (e.g., self-esteem, life satisfaction, depression, and loneliness) were of small-to-medium magnitude as reported in previous meta-analytic studies, ranging from − 0.11 to − 0.32 [[61](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR61)•, [62](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR62)].

Four longitudinal cohort studies reported mixed findings between SMU and mental health [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR41), [63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR63), [64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR64)•, [65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR65)]. Two cohort studies conducted in the USA and China reported that frequent and problematic SMU were significantly associated subsequent mental health issues [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR64)•, [65](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR65)]. Interestingly, the authors identified substantial sex differences in the mental health trajectories, with only girls showing a deteriorating linear trend (_β_ = 0.23, _p_< 0.05) [[64](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR64)•]. On the contrary, the other two longitudinal studies conducted in Sweden and UK reported that although frequent SMU was associated with increased levels of mental problems at a single timepoint, there was no longitudinal association [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR41), [63](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR63)], which suggests that SMU may be only an indicator for mental health instead of a risk factor.

### SMU, Sleep, and Mental Health

A total of 7 studies measured both sleep and mental health outcomes [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR31), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR45)•, [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46)–[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR48), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR50), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR59)]. Five of these studies reported significant associations among SMU, sleep, and mental health outcome [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR31), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR45)•, [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR50), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR59)]. It was reported that SMU was significantly associated with poor sleep quality and increased mental health issues [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR31), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR45)•, [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR50), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR59)], and sleep was found to mediate the negative impacts of SMU on mental health and emotional symptoms in adolescents [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR45)•]. Poor sleep was also shown to be significantly associated with mental health outcomes [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR31), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR50), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR59)]. Furthermore, adolescents with higher level of depressive symptoms were at higher risk of experiencing negative impacts of bedtime SMU on sleep outcomes [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46)]. Indeed, these findings preliminarily unveiled the complex interplay among SMU, sleep, and mental health.

Nevertheless, it is essential to highlight that recent research has also recognized the positive impacts of SMU on mental health, particularly in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, at which physical social interactions were significantly disrupted [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR56)•, [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR58)]. Adolescents in Australia and UK were found to use social media as an active coping strategy to relieve external stressors (e.g., exam pressure), to seek support for suicidal ideation or self-harm behavior, and to support others via social media [[56](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR56)•, [58](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR58)].

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475)Discussion

This scoping review synthesized recent publications from the past 3 years that investigated the impact of SMU on sleep and/or mental health outcomes in youth. The majority of the studies provide supporting evidence for an association between SMU, poor sleep quality, and adverse mental health outcomes. Problematic SMU or addiction, as well as the duration of SMU, were identified as the most prevalent aspects of social media examined in the included studies. Sleep duration, bedtime, and insomnia emerged as the most commonly assessed sleep problems, while depression and anxiety were the most frequently measured mental health outcomes. However, it is important to note that despite the significant associations identified among these variables, the directionality of the relationship remains unclear in view of inconsistent findings across studies.

### Underlying Mechanism Between SMU and Sleep

Numerous mechanisms have been proposed to elucidate the relationship between social/digital media usage and sleep quantity and quality [[66](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR66)]. Hyperarousal, a core mechanism in explaining insomnia [[67](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR67)], plays a role in explaining how night-time SMU disrupts sleep. Active engagement in media activities can directly induce physiological and psychological arousal, leading to longer sleep onset latency [[68](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR68)]. This effect is particularly noticeable when individuals actively engage in interactive digital media, such as social messaging and social media, as opposed to passive media consumption like television viewing [[69](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR69)•], likely due to the heightened arousal associated with interactive activities [[70](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR70)]. Interestingly, a study found that engaging in phone conversations near bedtime was associated with longer sleep duration, while the use of social media and texting displayed a negative association [[71](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR71)]. It has been hypothesized that conversing with a friend may positively influence emotional well-being, thereby promoting sleep [[72](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR72)]. However, social networking, despite its potential for fostering friendships, may also trigger FOMO and social media stress. In addition to the psychological arousal induced by electronic media usage, the light emitted from device screens is another hypothesis explaining the detrimental effects of digital media on sleep. Specifically, the light emitted by electronic devices, especially blue light (at a wavelength of 480 nm), has a significant impact on the suppression of melatonin, a hormone that promotes sleep [[73](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR73)]. Moreover, a recent study indicated that high-risk adolescents whose parents with bipolar affective disorder have lower level of nocturnal melatonin secretion. It might be possible that adolescents with certain risk factors (even without psychopathologies) may be particularly hypersensitive and vulnerable to light suppression of melatonin secretion [[74](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR74)], which are considered as high-risk group that require early intervention. Furthermore, it is plausible that an interaction or interplay might exist between arousal and light exposure, and the combination of these conditions could potentially heighten the risk of sleep disturbances. Additionally, the direct displacement of sleep resulting from engagement in social media activities may also lead to shorter sleep duration. Although initial evidence suggests a negative impact of both content and light emitted by electronic devices on sleep, the precise underlying mechanism remains poorly established. Last but not least, some preliminary studies have also investigated other sleep- and circadian-related factors such as chronotype preference and daytime sleepiness in mediating and/or moderating the relationship between SMU and sleep [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR32)•, [44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR44), [54](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR54)], albeit the findings have been inconclusive. Future studies are warranted to thoroughly explore the role of these factors in the interplay between SMU and sleep.

### Underlying Mechanism Between SMU and Mental Health

It has been suggested both behavioral and cognitive factors mediate the impact of SMU on mental health. Among the behavioral factors, sleep has been identified as one of the notable mediators of the association [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR31), [44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR44), [45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR45)•, [46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR46), [50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR50), [59](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR59), [75](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10948475#CR75)]. Physiologically, prolonged SMU before bedtime delays sleep onset, reduces sleep duration, and mediates the association between eveningness and sleep as well as daytime sleepiness [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles
</webpage_content>

args.summary:
This scoping review, published in Current Psychiatry Reports (2024), examines the impact of social media use (SMU) on sleep and mental health in youth (ages 15-24). The authors (Yu, Wing, Li, and Chan from The Chinese University of Hong Kong) synthesized 33 studies published between January 2020 and July 2023.

**Key Findings:**
- 26 of the 33 studies were cross-sectional; only a few used representative samples
- Most studies support an association between SMU and poor sleep outcomes (sleep quality, duration, bedtime, sleep-onset latency), with 16 of 17 cross-sectional studies finding significant associations
- Cohort studies showed mixed results: some found SMU predicted later bedtime and shorter sleep duration after 1-2 years, while others found no longitudinal association
- SMU was associated with increased risk of depression, anxiety, self-harm, and lower self-esteem, though effect sizes were small-to-medium (ranging from -0.11 to -0.32)
- Sleep was found to mediate the negative impacts of SMU on mental health
- Some positive benefits of SMU were noted, particularly during COVID-19 (social support, coping strategy)

**Proposed Mechanisms:**
- Hyperarousal from interactive media activities disrupting sleep
- Blue light from screens suppressing melatonin secretion
- Displacement of sleep time by social media engagement
- Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) and social comparison contributing to mental health issues

**Gaps and Future Directions:**
- Limited longitudinal research hinders establishing directionality and causality
- Need for representative samples, validated questionnaires, objective measurements
- Need for randomized controlled interventional trials to reduce problematic SMU

## Abstract

**Introduction:** Public health concerns over the impact of social media use (SMU) on adolescent health are growing. We investigated the relationship between SMU and sleep health in adolescents in Canada aged 11 to 17 years.

**Methods:** Data from the 2017–2018 Health Behaviour in School-aged Children study were available for 12 557 participants (55.2% female). SMU was categorized by frequency of use (non-active, active and intense) and the presence of addiction-like symptoms (problematic). Mixed effects logistic regression models identified associations between SMU and seven sleep health indicators (insomnia symptoms, daytime wakefulness problems, screen time before bed, meeting sleep durationrecommendations, sleep variability and late bedtime on school and non-school days).

**Results:** Compared to active SMU, non-active SMU was associated with better sleep indicators, except for insomnia symptoms. Intense SMU was associated with greater odds of having poor sleep health indicators (adjusted odds ratio [aORs] from 1.09 to 2.24) and problematic SMU with the highest odds (aORs from 1.67 to 3.24). Associations with problematic SMU were greater among girls than boys, including having a later bedtime on school days (aOR = 3.74 vs. 1.84) and on non-school days (aOR = 4.13 vs. 2.18). Associations between SMU and sleep outcomes did not differ by age group.

**Conclusion:** Intense and problematic SMU were associated with greater odds of poor sleep health among adolescents in Canada, with stronger associations among girls than boys. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms underlying associations between SMU and sleep to inform public health recommendations.

**Keywords:** adolescents, social media use, sleep, insomnia, daytime wakefulness, sleep duration, sleep variability

## Highlights

## Introduction

Social media use (SMU), defined as
the time spent on social media platforms (e.g. Facebook, Twitter, TikTok, etc.)
to connect with other users and exchange user-generated content, is an integral
part of adolescents’ lives around the world.[Footnote 1](#fn1)[Footnote 2](#fn2) In the United States, the percentage of adolescents reporting intense SMU
(i.e. being online almost constantly) increased from 25% to 45%.[Footnote 3](#fn3) One cross-national study estimated that 40% of adolescents aged 15 to 19 years
increased their SMU during the COVID-19 pandemic.[Footnote 4](#fn4)

In the current literature, a
distinction is made between intense and problematic SMU. Intense SMU is defined
as spending a lot of time on social media, whereas problematic SMU implicates
the presence of behavioural and psychological symptoms of addiction that affect
daily functions.[Footnote 2](#fn2)[Footnote 5](#fn5) While social media offers
opportunities to strengthen friendships, promote social support and reduce
social isolation, intense and problematic SMU may negatively impact youth
health and well-being, including sleep.[Footnote 2](#fn2)[Footnote 5](#fn5)[Footnote 6](#fn6)

Sleep is essential to the health
and development of adolescents and a contributor to their well-being through
its influence on learning capacities, emotional regulation and memory
processes.[Footnote 7](#fn7)Sleep health encompasses not just sleep
duration but also sleep quality, regularity, satisfaction, appropriate sleep
timing alertness during the day, and sleep-facilitating behaviours.[Footnote 8](#fn8)[Footnote 9](#fn9) These
components of sleep have been proposed in a sleep health framework called Peds
B-SATED (**B**ehaviour, **S**atisfaction/Quality, **A**lertness/Sleepiness, **T**iming, **E**fficiency and **D**uration).[Footnote 9](#fn9) In Canada, one in three children and adolescents do not meet sleep duration
recommendations,[Footnote 10](#fn10)[Footnote 11](#fn11) and at least 25% have symptoms of insomnia and daytime wakefulness problems[Footnote 10](#fn10)

Numerous studies have linked SMU with
poor sleep health in adolescents.[Footnote 12](#fn12)[Footnote 13](#fn13) SMU is hypothesized to impact sleep via four mechanisms: (1) exposure to
blue light, which affects circadian timing; (2) psychophysiological activation
due to the emotional content of social media; (3) the “never-ending” nature of
SMU; and (4) the constant alerts that disturb sleep.[Footnote 2](#fn2)[Footnote 6](#fn6)[Footnote 14](#fn14) Studies linking SMU to sleep have generally focused
on one aspect of sleep, most often sleep duration, but interest is growing in
understanding the association between SMU and other aspects of adolescent
sleep, such as sleep quality and sleep-facilitating behaviours.[Footnote 8](#fn8)[Footnote 9](#fn9)[Footnote 15](#fn15) Yet, according to a 2019 census on SMU in children and youth aged 8 to 18 years
in the United States, only 14% reported that their parent monitored their time
spent on social media.[Footnote 16](#fn16)

Associations between SMU and sleep may vary by gender
and age. A study of adolescents in the United States and the United Kingdom
found that the association between time spent on social media and lower
well-being was greater among girls than boys.[Footnote 17](#fn17)Another study also identified significant differences
in SMU by age group, with 11-year-olds reporting less intense SMU than 13- and
15-year-olds and significantly better mental health across most measures,[Footnote 2](#fn2) suggesting a need to look at age differences more closely. Studying gender and
age differences in the associations between SMU and different sleep health
indicators may offer a clearer picture of the factors in the relationship
between SMU and sleep.

The aim of the current study is to investigate the
association between SMU and sleep health indicators among adolescents in Canada
and to examine any gender and age differences. We examined SMU with a
previously developed scale[Footnote 2](#fn2) that combines intensity and problematic
symptoms. We hypothesized that intense and problematic SMU would be associated
with worse sleep health, compared to active SMU, and that associations would be
stronger in girls than boys and in older than younger adolescents.

## Methods

### Data and participants

Data were from the 2017–2018 Health
Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study, a cross-national research study
and World Health Organization collaboration, that collects data every 4 years
from a representative sample of students in Grades 6 to 10 in the school
setting. The Canadian part of the survey used a random two-stage cluster sample
of students from all provinces and two territories (Yukon and Northwest
Territories). Data were collected between January and May of 2018.
Participation was voluntary and anonymous. The Canadian HBSC study obtained
student assent and active and/or passive parental consent, depending on school
board requirements.

The General Research Ethics Board
at Queen’s University (GMISC-062-13) and the Health Canada–Public Health Agency
of Canada Research Ethics Board provided ethics approval.

A total of 21 745 students from 287 schools
participated in the survey. For this study, we excluded adolescents in Grade 5
(n = 40) and Grade 11 (n = 163) because the HBSC survey is
representative of students in Grades 6 to 10. We excluded adolescents who
responded to “neither term describes me” for gender (n = 325) because
of the small sample size, and those with information missing on SMU (n = 6226)
and on the variables in our analyses (n = 2434), resulting in a final
sample of 12 557 students with
complete data.

### Measures

#### Social media use

To assess SMU
intensity, the survey asked participants to identify how often they had online
contact with the following four categories of people: close friends; friends
from a larger friend group; friends they met through the Internet; and other
people (such as classmates, siblings or teachers). Response options were:
“never or almost never,” “at least every week,” “daily or almost daily,”
“several times each day” and “almost all the time throughout the day.” The
highest frequency reported across the four categories was used to establish
three levels of SMU intensity: (1) non-active (never or at most weekly); (2)
active (daily/several times a day); and (3) intense (almost all the time), as
previously described by Boniel-Nissim et al.[Footnote 2](#fn2)

We assessed problematic SMU using
the Social Media Disorder Scale.[Footnote 18](#fn18) The scale has previously demonstrated appropriate validity in a large
international sample of adolescents.[Footnote 19](#fn19) The scale includes nine “yes/no” items that identify addiction-like symptoms of
SMU during the past year (e.g. having conflict with family, lying about the
amount of time spent on social media, feeling bad when cannot use social media,
among others). Participants who responded yes to six or more items were
classified as problematic users, regardless of their SMU intensity level.[Footnote 2](#fn2)

Participants were classified into one of four mutually
exclusive categories: non-active SMU (non-active SMU and nonproblematic use);
active SMU (active SMU and nonproblematic use); intense SMU (intense SMU and
nonproblematic use); and problematic SMU (problematic use regardless of SMU
intensity).[Footnote 2](#fn2)

#### Sleep health

We investigated seven
indicators of sleep health, based on availability in the dataset: insomnia
symptoms, daytime wakefulness, screen time before bed, sleep duration, sleep
variability, and sleep timing on school days and on non-school days (weekends
and holidays). Many of these sleep health measures align with the Peds B-SATED
framework, with four of the six domains included.[Footnote 9](#fn9) We were unable to investigate sleep satisfaction/quality and efficiency
with the current data source.

#### Insomnia symptoms

Participants were asked how often
they have trouble going to sleep or staying asleep. There were five response
options: “never,” “rarely,” “sometimes,” “most of the time” and “all the time.”
The variable was dichotomized as those with insomnia symptoms (“most of the
time” and “all the time”) and those without (“never,” rarely” and “sometimes”),
in line with previous work.[Footnote 20](#fn20)

#### Problems with daytime wakefulness

Participants were asked how often
they have trouble staying awake during the daytime when they want to be awake.
There were five response options: “never,” “rarely,” “sometimes,” “most of the
time” and “all the time.” “Never” and “rarely” were grouped to create a
dichotomous variable defined as no daytime wakefulness problems.

#### Screen time before bed

To assess
sleep-facilitating behaviours, the survey asked participants how often they
watched television or used a cellphone or computer/tablet in their bedroom in
the last hour before going to sleep. There were five responses options: “never,”
“1 or 2 nights a week,” “3 or 4 nights a week,” “5 or 6 nights a week” and
“every night.” Participants who responded “never” or “1 or 2 nights a week” were
categorized as using screens before bed less than 2 nights a week, and all the
other participants were categorized as using screens before bed 3 or more
nights a week.

#### Sleep duration

To assess sleep duration, the survey
asked participants when they usually go to bed and when they usually wake up,
on school days and non-school days (weekends and holidays), separately.
Participants could answer within 15-minute increments. Sleep duration on school
days and non-school days was calculated and used to determine average daily
sleep duration, which was compared to sleep duration recommendations for
adolescents. Sleep duration recommendations differ depending on age group: 9 to
11 hours per night for 11- to 13-year-olds and 8 to 10 hours per night for 14-
to 17-year-olds.[Footnote 21](#fn21) Taking into account sleep duration
recommendations by age, we separated participants into two categories, meeting
the sleep duration recommendation or not meeting the sleep duration
recommendation.

#### Sleep variability

To assess sleep variability/regularity, we calculated for each
participant if there was more than a 2-hour difference between bedtime during
the week and weekend nights.[Footnote 22](#fn22) Participants with less than a 2-hour
difference between bedtime during the week and weekend nights were categorized
as having little or no sleep variability.

#### Sleep timing

As wake times can largely depend on
school start times, we used bedtimes as an indicator of sleep health. We
calculated bedtime tertiles on school and non-school days for each age category
(11–13 years and 14–17 years), given the shift towards a later bedtime during
adolescence due to biological changes in circadian rhythms. We then categorized
participants as having an early/moderate bedtime (first and second tertile) or
a late bedtime (third tertile) on school days in comparison with peers. For those
aged 11 to 13 years, late bedtimes on school and non-school days were after
10:30 p.m. and 12:00 a.m., respectively. For youth aged 14 to 17 years, late
bedtimes on school and non-school days were after 12:00 a.m. and 1:00 a.m.,
respectively.

### Sociodemographic variables

We included information on gender (boy/girl), cultural/ethnoracial
background (categorized as White vs. non-White) and family affluence. Family affluence was measured using the Family Affluence
Scale, a reliable and valid measure of socioeconomic status.[Footnote 23](#fn23) The FAS is a composite score based on household characteristics, including
the number of cars, bathrooms, computers, having an unshared bedroom and the
number of family holidays abroad during the past year. The responses were
summed and categorized into three groups (0–6: “low affluence”; 7–10: “medium
affluence”; and 11–13: “high affluence”).[Footnote 23](#fn23)

### Statistical analysis

We first conducted descriptive
analyses of the sample across the four SMU categories. To examine the
associations between the four SMU categories and sleep variables, we used mixed
effects logistic regression models, with separate models for each of the seven
sleep health outcomes. From the logistic regression models, we report both the
odds ratio and 95% confidence interval (CI). All models were adjusted for
gender, cultural/ethnoracial background, age and family affluence.

We then conducted additional
exploratory analyses to examine gender and age differences by rerunning the
models stratified by gender and age group. All models were controlled for
clustering by schools using mixed effects models, and survey weights were
applied to ensure results were representative of Grade 6 to 10 students in
Canada. An alpha value of 0.05 was used to detect statistically significant
results.

We conducted analyses in SAS Enterprise Guide version 7.1
(SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, US).

## Results

### Descriptive characteristics

The most common SMU category was active users (43.7%)
followed by intense users (35.4%), non-active users (14.2%) and problematic
users (6.7%). Problematic and intense users were generally more likely to be
girls and non-White compared with active users. Conversely, non-active users were
generally more likely to be boys and younger than the active SMU groups ([Table
1](#t1)).

### Association between SMU and sleep health indicators

Non-active SMU was associated with significantly lower odds
of problematic sleep health indicators compared with active SMU (aORs from 0.42
to 0.78), except for insomnia symptoms, where the association was not
significant. Intense SMU was associated with significantly worse sleep for all
sleep health indicators except insomnia symptoms (aORs from 1.14 to 2.24).
Finally, problematic SMU had the highest odds of having poor sleep health
indicators (aORs from 1.67 to 3.24). All of the aORs for problematic SMU and
insomnia symptoms, were consistently greater than the aORs for intense SMU,
although some not significantly ([Table 2](#t2)).

## Discussion

In this study, we examined
associations between SMU and seven sleep health indicators in a nationally
representative sample of adolescents in Canada. Our results show that both
problematic and intense SMU were associated with worse sleep health across a
range of indicators, compared to active SMU, while non-active SMU was
associated with better sleep health. The presence of insomnia symptoms was the
only indicator not associated with SMU. Associations were stronger for girls
than for boys, but did not differ by age group. The associations for
problematic SMU were generally stronger than for intense SMU with all the sleep
health indicators.

Compared to previous research
exploring the relationship between SMU and sleep,[Footnote 12](#fn12)[Footnote 24](#fn24)[Footnote 25](#fn25)[Footnote 26](#fn26) our study offers a comprehensive examination
of the relationship between SMU and different indicators of sleep health. Few
studies have made a distinction between intense and problematic SMU and their
associations with sleep. Our results point to both the intensity and
problematic nature of SMU affecting many aspects of healthy sleep. A few
explanations for these associations have been proposed. First, electronic
devices (e.g. cellphones, tablets, computer screens) emit blue light, which
affects the production of melatonin, a hormone that regulates circadian rhythms
and sleep.[Footnote 6](#fn6)[Footnote 7](#fn7) Second, social media activities can lead to psychophysiological arousal, in
part because of the emotional content of social media, which can lead to
difficulties falling asleep.[Footnote 14](#fn14)[Footnote 27](#fn27) Third, the “never-ending” nature of social media can make it difficult to stop
use at night, particularly for adolescents, who are still developing their
capacity to self-regulate.[Footnote 14](#fn14)[Footnote 24](#fn24) Fourth, the constant alerts may disrupt the sleep of the large number of
adolescents who keep their phones in their bedrooms at night.[Footnote 14](#fn14)[Footnote 24](#fn24) Research has found that 15%
of those in France report disturbance of sleep because of text messages
alerts.[Footnote 28](#fn28) Further, “fear of missing out,” a general state of anxiety
at missing out on experiences, may prevent young people from turning off their
phones at night and disengaging from social media at bedtime.[Footnote 15](#fn15) This fear may contribute to
psychophysiological activation before bedtime and to delayed bedtimes.[Footnote 15](#fn15)

Previous findings on the link
between SMU and various health outcomes (e.g. mental health, physical activity)
suggest a curvilinear relationship where both non-active and problematic use are
associated with health risks relative to active use; this is referred to as the
Goldilocks hypothesis.[Footnote 29](#fn29) However, we found that non-active use was associated with better sleep
indicators than active use, suggesting a monotonic relationship between SMU and
poor sleep health. Notably, intense users had worse sleep health outcomes than
non-active and active users, even if their use was not problematic.

We found a stronger association
between problematic SMU and sleep indicators among girls than boys. Previous
work has shown that, even when using screens for less than 2 hours per day,
girls were more likely to experience insufficient sleep than boys.[Footnote 30](#fn30) However, to our knowledge, no study has examined gender differences in
intense and problematic SMU and sleep. There is evidence that girls and boys
use social media differently and that girls may be more susceptible to the
negative impacts of SMU.[Footnote 14](#fn14) For example, girls are more likely to engage in social comparison and seek
feedback on social media, which may influence their body image concerns and
possibly explains why their sleep is affected to a greater extent.[Footnote 17](#fn17)[Footnote 31](#fn31) They may also be more susceptible to the psychophysiological arousal effects
of social media; they report greater emotional investment and increased stress
linked to SMU.[Footnote 26](#fn26) A longitudinal study of
adolescents in the Netherlands found that social media stress was associated
with greater daytime sleepiness among girls but not boys.[Footnote 26](#fn26) Finally, research also suggests a difference between active (e.g. posting or
commenting) and passive (e.g. viewing posts, scrolling) SMU. Passive SMU is
associated with lower well-being, with a stronger effect in girls,[Footnote 32](#fn32) that might translate
into girls spending more time on social media at night and more sleep
difficulties.

Overall, we did not find statistically significant
differences between 11- to 13-year-olds and 14- to 17-year-olds in associations
between SMU and sleep indicators. To the best of our knowledge, our study is
among the first to examine age differences in the association between SMU
categories and sleep health indicators. Sleep health tends to change with age,
with older adolescents sleeping less and going to bed later, partly due to
biological changes.[Footnote 7](#fn7)[Footnote 11](#fn11) Time spent on social media also increases as adolescents age, which could
explain why the associations between SMU categories and sleep health remain
similar with age.

### Strengths and limitations

There are several strengths to
this study. First, it uses nationally representative data, with data collection
following a standardized protocol. The study also included a distinction
between intense and problematic SMU, using a validated scale for problematic
SMU, and examined seven sleep health indicators that offer a broad picture of
sleep health.

Some limitations need to be acknowledged. The use of
cross-sectional data does not allow for causal inferences. There may have been
unmeasured confounding that we were not able to adjust for in our analysis. In
addition, the data were self-reported. Some studies suggest that self-reported
sleep duration correlates moderately with actigraphy-measured sleep but that
self-reports often overestimate sleep duration, which may have introduced some measurement
error.[Footnote 33](#fn33) Only 58% of the Canadian HBSC sample had complete data and were
included in our analyses. When comparing the characteristics of our included sample
against the excluded samples, we found significant differences in gender, age
group, culture/ethnoracial background, SMU and screen time before bed, which
may indicate a risk of sampling bias in our study impacting the generalizability
of our results (data available from the authors on request). Many of the
measures used in this study have not been validated, representing an important
area of future research. Our measure of SMU does not specify if the use was
active (e.g. communicating with friends and creating content) or passive (e.g.
scrolling through feeds), and our study could not distinguish between SMU and
exposure to screens in general. We also did not have information on the type of
device (i.e. phone, tablet, computer) that may play a moderating role in the
associations with sleep health. To more precisely understand how SMU affects
sleep, further studies should distinguish between active and passive SMU and
account for other types of screen use.

## Conclusion

In our study, intense and
problematic SMU were associated with worse sleep health compared to active SMU,
whereas non-active SMU was linked to better sleep health. These associations were
stronger among girls than boys.

Further research is needed to understand the underlying
mechanisms between SMU and sleep and to investigate potentially important
gender differences. To guide public health recommendations, further studies
could collect data on specific social media activities and use objective
measures of sleep and SMU (such as time spent on social media apps). During the
COVID-19 pandemic, adolescents increased their time spent on social media.[Footnote 4](#fn4) Considering our findings, it will be important to examine how changes in
youth SMU due to the pandemic have impacted sleep health in adolescents.

args.summary:
This is a peer-reviewed original quantitative research article published in Health Promotion and Chronic Disease Prevention in Canada (HPCDP Journal) examining the relationship between social media use (SMU) and sleep health among Canadian adolescents aged 11-17 years.

**Data and Methods:** Data came from the 2017-2018 Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study, comprising 12,557 participants (55.2% female). SMU was categorized into four mutually exclusive groups: non-active (14.2%), active (43.7%), intense (35.4%), and problematic (6.7%). Sleep health was assessed across seven indicators: insomnia symptoms, daytime wakefulness problems, screen time before bed, meeting sleep duration recommendations, sleep variability, and late bedtime on school and non-school days. Mixed effects logistic regression models were used, adjusting for gender, age, cultural/ethnoracial background, and family affluence.

**Key Findings:**
- Non-active SMU was associated with better sleep indicators compared to active SMU (aORs from 0.42 to 0.78), except for insomnia symptoms.
- Intense SMU was associated with worse sleep across all indicators except insomnia symptoms (aORs from 1.14 to 2.24).
- Problematic SMU had the strongest associations with poor sleep health (aORs from 1.67 to 3.24).
- Associations were stronger for girls than boys. For example, problematic SMU among girls vs. boys was associated with late bedtime on school days (aOR=3.74 vs. 1.84) and non-school days (aOR=4.13 vs. 2.18).
- No significant differences were found between age groups (11-13 vs. 14-17 years).

**Conclusion:** Intense and problematic SMU were associated with greater odds of poor sleep health among Canadian adolescents, with stronger associations among girls. The authors note that the cross-sectional design prevents causal inferences, and further research is needed to understand underlying mechanisms and inform public health recommendations.

--- SOURCE 1: The EU Commission’s Approach to Age Verification: Mobile Apps, DSA Enforcement, and Challenging National Social Media Bans ---
URL: https://fpf.org/blog/the-eu-commissions-approach-to-age-verification-mobile-apps-dsa-enforcement-and-challenging-national-social-media-bans

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On April 29, 2026, the European Commission published a non-binding Recommendation for a common EU-wide approach to age verification technologies, aiming to harmonize measures for protecting children online. Key takeaways include:

- The Commission is accelerating age verification roll-out, urging Member States to implement solutions by December 31, 2026, partly in response to growing tensions over potential social media bans in countries like France (under 15), Spain (under 16), and Germany (under 14/17).
- Under the Digital Services Act (DSA), it remains unclear whether age verification will be mandatory or voluntary, though DSA enforcement actions (e.g., preliminary findings against Meta for minors under 13 accessing Instagram/Facebook, and an investigation into Snapchat) show existing age assurance methods are being deemed inadequate.
- The Commission will develop an EU age verification "blueprint" — a technical specification including a customizable mobile app — and an age verification "scheme" establishing requirements for "proof of age attestations" from EU-based trusted providers.
- While the Recommendation emphasizes "privacy-preserving" age verification (limiting shared info to true/false age responses, using zero-knowledge proofs), it notably lacks reference to the GDPR, and specific technical safeguards remain undefined. This gap follows security flaws found in the EU's early April "age checking app."
- The Recommendation invokes Directive 2015/1535 to make it procedurally challenging for individual Member States to implement social media bans. Member States must notify the Commission of any proposed technical restrictions before adoption, triggering a 3-month standstill period. Failure to do so renders the measure unenforceable against individuals, citing CJEU cases C-194/94 and C-443/98.
- The Commission's approach is compared globally to New York's SAFE for Kids Act rulemaking, Australia's Age Assurance Technology Trial, and social media restrictions in Brazil, Indonesia, and pending U.S. legislation.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: Mind the Gap ---
URL: https://www.interface-eu.org/publications/age-assurance-gap

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This policy brief, published October 13, 2025, by Interface EU and authored by Jessica Galissaire, examines the gap between EU laws protecting minors online and their actual enforcement, focusing on age assurance mechanisms.

**Key Findings:**

The paper's central argument is that the key problem today is not a lack of legislation or awareness but a failure of implementation and enforcement. Despite a dense EU legal framework (GDPR, AVMSD, DSA, AI Act, BIK+ Strategy), minors remain insufficiently protected online.

**Empirical Testing Results:**
The research tested eight popular platforms among EU minors—Discord, Fortnite, Instagram, Roblox, Snapchat, TikTok, Twitch, and YouTube. Results show all rely on self-declaration for age checks at account creation. None have implemented robust age assurance, and existing parental consent tools (on YouTube and Fortnite) can be easily bypassed or applied only after account creation.

**Three interrelated issues identified:**
1. Ineffectiveness of self-declaration as an age assurance method
2. Systematic absence of compliance (e.g., platforms using 'performance of a contract' as legal basis for processing minors' data without checking legal capacity)
3. Overall failure of enforcement by competent authorities

**EU Political Context:**
In June 2025, French President Macron announced intentions to ban social media for under-15s. 21 ministers from 13 Member States signed an op-ed calling for mandatory EU-wide age verification. The European Commission released DSA Article 28 guidelines emphasizing age assurance. Member States including France, Denmark, and Greece are pushing for EU-wide mandatory age checks or social media bans.

**Case Studies:**
- **France:** Loi SREN mandates age verification for pornographic websites, enforced by Arcom. However, jurisdictional issues persist with EU-based platforms. France's digital majority law (under-15s requiring parental consent) has never been enforced due to EU notification procedure issues.
- **Germany:** The JMStV (Youth Media Protection Interstate Treaty) has been in effect since 2003, using a 'regulated self-regulation' model with 120 certified age-assurance mechanisms. Enforcement remains difficult for foreign-based platforms.

**Key Contributions:**
1. Maps the regulatory framework highlighting overlaps and contradictions
2. Documents the implementation gap through empirical testing
3. Offers actionable recommendations focused on enforcement rather than new legislation

**Central Message:** More legislation is not the solution. The EU and Member States should focus on making existing rules work by ensuring minors' rights are protected in practice, not just recognized in law.
</summary>

None have implemented robust age assurance, and where parental consent tools do exist, they can either be easily bypassed or they are applied only after the account has already been created.", "The central message is that, in the short run, more legislation is not the solution. Instead, the EU and Member States should focus on making the existing rules work by ensuring that minors' rights are not just recognised in law but protected in practice.", "Above all, mandatory age verification mechanisms must be implemented across all social networks.", "In practice, minors can thus access these services freely, while platforms remain noncompliant with provisions that legally oblige them to treat minors differently than other users."

--- SOURCE 4: Key developments in online age verification laws | Arthur Cox LLP ---
URL: https://www.arthurcox.com/knowledge/key-developments-in-online-age-verification-laws

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a legal briefing from Arthur Cox, dated December 12, 2024, titled "Key developments in online age verification laws." It outlines the evolving legislative landscape for online age verification at both Irish and EU levels, moving from minimal obligations to stricter requirements for certain entities.

**Current Legal Framework:**

- **GDPR (Article 8):** Requires "reasonable efforts" to verify a child's age for data consent, with a proportionate, risk-based approach. Self-declaration may suffice for low-risk activities, but excessive data collection should be avoided.
- **Digital Services Act (DSA):** Requires Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and Very Large Online Search Engines (VLOSEs) to implement age verification as a mitigation measure. However, Article 28(3) clarifies that smaller platforms are not obliged to process personal data to assess if a user is a minor. The European Commission is expected to issue guidelines in 2025 that may broaden these obligations.
- **Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD):** Requires Member States to ensure video-sharing platform services (VSPSs) have age verification systems, with appropriate measures *shall* include age verification for content that may impair minors.
- **Online Safety and Media Regulation Act 2022 (OSMRA):** Empowers Coimisiún na Meán to make binding codes. On 21 October 2024, Coimisiún na Meán published an Online Safety Code for VSPSs, and on 5 December 2024, a Media Service Code and Rules for Audiovisual On-demand Media Service Providers.

**Key Implications of Coimisiún na Meán's Codes:**

- Age verification is mandated for VSPSs in two broad circumstances: (1) content that may impair minors' physical, mental, or moral development, and (2) adult-only content (pornography or gratuitous violence).
- Self-declaration of age is no longer considered an effective age verification measure for these purposes.
- The Code does not define what constitutes "content that may impair... development," leading to potentially broad interpretations.
- While the Code is Irish, it is likely to have EU-wide impact as the ten designated VSPSs operate across Europe.
- The Media Service Code extends "age assurance" obligations to audiovisual on-demand media service providers.

**Key Takeaways:**

- Entities should assess what online age verification obligations apply to them and adopt proportionate, risk-based mechanisms.
- Self-declaration is no longer sufficient for VSPSs and audiovisual on-demand providers in the specified circumstances.
- Entities should monitor future developments, as obligations may extend to non-VLOPs.
- The law is still developing, with regulators balancing child protection against privacy and fundamental rights.
</summary>

<summary>
The Online Safety Act 2023 (OSA) is an Act of the UK Parliament that received royal assent on 26 October 2023, regulating online content. It imposes a duty of care on online platforms to take action against illegal content and content harmful to children, with fines up to £18 million or 10% of annual turnover. The Act empowers Ofcom to block access to websites and requires platforms—including end-to-end encrypted messaging services—to scan for child pornography and terrorism content, though enforcement of this provision is deferred until "technically feasible." It also requires age verification for pornographic content and creates new criminal offences including cyberflashing, sharing intimate images, encouraging self-harm, sending flashing images to people with epilepsy ("Zach's law"), and false communications.

The Act has drawn significant criticism from academics, human rights organisations, journalists, and tech firms who argue it threatens privacy and freedom of speech. Major tech companies (Apple, Meta/Signal threatened withdrawal over encryption provisions). Wikipedia launched a judicial review against potential designation as "category 1" service. The U.S. State Department's 2024 Human Rights report criticised the Act as a hazard to press freedom. Supporters including the NSPCC and Samaritans endorsed it for child protection.

Subsequent enforcement actions include fines against 4chan (£20,000 + £100/day, later £520,000), Itai Tech (£50,000), and AVS Group (£1 million). A petition to repeal the Act attracted over 500,000 signatures. The Act has been amended by several subsequent laws including the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026. Some websites have closed or blocked UK users in response. The Act was amended by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 Part 3.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the official legislation.gov.uk page for the **Online Safety Act 2023** (2023 c. 50), a UK Public General Act passed on 26 October 2023. The Act establishes a new regulatory framework for internet services, overseen by OFCOM, with the general purpose of making internet use safer for individuals in the UK.

**Key Provisions:**
- **Part 1 (Introduction):** Sets out the regulatory framework requiring providers to identify, mitigate, and manage risks of harm from illegal content and activity, and content harmful to children. # Online Age Verification Laws by Country (Wikipedia Article)

This Wikipedia article provides a comprehensive overview of online age verification laws across the globe, primarily from 2023 onward. It covers the background, laws in effect, and criticisms of these regulations.

## Key Overview

Since 2023, many countries have passed or proposed laws requiring age verification for social media and digital services to protect young people from harmful content. Methods include government-issued IDs, facial scans, or credit cards. Laws vary from restricting certain features (e.g., US Kids Online Safety Act) to outright bans on users under a certain age (e.g., Australia's ban on under-16s).

## Criticism

These laws have faced backlash from civil rights organizations (EFF, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, UNICEF) for:
- Normalizing mass surveillance
- Restricting freedom of speech through elimination of anonymous accounts
- Privacy violations
- Potential to backfire
- Being bypassable by VPNs

## Countries with Laws in Effect

- **Australia**: First country to ban social media for under-16s (effective December 2025). Platforms include YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Twitch, Reddit, etc. Fines up to 50 million AUD (increased to 99 million AUD in June 2026). Over 310,000 accounts deactivated by March 2026.

- **Brazil**: Passed law September 2025, effective March 2026. Bans social media for under-16s without parental consent. Also bans lootboxes, digital rewards, and in-app purchases for under-18s. Fines up to 50 million BRL.

- **China**: Existing strict internet censorship with Great Firewall. "Minor Mode" (Youth Anti-Addiction System) since January 2024 cuts internet access for under-18s between 22:00-06:00, with daily time limits based on age.

- **Indonesia**: Banned social media for under-16s on March 28, 2026. First non-Western, Asian, and Muslim country to do so. By July 2026, 4.7 million accounts terminated.

- **Malaysia**: Banned social media for under-16s effective June 1, 2026, for platforms with over 8 million users.

- **Singapore**: Since April 1, 2026, app stores must prevent under-18s from downloading age-inappropriate apps using ID or facial scans.

- **United Kingdom**: Online Safety Act 2023 enforced since July 25, 2025. First country to enforce age verification for harmful content. Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026 will ban under-16s from social media by spring 2027, with a proposed curfew for 16-17 year-olds (00:00-06:00).

- **United States (state level)**: No federal law enacted. Florida (effective November 2025, bans under-14), Mississippi (effective July 2025, parental consent for under-18), Tennessee (effective January 2025, parental consent for under-18), and Ohio (effective June 2026, parental consent for under-16) have laws in effect.

## Effects on Platforms

- **Discord**: Blurs sensitive content; requires age verification for UK/Australia/Brazil users; expanded to DMs in late 2025; announced teen safety protections worldwide (delayed to late 2026).
- **Google**: Blocks searches for harmful material without age verification in UK and France; Play Age Signals API deployed in Brazil and Texas.
- **X (Twitter)**: Locks certain content behind age verification in EU since July 2025.
- **Reddit**: Blocks underage European users from NSFW content (July 2026).

## Countries with Proposed/Rejected Laws

Numerous countries across all continents (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, Oceania) have proposed or are considering similar legislation. Some countries like France, Italy, Estonia, Croatia, Hong Kong, and New Zealand have rejected online age verification laws.
</summary>

## EU Kids Online Study: Tech & Teens

This webpage summarizes a comprehensive research project conducted by the Interdisciplinary Research Team on Internet and Society (IRTIS) in the Czech Republic over six years, involving 15 rigorous studies using advanced methods (longitudinal studies, experiments, and real-time assessments). The research investigated how digital technologies (smartphones, social media, online games) impact adolescents' psychological, social, and physical well-being.

### Key Findings:

- **Not all adolescents are the same:** Impacts vary significantly by gender, age, individual traits, and frequency/type of media use, making generalizations difficult.
- **Well-being is multi-dimensional:** Technology use can be positive in one area of well-being and negative in another simultaneously.
- **Psychological well-being:** Increased smartphone use and consistent daily usage can raise stress levels. More time on social networking apps slightly decreases positive affect and increases negative affect (though minimal). No causal effect was found for entertainment apps (videos, games).
- **Social well-being:** No negative or positive causal impacts were found regarding social skills, social support, or sexting from smartphone/social media use.
- **Gender differences:** Reading comments praising idealized beauty standards causally impacts body dissatisfaction, but only among adolescent girls.
- **What adolescents do matters:** The specific type of activity (e.g., social media vs. entertainment apps) determines the impact.
- **Short-term vs. long-term effects:** Short-term impacts on affect may not correlate with long-term life satisfaction.
- **No simple answers:** Simplistic conclusions should be avoided.

The study (2025) is authored by Smahel, D., Šaradín Lebedíková, M., Lacko, D., Kvardová, N., Mýlek, V., Tkaczyk, M., Svestkova, A., Gulec, H., Hrdina, M., Machackova, H., & Dedkova, L., and published by EU Kids Online, Leonie Lemke, Stiftung Digitale Chancen. - No evidence that bans work to improve children's lives; many researchers and children's organizations oppose them.

Key findings: (1) Links between social media use and life satisfaction are bidirectional and small at best; (2) lower life satisfaction led to increased social media use, and vice versa, but these effects were trivial in size; (3) bidirectional effects were more consistent for females than males, though still modest; (4) more than half of the statistical models tested were not significant. The researchers—Professor Andrew Przybylski, Amy Orben, and Dr. Tobias Dienlin—emphasized that previous literature relied on correlations without disentangling causality. This submission from Professors Przybylski, Weinstein, and Orben (Oxford and Cardiff Universities) to the UK Parliament addresses the evidence gap regarding social media and screen-use effects on young people's mental health. The authors argue that the evidence base is weak, mixed, and generally low in empirical quality, with most studies showing small or null effects when proper controls are used. They cite a study of 120,000+ British adolescents showing a non-linear relationship between digital screen time and well-being. --- SOURCE 38: Windows of developmental sensitivity to social media | Nature Communications ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study published in Nature Communications (2022) investigates how the relationship between social media use and life satisfaction changes across development. The researchers analyzed two UK datasets: a cross-sectional sample of 72,287 participants aged 10–80 from the Understanding Society household panel, and a longitudinal sample of 17,409 participants aged 10–21.

Key findings include:

1. **Cross-sectional results**: The negative relationship between social media use and life satisfaction was most pronounced in younger adolescents. Significant sex differences emerged only during adolescence (ages 12–15), with females who reported very high social media use scoring substantially lower on life satisfaction than males.

2. **Longitudinal results (RI-CLPM models)**: The study found distinct developmental windows of sensitivity to social media:
   - For females: Ages 11–13, when higher social media use predicted decreased life satisfaction one year later.
   - For males: Ages 14–15, when higher social media use predicted decreased life satisfaction one year later.
   - For both sexes: Age 19, suggesting a later window of sensitivity possibly related to social environment changes.

3. **Bidirectional relationship**: Lower life satisfaction also predicted increased social media use one year later, but this effect was consistent across age and sex.

The study suggests that puberty may underlie the earlier window for females, while the age 19 window for both sexes may relate to social transitions like leaving home. The authors note that effect sizes were small but meaningful, and that individual differences likely matter. Limitations include reliance on self-reported social media use, the one-year time interval between observations, and the observational nature of the data preventing causal conclusions.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A May 4, 2021 Oxford University study published in Clinical Psychological Science examined data from over 430,000 adolescents in the UK and US to investigate how associations between technology use and mental health have changed over 30 years. Researchers analyzed links between social media use and depression, emotional problems, and conduct problems, as well as television viewing and digital device use with suicidality. The study found little evidence for increases in these associations over time. Of eight associations studied, only three showed small changes: social media and TV became less associated with depression, while social media's association with emotional problems increased slightly. Lead author Dr Matti Vuorre noted the importance of examining historic data, while senior author Professor Andrew Przybylski cautioned that it is too soon to draw firm conclusions or base policy on these findings, urging access to industry data for neutral investigation.
